title: Firm Capabilities under Stress: Business Environment Pressures and Establishment Scale in Bolivia
affiliations: Universidad Católica Boliviana San Pablo

detail.title: Firm Capabilities under Stress: Business Environment Pressures and Establishment Scale in Bolivia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The study was developed independently of any organization.
declarations.funderStatement: The study was not funded by any organization, only by me, in free use of my time.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how business environment pressures, firm capabilities, and establishment scale are related among formal enterprises operating under economic stress. Using the 2025 Bolivia Enterprise Survey, it estimates a survey-weighted path analytic structural equation model linking infrastructure stress, intensity of regulatory and tax interaction with the state, informal competition, and political instability to formal finance, adaptive, technology and standards, and digital transactional capabilities, and subsequently to sales and employment. The preferred model uses 567 establishments. Digital transactional capability, measured by electronic receipt of sales, is positively associated with both sales and employment and remains robust across alternative digital measures, the small-firm subpopulation, corruption controls, and trade extensions. Informal competition is negatively associated with digital transactions and has negative total associations with both outcomes. Formal finance and adaptation are particularly related to employment, while technology and standards are more closely related to sales. Greater interaction with the state is positively associated with formal capabilities and establishment scale, a relationship that remains distinct from corruption. International market integration adds explanatory content for sales without eliminating the digital transaction result. By contrast, the capability structure does not explain recent sales or employment growth. The findings support a framework for capabilities under stress in which heterogeneous external pressures are associated with distinct capability profiles rather than a uniform deterioration in firm performance. Because the data are cross-sectional, the estimated paths are interpreted as conditional associations rather than causal effects.

title: Employee Social Bridging: A Multilevel Theory of Employee Relationships, Workforce Capabilities and Organizational Outcomes
affiliations: Innovation Management Research Institute (IMRI)

detail.title: Employee Social Bridging: A Multilevel Theory of Employee Relationships, Workforce Capabilities and Organizational Outcomes

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: KEYSS AI provided some funding to initiate the research.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary indicators describe a corporate workplace in crisis: global employee engagement has fallen to 20 percent, mental-health-related productivity losses are measured in billions of working days, and loneliness has been declared a public-health epidemic. The condition keeps deteriorating while industry and academia pour research into it, and that is the puzzle this paper explains. It is a theory-building paper whose method is systems thinking and systems modeling. It models the enterprise as one system and the employee as the element within it whose corporate life is the object of study, and it integrates established scholarship into ten operational models (five frameworks, three models and two systems of systems) that together yield a single causal account of the employee's state of mind, where prior research has measured its conditions separately and reported their correlations.

The diagnosis is structural. After the Second World War the enterprise became a social system; in 1970 its governance passed to shareholder capitalism, a doctrine that corresponds to no conception of the enterprise at all and governs it by a single metric, total shareholder return, which hardened into the Employee Performance Extraction Industrial Complex: the apparatus that harnesses every employee need to extract discretionary performance, except the one need that cannot be harnessed, the need to bond. Its deprivation drives the Employee Psychological Erosion Cascade, seven stages from pressure to voluntary turnover, driven by three reinforcing loops and lacking any balancing loop.

The solution supplies the missing balance at the stage where the need lives. The mechanism is Directed Propinquity: propinquity applied deliberately across departments, functions, levels, locations and tenure. The act it produces is Employee Social Bridging: employees form Work Contacts (ties) and, through repeated encounters, Work Friends (bonds). Accumulated across the enterprise, ties and bonds form the Employee Social Bridging Fabric, the Core Competence of the Corporation. From the Employee Social Bridging Fabric the Workforce Social Bridging Maturity Cascade derives three Core Capabilities of the Workforce, and from those capabilities four enterprise outcomes, along three causal chains: Workforce Resilience to Employee Performance and Retention; Workforce Learning to Organic Innovation; and Workforce Agility to Organizational Adaptability. 

These outcomes drive total shareholder return by an indirect, long-horizon route. Employee Social Bridging therefore does two things: as the balancing intervention it defuses the pressure that shareholder capitalism places on the employee for ever-rising total shareholder return, the pressure that starts the Employee Psychological Erosion Cascade; and as an institutionalized, enterprise-wide intervention, sustained over the years in which the Employee Social Bridging Fabric matures, it creates the conditions under which total shareholder return rises.

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: Market microstructure studies how trading rules turn orders into prices and allocations. Those rules have been rebuilt repeatedly: for floor traders, electronic limit order books and highfrequency trading, batch auctions and dark pools, blockchains run by automated market makers and block builders, and now AI agents that discover, pay for, and compete over resources. This survey traces that evolution through one question: can a market allocate scarce goods efficiently and fairly without participants revealing everything they know and want? Each technological shift moved the binding constraint of market design from trader rationality to speed, to control over transaction ordering, to the dimensionality of what participants can report. Impossibility results persist; only their cost moves. We review evidence on high-frequency trading, trading venues, automated market makers, extractable value and algorithmic collusion, and identify allocation as the missing layer of the agent-commerce protocol stack.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how industrial policy affects equity valuations through expectation channels. We develop a structural framework in which announcements under government policy shift posterior beliefs about long-run US technological leadership in semiconductors. Firms differ in exposure to policy benefits, generating a cross-sectional gradient in stock-price responses to belief shocks. Directly eligible semiconductor firms exhibit the strongest valuation gains due to anticipated profitability improvements and reductions in effective capital costs. Complementary sectors benefit with attenuated effects, while input-competing firms may experience weaker or negative reactions, reflecting resource reallocation in domestic factor markets. The mechanism operates through forward-looking expectations rather than contemporaneous cash-flow changes. The findings provide evidence that industrial policy reshapes firm valuations by altering beliefs about future technological leadership and competitive advantage.

detail.abstract: Whether women exert control over household resources when given the choice, and when they do not, is central to understanding gender inequality in developing countries. We study this through an original lab-in-the-field experiment with 422 married couples in western Kenya, randomly giving wives the agency to decide who divides a household endowment before a voluntary contributions game played over five repeated rounds. Most women retain the decision, but about a third defer to their husbands at least once. Deferral shifts resources against women: a wife's endowment share falls by about 9.6 percentage points and her earnings share by 4.5 to 6 percentage points. Women who sometimes defer reported higher preexperiment exposure to intimate partner violence, suggesting that deferral reflects a fear of backlash. These findings highlight the value of repeated measurement for identifying the women who occasionally cede agency, and its potential reasons.

detail.abstract: Premier League financial enforcement depends on the information clubs provide and on the rules governing what happens after the League receives it. This article examines the relationship between disclosure and procedural time through the published 2020 CAS award in Manchester City FC v. UEFA and the Premier League's 2024/25 Handbook. It argues for a knowledge-based limitation period coupled with a charging window and a reasoned timetable for adjudication. The proposal develops an existing suggestion in the sports-law literature by addressing the interval between discovery, inquiry and determination. The CAS award supplies the interpretative problem; the Handbook supplies the contractual setting. Chelsea's published financial sanction agreement illustrates the acknowledged value of self-reporting. How clubs would respond to a different limitation rule remains an empirical question. Table 1 translates the proposal into model rules. Their operation is tested through a constructed example and objections concerning knowledge, procedural fairness and historical evidence. The argument concerns regulatory design and makes no assessment of the merits or outcome of Manchester City's separate Premier League proceedings.

detail.abstract: This article examines the systemic consequences of the United States-Iran war for global energy security. It argues that the conflict is not only a regional military confrontation but also a geoeconomic struggle in which sanctions, blockades, energy infrastructure, maritime insurance, and strategic straits operate as instruments of coercion. US economic strangulation and Iranian asymmetric countermeasures have sharply constrained navigation through the Strait of Hormuz. Simultaneously, Houthi advances along Yemen's western coast and near Bab el-Mandeb have increased the vulnerability of the route used by Saudi Arabia to redirect oil exports toward the Red Sea. The article conceptualises this configuration as a dual maritime chokepoint: pressure at both ends of the Arabian Peninsula reduces route substitutability and transforms a regional confrontation into systemic energy risk. Using a qualitative embedded case study, process tracing, and triangulation of institutional, maritime, economic, academic, and carefully classified expert sources, the analysis identifies four transmission mechanisms: physical supply contraction; maritime and geopolitical risk repricing; forced logistical reconfiguration; and the inflationary internationalisation of the shock. The Middle Eastern crisis also overlaps with the fragmentation of the Eurasian energy order caused by the war in Ukraine. The contraction of Russia-EU energy trade strengthened the strategic role of liquefied natural gas and, consequently, Europe's exposure to maritime supply chains. The article's principal theoretical contribution is the concept of recursive coercive externalities: coercion directed at an adversary embedded in critical global networks imposes costs on the target 2 while recirculating part of those costs to the initiating state, its allies, and third countries. The article concludes that a durable settlement requires reciprocal de-escalation, maritime guarantees, economic sequencing, an autonomous Yemeni peace process, and structural energy resilience.

detail.abstract: This paper provides the first systematic analysis of how high-profile police killings affect state policing legislation and public attitudes toward the police. Using a difference-indifferences design and a novel dataset on state-level policing laws, I find that these incidents generate large legislative responses, concentrated in states with Democratic-controlled legislatures and among incidents drawing greater media and protest attention. They also polarize public opinion: support for police falls among Independents and rises among Republicans. Evidence from California shows public opinion shapes legislative response, as Democratic (Republican) legislators introduce more bills when constituent support for police declines (increases) following an incident.

detail.abstract: This article examines the legal influence of ethnic legal traditions on the development of Hungarian law during the reign of King Stephen I. The extent of this influence is explored through an analysis of the social and political context, enabling a logical tracing of the cultural impact on Stephen I’s legislation. Particular attention is paid to the Nitra Slavs; the author concurs with Jan Steinhubbel’s view regarding the greater continuity of traditions that occurred under the Hungarian monarchy. To ensure a comprehensive understanding, the author analyses the influence and determines the role of Magyar legal traditions and the conditions under which they could spread and take root, drawing attention to the possibility of gradual assimilation and blending of legal traditions. The role of Roman law, which spread with Stephen I’s adoption of Christianity, is examined. The Frankish influence is mentioned separately. The author concludes that Stephen I’s legislation was an integral element of his open policy. The research demonstrates that both the king and the highest Hungarian nobility effectively and justifiably integrated Slavic administrative traditions and Western European legal standards into the framework of evolving Hungarian law.

detail.abstract: Frontier artificial intelligence governance increasingly relies on capability evaluations, catastrophic-risk thresholds, model-weight security, deployment safeguards, incident reporting, and commitments to pause development or deployment where risks cannot be adequately mitigated. These measures are necessary but insufficient because predeployment evidence is generated under bounded conditions, while frontier models may gain capabilities through scaling, post-training, scaffolding, tool access, model updates, or changed deployment contexts. This article introduces FORECAST-AI, a human-governed, cloud-capable conceptual research framework for Prediction-to-Outcome Accountability in frontier AI risk governance. Methodologically, the article uses interdisciplinary literature synthesis, comparative policy analysis, theory integration, systems design, and design-oriented normative reasoning to translate recurrent governance obligations into testable constructs, non-additive risk domains, response pathways, and a staged validation architecture. FORECAST-AI is grounded in sociotechnical systems theory, system-theoretic safety and feedback, high-reliability organising, responsive regulation, procedural justice, and principal-agent accountability. It integrates a Frontier Capability Forecast Register, Severe-Risk Prediction Ledger, Safeguard-to-Outcome Traceability Matrix, Frontier AI Outcome Observatory, Prediction-Outcome Discrepancy Engine, Counterfactual Safety Remedy Generator, and Institutional Proof Ledger. Its FORECAST-P cycle specifies Forecast, Observe, Reconcile, Evaluate, Correct, Authorise or Suspend, Share, and Trace. The framework is non-additive: cyber, biological or chemical enablement, autonomy, model security, manipulation, critical infrastructure, human control, and large-scale impact remain separate so favourable average performance cannot cancel catastrophic failure in one domain. FORECAST-AI responds to the EU AI Act and General-Purpose AI Code of Practice, G7 Hiroshima AI Process, Frontier AI Safety Commitments, OECD AI Principles and Due Diligence Guidance, NIST AI Risk Management Framework and deployed-system monitoring work, United Kingdom frontier-model evaluation practice, and California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act. The proposed implementation paper  provides the protected guidance for the future development of FORECAST-AI as a modular, cloud-based and federated accountability platform. No operational platform is claimed in this article. The companion validation protocol is prospectively registered and under embargo. The separate technical implementation paper is withheld and is not included in, attached to, or offered for publication with this article. FORECAST-AI does not guarantee safety and cannot justify deployment where prospective evidence is inadequate or plausible harm may be irreversible. Its contribution is to make predictions, safeguard commitments, and authorised decisions continuously traceable to observed outcomes, discrepancies, corrective action, and institutional proof.

title: Colour Value and Affective Response
affiliations: Renmin University of China and Tilburg University - Department of Finance

detail.title: Colour Value and Affective Response
detail.abstract: Hedonic models of auctioned art prices include artist reputation, medium, size, provenance, topics, and sale characteristics (such as auction house branches) as price determinants, but omit an important attribute a viewer perceives first: colour. This paper examines whether colour is a priced characteristic of paintings and whether value is affected by specific psychological channels. We address four questions: whether the colour dimensions hue, luminosity and saturation carry shadow prices; whether colours trigger specific emotions; which emotions drive the willingness-to-pay (captured by the bids); and whether these relations are culture-specific or universal. Building on the pleasure-arousal model of affect, we describe incentive-compatible bidding experiments with re-hued Rothko compositions conducted by Ma, Noussair and Renneboog (2022) in Europe, the US and China. These experiments were complemented by a hedonic pricing model on a large sample of non-figurative auctioned paintings. The evidence depicts a consistent colour hierarchy across all three cultures: blue and red paintings attract the highest bids (premiums of 18.6% and 17.3% respectively), followed by green, and then orange, purple, and yellow. In experiments with dual-colour paintings, red-blue and green-blue also command higher bids. Of the colour dimensions, hue dominates saturation and luminosity. Colour affects both pleasure and arousal, but only the pleasure emotional channel impacts the bidding. Arousal raises purchase intentions without affecting bidding behaviour. In the auction market, a one-standard-deviation increase in the blue (red) surface raises hammer prices by 10.6% (4.2%). The paper contributes to cultural economics by showing that part of the aesthetic dividend is measurable and largely universal. This supports affect-as-information and ecological valence theories, and rejects arousal-based explanations of colour effects in art auctions.

detail.abstract: This paper studies how students of the Faculty of Economics and Business of the University of Cantabria choose between bus, walking and private car for their trip to campus in Santander. With an original survey of 218 students, I estimate a multinomial logit on the 98 respondents who live in the municipality of Santander and report complete information, and test every coefficient against bootstrap resampling, a probit specification, lasso selection, a random forest and a separate sample of students living elsewhere in Cantabria. Travel time and monetary cost of the commute are the attributes most consistently associated with the mode chosen, and the only ones that pass all of these checks. Because both are reported for the chosen mode only, they are read as associations rather than as causal determinants. Sex, age, household size and parental education, some of which look significant in the conventional logit, do not survive, and household income keeps only a weak effect on walking. Aggregated by postcode, bus use is spatially autocorrelated (Moran's I = 0.291), yet the autocorrelation disappears once distance to campus and cost are controlled for. Expressed in consistent units, the value of travel time implied by the logit (about 5 e to 9 e per hour) is of the same order as an opportunity cost value based on the cost of a university education (8.67 e per hour), a figure to be taken as indicative. Four stated preference questions (a free bus line, a nearby line, a paid car park and environmental concern) respond to cost, sex and age in Santander, but their main predictors change outside the city, so they are read as local results.

detail.abstract: This investigation analyzes the comparative advantages of artificial intelligence (AI) relative to human judgment within the asset management process. A distinction is drawn between the naive investor-a private actor relying on autodidactic knowledge-and the professional investor, characterized by a mandate-driven process and institutional accountability. The analysis prioritizes asset allocation decisions, while security selection is evaluated specifically for government and corporate bonds, as well as globally diversified equity holdings, including funds and ETFs. The theoretical framework is grounded in behavioural finance evidence and the empirical record of implemented AI systems.

detail.abstract: Earlier work (Portugal Ribeiro, Sande and Jordão, 2024) argued that renegotiation programs for public contracts, such as the one created by Normative Instruction No. 91/2022 of the Brazilian National Audit Office (TCU), should admit only economically unsustainable contracts, lest they create moral hazard and systemic risk. This article develops that criterion in two directions. It distinguishes degrees of unsustainability-operational, investment-related and nonexistent-and shows that the quality of the service delivered reveals which one applies: a concessionaire that cannot operate meets no indicator at all; one that operates but does not invest meets the operating indicators and fails the investment ones; one with margin for both that still delivers substandard service does not have a contract problem. The article proposes that crossing quality with financial condition serve as the admissibility test for renegotiation and as the criterion for retaining the incumbent, and it identifies the legal instruments for replacing it: rebidding at the concessionaire's request, or early termination for default of the concessionaire followed by ordinary rebidding. The evidence comes from a panel of the six Brazilian federal airport concessions of the first and second rounds, from 2013 to 2025. The concessionaire with the highest operating margin in every year was the only one whose quality fell below the contractual standard, and it did so in operating items; the other four, which went through judicial reorganization, rebidding, demand collapse or near-zero margins, kept quality positive in every year, three of them at the ceiling.

detail.abstract: The European Union Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism converts EU allowance auction prices into regulated import liabilities. This paper measures regulatory window risk: the pricing interval determines how far an auction-day carbon price can lie from the regulated price assigned to that date. Using 2,676 official European Energy Exchange EUA primary auctions from 2013 through 2025, I apply weekly, 14-day, monthly, and quarterly volume-weighted pricing rules to identical realized price paths. Mean quarter-level absolute basis rises monotonically from 1.927 percent under weekly pricing to 6.145 percent under quarterly pricing, and weekly pricing lowers it in all 52 quarters. The 4.218-percentage-point paired reduction is highly significant under t, signed-rank, and 200,000-draw sign-flip inference. For squared loss, lower error under a nested weekly partition follows from an exact weighted-variance decomposition; the empirical contribution is its magnitude and state dependence. Between-week variation accounts for 86.0 percent of quarterly weighted squared error on average, and the quarterly-to-weekly MAE reduction correlates 0.950 with withinquarter auction-price variation. Actual calendar weeks differ from quarter-contained weeks by at most 0.188 percentage points of quarter MAE. Exact reproduction of the first two official 2026 prices validates the regulatory construction. The 2027 shift therefore materially compresses liability basis, especially when a quarter spans different carbon-price states.

title: Paying for Itself? Value (Mis)Alignment in Subscriptions

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no conflicts of interest to declare with the platforms studied in this paper.

detail.abstract: Cost-reducing subscriptions (e.g., DoorDash DashPass and Instacart+) promise to "pay for themselves" by waiving per-order fees in exchange for a fixed recurring charge. To examine whether these programs can create value for both consumers and platforms, this article develops a consumer-platform value alignment framework that maps subscription program outcomes along two dimensions: subscriber savings and platform profit. Waived fees are foregone revenue, but spending increases attributable to the program can create value, in principle enabling "win-win" outcomes. Applying the framework to nearly half a million subscribers across eight food delivery programs and using staggered difference-in-differences and causal forests to measure spending lift, the authors find that win-win outcomes are rare: thin contribution margins offset even substantial increases in consumer spending, resulting in a near-zero-sum relationship between subscriber gains and platform profit. Despite consumers with high baseline demand self-selecting into subscriptions, approximately half of subscription relationships do not generate positive lifetime savings. More selective targeting by the firm or lower-friction subscription and cancellation decisions by consumers can shift the allocation of value, but do not meaningfully increase value creation. These findings speak to program design, "pays for itself" claims, distributional outcomes, and sustainability of subscription programs in low-margin markets.

detail.abstract: Industrial and information Technology (IT) infrastructures are becoming more large and massive, making manual fault management more and more difficult, and leading to sustained research in self-healing and autonomous fault-recovery architectures. Several important and proven design paradigms, facilitating mechanisms, and methods to evaluate the effectiveness of self-healing systems are considered in this paper with respect to present-day systems in industrial automation, cloud-native computing and networked systems. Returning to the paradigm of autonomic computing, using the MAPE-K reference model, the review is based on 46 papers published mainly in the 2019-2025 period, as well as some foundational papers, and on studying how Monitoring, Diagnosis and Planning operations and Execution are implemented through a Rule-based Logic, Statistical Inference, Supervised and Reinforcement Machine Learning, and Hybrid Ensembles. Also, the paper reports a comparison between meantime to reduction and fault-detection accuracy per technique category, supported with figures and tables, and a description of respective open problems, namely: explainability, safety assurance, and cross domain generalisation. The results show that hybrid architectures using the models learned in addition to deterministic safety constraints are generally more successful than purely reactive or purely data-driven architectures, especially in safety-critical industrial applications. The paper concludes that future, self-healing architectures need to include explainable decision layers, formally verifying recovery actions, and governance in order to be viable in regulated critical infrastructure and proposes future research agendas for academic and industry practitioners to address.

title: Organisational Differentiation in Reported AI Use: Evidence and Temporal Constraints from Linked Enterprise Surveys in India
affiliations: University of Kerala

detail.title: Organisational Differentiation in Reported AI Use: Evidence and Temporal Constraints from Linked Enterprise Surveys in India
detail.abstract: Linked enterprise surveys can appear longitudinal while still leaving the timing of the phenomenon ambiguous. This study examines which observable organisational characteristics measured in the baseline India World Bank Enterprise Survey distinguish establishments reporting AI use from those reporting no AI use in the subsequent AI follow-up, while testing whether reported first-use timing supports a prospective interpretation. The linked sample contains 1,355 establishments; 520 reported AI use at follow-up. Of these, 383 (73.7%) reported first use before their own baseline interview month, 29 (5.6%) in the same month, and 108 (20.8%) afterwards. The primary analysis therefore treats the linked data as a status/profile association study rather than a model of subsequent first adoption. Weighted binomial logit models used follow-up survey weights normalised to mean one within the analytical sample and HC1 heteroskedasticity-robust covariance estimates. Sectoral context showed strong and stable differentiation in reported AI-use status. Formal employee training showed a large positive association whose weighted magnitude was information-constrained; internationally recognised certification showed a negative primary association that attenuated substantially after geographic adjustment. Website presence and establishment size remained inconclusive, whereas establishment age and top-manager sector experience yielded bounded evidence excluding substantively large conditional differences under the prespecified criterion. The study therefore provides bounded evidence on organisational differentiation in reported AI-use status among covered Indian establishments rather than a prospective model of the determinants of first AI adoption.

detail.abstract: AI agents capable of taking action, making decisions, and shaping experiences on a brand's behalf are moving from peripheral channels to central ones, joining algorithmic, platform, influencer, partner, co-creator, and employee agents in an increasingly distributed system of brand performance. This distribution of brand agency has outpaced the frameworks brands use to manage it: brand-safety standards govern adjacency, privacy regimes govern data, and AI-ethics frameworks govern algorithmic accuracy, but none addresses what happens when many agents represent a brand at once and make promises the brand must keep. Drawing on service-dominant logic, agency theory, and the emerging literature on consumer trust in AI, this article develops a conceptual framework for agentic brand orchestration: the coordination of a brand's distributed agents into a single, accountable performance. The framework identifies six pillars of orchestration responsibility (Purpose, Platform, Phygital Experience, Participation, Personalization, and Partnerships), each paired with a governance mechanism that operationalizes it, and three levels of governance maturity (Compliance, Differentiation, Leadership) that together yield an eighteen-cell diagnostic matrix, operationalized in an appendix as a seventy-two-item scorecard. The article develops eight formal propositions linking orchestration maturity to brand trust, resilience, and performance, illustrates the framework with recent brand failures and regulatory developments, and outlines a research agenda for testing the framework empirically.

detail.abstract: Kubernetes nodes rotate, compress, and delete container log files on their own schedule, and none of these actions reaches the application that wrote the lines. This paper documents three mechanisms that remove container logs without an error: rotation lag under sustained writes, disk-pressure eviction, and a race between kubelet rotation and the log shipper. It specifies a detection layer built on application-level sequence markers and ordered classification rules, and adds three node-side parts: a high-water gauge that exposes losses at the end of a stream, an offset auditor that measures lost bytes without application changes by comparing each log file's final size with the shipper's saved offset, and log escrow, which hard-links log files so they outlive the kubelet's cleanup until their data has been read. A node emulator that ports the kubelet's rotation sequence and performs real file operations measured each part. With a shipper reading 32 MB/s, loss began once writes passed that rate and reached 14%, 28%, and 46% of lines at 40, 48, and 64 MB/s. A longer Rotate_Wait delayed the first loss linearly but did not prevent it. Shortening the kubelet's monitor interval cost a polling shipper 50% to 89% of lines. After eviction, gap checks found none of the lost lines, while the auditor measured over 99% of the lost bytes. Escrow prevented all loss in uncapped runs, at the cost of up to 3 GB of held disk and about 0.6% duplicate lines. The code, raw results, and a cluster evaluation kit are published.

detail.abstract: This conceptual study examines brand name changes and their implications for product competitiveness through the perspectives of brand identity, brand positioning, brand equity, and consumer responses. The study aims to analyze why companies change brand names, how changes affect consumer perceptions and brand value, and how they relate to product competitiveness. A conceptual approach is used by reviewing relevant branding literature and analyzing four cases: BreadTalk to MAKO, Carrefour to Transmart, Dunkin' Donuts to Dunkin', and Aunt Jemima to Pearl Milling Company. The analysis indicates that brand name changes are not merely changes in terminology but can involve adjustments to identity, positioning, communication, and consumer relationships. The cases also show that maintaining continuity between old and new brand identities is important for preserving recognition, associations, and brand equity. Overall, brand name changes can support product competitiveness when companies consistently connect the new identity with consumer perceptions, experiences, relationships, and market positioning.

title: The Two-Clock Model: Structural Presence and AI Perception of Technology Entities

detail.abstract: A structural answer engine optimization (AEO) score measures whether a website is machinereadable. It does not measure whether AI platforms have updated what they know and cite about the entity behind that website. We propose the two-clock model: structural presence S(t) and AI perception P(t) are the same underlying construct-how established an entity is-measured from two viewpoints that move at different speeds. The perception gap G(t) = S(t)-P(t) is predicted to be largest at birth and to close as third-party citation accumulates. We assemble five mechanisms from research on knowledge cutoffs, temporal misalignment, fact decay, retrieval staleness, and long-tail knowledge to explain why the gap is a structural property of how language models work, not evidence of failed optimization. We then test these predictions empirically on a panel of fifty technology entities launched between January 2023 and March 2025. Using a model-cutoff natural experiment with dated OpenAI snapshots, we reconstruct AI perception at five frozen moments; archived homepage snapshots measure structural presence; weekly GDELT news mentions provide a citation series. Three findings follow. First, the birth gap is universal in this panel: structure averages 64.2% of maximum at birth while perception averages 0.5%-a mean gap of 63.6 percentage points with zero counterexamples. Second, citation precision is bimodal: distinctive entity names exceed 70% precision, common-word names collapse entirely, a methodological result for any entitymention measurement. Third, citation ramps precede perception onsets in 28 of 33 entities (85%; median lead 83 days; two-sided exact sign test p = 6.6 × 10-5), consistent with the citation-transmission hypothesis. We report these as supporting evidence for the mechanism, not as established causation. A three-run repeat-scoring pass on the perception measure (750 entity-model-run cells) finds 96.0% of cells agree within one point across runs (81.6% exact), bounding the run-to-run instability of the pilot P(t) series. The paper contributes a measurement framework for distinguishing expected lag from genuine failure in AEO practice, operationalizes diagnostic thresholds (perception should measurably narrow by month six), and identifies three levers that narrow the gap: citation building, external mentions, and answer-format content.

detail.abstract:
Cost-related medication non-adherence is prevalent across many healthcare systems and is associated with poorer health outcomes. Pharmaceutical expenditure ceiling policies that reduce patient copayments once cumulative spending reaches a defined limit offer financial protection against high out-of-pocket medication costs.

Using whole-of-population administrative prescription claims data, we provide the first population-level quasi-experimental evidence on the effects of reaching Australia's Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme Safety Net on medication utilisation (n=1,537,885). We apply a dynamic difference-in-differences framework, comparing prescription use before and after individuals reach the safety net, using future threshold-crossers as controls.

Reaching the safety net increased average monthly prescriptions dispensed by 0.715 (a 15% increase). Effects were driven primarily by pre-existing medications, particularly those used to treat chronic conditions. Responses were largest among lower-income individuals, especially those not eligible for government concession pricing, people with chronic health conditions, and individuals aged 40-69 years.

These findings suggest that reducing out-of-pocket medicine costs increases medication utilisation, with the strongest effects observed among populations at elevated risk of cost-related non-adherence. The results provide new evidence on the distributional effects of pharmaceutical expenditure ceiling policies and have implications for the design of policies intended to improve equitable access to medicines.

detail.abstract:
AI-agent benchmarks commonly collapse several questions into one number: whether the agent
completed a business task, whether it produced the publicly specified delivery, and whether it
matched an evaluator’s exact internal representation. This paper introduces an auditable
separation for a lightweight RHIS runtime: business fact topology T_B, public-contract delivery
projection P_D(T_B), and evaluator-compatibility projection P_E(T_B). The projections are
prohibited from writing back into the fact topology. We evaluate four completed configurations on
one WorkBuddyBench Office task using DeepSeek V4 Pro and exactly four tools: Read, Write, Edit,
and Bash. The only intended varying policy parameter is a bounded visible-obligation coverage
tolerance theta; hard authorization, source, time, role, site, schema, acyclicity, connectivity, and
public-delivery-closure constraints remain unchanged. All completed runs had zero admitted
noncoverage deviation. Nevertheless, request counts fell from 68 to 13 across theta = 0.00, 0.30,
0.60, and 0.90, while official raw scores were 32.67%, 47.94%, 22.14%, and 21.98%. The request
trajectory is a runtime observation recorded before scoring. The score trajectory is not evidence
about objective business correctness, because the scorer’s fixed but pre-run non-derivable
representation obligations confound that inference. The study establishes the implementability
and auditability of mathematical admission objects in an agent runtime; it does not establish a
general causal optimum, business-correctness rate, cost-quality improvement, or full-RHIS
validation.

detail.abstract: Typed decision layers such as TypeSafe Jev return isolated Nouls and no rationale [1], [2]. The Fréchet-Hoeffding bounds already imply that those Nouls do not determine a conjunction: at marginals 0.6 and 0.6, P (R ∧ D | s) lies in [0.2, 0.6]. That interval is the lemma. The result is that no function of the Nouls repairs it. Let L and U be the lower and upper ends of the interval, and let a probability policy allow when the conjunction probability is at least τ. If L < τ ≤ U , every combiner g(nR, nD) disagrees with that policy on some coupling that has the same Nouls. We call this the straddle theorem: there is no safe combiner. At 0.6, 0.6 and τ = 1/2 the cut sits inside [0.2, 0.6]. The product bit denies. A still-feasible coupling has probability 0.6 and the probability policy allows. A minimum, a maximum, or any other published formula is some other g, and each of them fails on one of the two couplings. The bit agrees with the probability policy on the whole interval only when U < τ or L ≥ τ , a check that uses the Nouls and does not need the joint. The product fails that check because it is the maximum-entropy coupling, which sets I(R; D) = 0 and lands at 0.36. A PEP, store-backed state, perfect calibration, and a published cut all survive. ISO/IEC 42001, the NIST AI RMF, OWASP inventories, and policy-as-code do not name the straddle [3]-[10]. The paper is a representation and audit argument, not an accuracy measurement.

detail.abstract: Research on trust in AI-generated information is growing fast, but almost all of it looks at the same thing: whether one employee, in one moment, decides to check an AI output. Some studies look at motivation and personality. Others build economic models of when checking is "worth it" for a given worker. A newer group of studies calls this checking work "epistemic labor" but still does not ask how that labor gets spread across an organization. This paper argues that all three approaches miss the more important question: who, across an entire organization, is expected to verify AI-generated claims, and who actually has the time, expertise, and authority to do it? Drawing on research about information infrastructure, the paper shows that organizations already know how to build trust into a system at scalethis is exactly what protocols like DNSSEC do for the internet-but no equivalent system exists yet for AI-generated information. Drawing on Miranda Fricker's theory of epistemic injustice, the paper then argues that leaving this gap unaddressed is not neutral: the work of verification tends to fall on people with the least power to be credited for doing it. The paper ends with a practical framework for closing this gap and a set of research questions for studying it empirically.

detail.abstract: Network intrusion detection systems (NIDSs) operate in dynamic environments where traffic distributions, device populations, and attack strategies constantly evolve. Static training assumptions create a persistent mismatch between laboratory accuracy and operational reliability. This structured review examines a curated evidence base of 30 studies at the intersection of concept drift, continual learning, lightweight deployment, and open-world detection. Each study was systematically coded for problem context, drift characterization, adaptation mechanism, replay or forgetting mitigation, datasets, and computational evidence. The synthesis reveals that while the literature contains strong partial solutions, the complete operational lifecycle-detecting meaningful change, triggering economical updates, preserving previous knowledge, recognizing unseen attacks, and verifying resource cost-is rarely evaluated within a single, reproducible protocol. This review converts this fragmentation into a precise research gap and proposes an evidence-derived evaluation blueprint and research roadmap (DART-Lite) for future drift-aware continual NIDSs.

detail.abstract: This study reconstructs the estimation structure of drift-augmented linear Gaussian state-space models for dynamic beta estimation by clarifying the information sets and establishing a unified framework of conditional Gaussian distributions. By treating pre-and post-observation variables, which have not been explicitly handled in existing state-space models, as a bivariate normal distribution, the Kalman filter and the EM algorithm are derived in a coherent likelihood-based manner. The local model of Durbin and Koopman (2011) is designed for trend extraction and is structurally different from the present dynamic beta model, which incorporates explanatory variables, non-zero means of the observation error and the state error, and a drift term. In the EM algorithm, the conditional distribution of the dynamic beta is obtained in the E-step, and parameter updates are performed in the M-step. Because the state-error variance may lie on the boundary, its significance is evaluated using the LR test for boundary parameters of Self and Liang (1987). Empirical analysis shows that dynamic beta is unnecessary for many stocks, while some exhibit significant improvement, and the boundary-specific pileup phenomenon is also observed. Through the research process, a unified estimation foundation has been established that enhances the transparency and reproducibility of model selection in state-space modeling. All research design, analysis, mathematical derivations, and substantive writing were conducted by the author.

detail.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence does not merely accelerate the attention economy; it reconfigures the conditions under which attention is captured, organized, and monetized. This article develops an account of semiotic capitalism as an analytical formation in which signs, affects, communicative activity, and attention become central to processes of accumulation. Rather than treating capitalist regimes of capture as successive replacements, the article conceptualizes them as stratified formations in which new mechanisms reorganize and extend earlier forms of appropriation. The generative turn introduces a further transformation: the growing capacity to synthesize and personalize symbolic environments in response to users. The argument does not claim that AI produces perception itself. Rather, generative and agentic systems participate in producing the symbolic conditions through which users encounter, interpret, and navigate the world. The article therefore distinguishes attention capture from the synthetic production of symbolic environments. Whereas earlier platform economies selected, ranked, circulated, and monetized content within pre-existing environments, generative systems combine these functions with production of text, images, voices, narratives, and personalized interactions. Four propositions examine this transformation across political-economic, behavioral, phenomenological, and epistemic registers, addressing declining marginal costs of symbolic production, adaptive personalization, sensory alienation, and the destabilization of shared objects of interpretation. The analysis distinguishes empirical evidence from theoretical inference and speculative extension. It then proposes 'cognitive sovereignty' as a normative framework for governing attention, perception, memory, and meaning-making-ultimately shifting the focus from who captures attention to who shapes the environments that organize it.

detail.abstract: Fadeout is defined as the decline in an intervention's initial treatment effect in subsequent follow-up periods. This paper uses the Head Start Impact Study to examine heterogeneity in the fadeout of cognitive gains from access to Head Start preschool. I find that Black children experience substantially less fadeout than non-Black children and retain a 0.23 standard deviation gain at the end of kindergarten (p < 0.10). A selection-corrected decomposition attributes 74% of the Black-non-Black fadeout differential to differences in cognitive growth between Black and non-Black children under Head Start nonparticipation. Mediation analyses provide suggestive evidence that kindergarten school environments, particularly school achievement levels and time spent in adult-directed individual activities, partially contribute to these divergent growth trajectories. Counterfactual simulations show that reallocating existing Head Start offers toward centers serving predominantly Black applicants reduces aggregate fadeout only modestly because Black children constitute a relatively small share of applicants nationally. These findings suggest that meaningfully improving the persistence of Head Start's cognitive effects may require expanding the program and directing recruitment toward children for whom initial gains are more likely to persist.

detail.abstract: Germany faces growing congestion challenges and residential flexibility is seen as a promising solution, but it remains largely untapped. Uncertainty about financial benefits and limited smart meter rollout pose significant barriers to households. Motivated by residential flexibility's potential to address Germany's energy challenge, this paper builds a framework to answer when switching to a dynamic tariff is economically rational and how fast adoption can proceed given infrastructure constraints. An electricity bill simulation is constructed across household archetypes using EPEX spot price data (2023-2025) to calculate a break-even threshold S* under passive and automated load shifting scenarios. This feeds into a Bass diffusion model modified with a time-varying smart meter infrastructure ceiling to project adoption to 2035. Both analyses are supplemented by expert interviews with dynamic tariff providers, regulators, and consumer advocates. The break-even simulation finds modest private savings compared to the system-level flexibility value, reflecting a structural externality. Dynamic tariffs are only economically rational for households with large shiftable loads, particularly EV owners, and incentive compression from fixed charges suppresses the price signal. The adoption model projects between 0.73M and 5.35M additional adopters by 2035, with smart meter rollout, low policy activation, and limited consumer awareness acting as mutually reinforcing constraints. Beyond quantitative findings, expert interviews highlight that risk aversion poses a further barrier to adoption. In their current form, mass market adoption of dynamic tariffs is unlikely. To increase residential flexibility, the paper identifies several levers: accelerating smart meter rollout, enforcing dynamic tariff and grid fee availability, and making grid fees variable to reduce incentive compression, while aggregator models offer an alternative path.

detail.abstract: When does external adjustment become external normalisation? This paper studies why a narrowing current-account deficit need not signal the end of foreign-currency liquidity pressure when access to formal foreign exchange (FX) is rationed. The model separates current import-payment demand from debt-service pressure and short-term refinancing exposure inherited from earlier liabilities, and routes these gross payment requirements through a formal FX allocation that need not clear continuously at posted terms. A latent scarcity state captures pressure on effective formal-FX access. Using quarterly Egyptian data from 2001Q4 to 2025Q4 and a Bayesian state-space model, I trace conditional source-specific propagation. Under the maintained short-term refinancing process, the 90 per cent horizon-specific highest-posterior-density (HPD) interval for scarcity remains above zero throughout the twenty reported quarters, while the non-interest current-account-deficit response lies below zero from horizon 7 through horizon 19. The contribution is to introduce a settlement-allocation margin into the rollover-risk problem: gross refinancing pressure can remain transmitted through a rationed FX market after net external flows have begun to adjust. Current-account adjustment can therefore precede foreign-currency-liquidity normalisation. External surveillance should assess net external adjustment alongside debt maturities, rollover conditions and effective FX-market access.

detail.abstract: Something is amiss in empirical economics. Despite the advances of the credibility revolution, published estimates tend to be inflated and overconfident. We argue that this stems from a weakness in the dominant econometric framework: treating the researcher like a calculator that mechanically implements the econometric method. We use several examples to show how properties of estimators change dramatically with humans-in-the-loop. Under plausible assumptions on researcher behavior, low-power estimators such as instrumental variables exhibit high degrees of bias, even with a first-stage F-statistic of 200. Threshold testing on the first-stage F-statistic can reduce bias, contrary to Angrist and Kolesár (2024). And standard errors understate uncertainty, since they ignore variation due to researchers' subjective choices. Ignoring the role of humans "in the research loop" can lead to highly biased and unreliable findings. Modifying econometric practices to address the human factor is a critical frontier of the credibility revolution.

detail.abstract: Can banks maintain their advantage as liquidity providers when they are heavily exposed to a financial crisis?  The standard argument - that banks can - hinges on deposit inflows that are seeking a safe haven and provide banks with a natural hedge to fund drawn credit lines and other commitments. We shed new light on this issue by studying the behavior of bank deposit rates and inflows during the 2007-09 crisis.  Our results indicate that the role of the banking system as a stabilizing liquidity insurer is not one of the passive recipient, but of an active seeker, of deposits.  We find that banks facing a funding squeeze sought to attract deposits by offering higher rates.  Banks offering higher rates were also those most exposed to liquidity demand shocks (as measured by their unused commitments, wholesale funding dependence, and limited liquid assets), as well as with fundamentally weak balance-sheets (as measured by their non-performing loans or by subsequent failure).  Such rate increases have a competitive effect in that they lead other banks to offer higher rates as well.  Overall, the results present a nuanced view of deposit rates and flows to banks in a crisis, one that reflects banks not just as safety havens but also as stressed entities scrambling for deposits.

title: Dynamic Model Averaging under Scale Instability: Bounded Predictive Evidence for U.S. Inflation Forecasting

detail.title: Dynamic Model Averaging under Scale Instability: Bounded Predictive Evidence for U.S. Inflation Forecasting

detail.abstract: Dynamic model averaging adapts model probabilities to predictive performance, but the predictive law also determines how strongly a single observation can alter model credibility. This paper separates the strength of current relative predictive evidence from the persistence of accumulated evidence. Gaussian predictive densities generate unbounded one-period evidence in the tails, whereas common-tail predictive laws yield bounded evidence while preserving cumulative learning. In recursive U.S. inflation forecasts, Gaussian and robust updating behave similarly for ordinary surprises but differ sharply for tail observations, with little change in point accuracy. Monte Carlo experiments show less false switching under temporary scale disturbances without a material adaptation penalty after persistent mean change. In an operational block-DMA system with stochastic volatility, robust learning reduces mean RMSFE by 3.1% and improves average log predictive scores.

title: Trading Regulation: Markets for Regulatory Attributes in Banking
affiliations: Yeshiva University - Sy Syms School of Business and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Trading Regulation: Markets for Regulatory Attributes in Banking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Declaration of Interest
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding Received

detail.abstract: Can tradable regulatory claims undermine the activity regulation is designed to promote? We study India’s Priority Sector Lending Certificate market, where banks can satisfy lending mandates by purchasing regulatory credit without acquiring the underlying loans. Trading allows banks to separate regulatory attributes from balance-sheet lending and reallocates compliance toward institutions with comparative advantage. This lowers the real cost of meeting regulatory targets, but it also reduces incentives to originate qualifying credit. The results reveal a fundamental policy tradeoff: markets for regulatory claims improve compliance efficiency while potentially weakening the real activity that regulation seeks to encourage.

title: Monetary Tightening and Inflation-Risk Composition: The Role of Shock Identification
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: Monetary Tightening and Inflation-Risk Composition: The Role of Shock Identification

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research, authorship, and publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: Monetary tightening restrains demand but cannot directly remove supply disturbances, so its effect on inflation risk may depend on where adverse macroeconomic uncertainty originates. I combine Bekaert-Engstrom-Ermolov measures of bad supply and demand uncertainty with high-frequency FOMC surprises and estimate quarterly U.S. local projections for 1994-2019. Using the Bauer-Swanson surprise orthogonalised to pre-announcement public information, the one-quarter-ahead interaction between tightening and the supply share of bad structural uncertainty is economically small and statistically indistinguishable from zero for inflationinnovation skewness, while the variance decomposition reveals no stable reallocation from demand-to supply-related bad inflation risk. Positive interactions under raw Bauer-Swanson and Jarociński-Karadi measures weaken under leverage-sensitive inference and acute-GFC exclusion. Apparent state dependence in inflation-risk composition is therefore identification-sensitive, limiting structural interpretations of distributional monetary transmission.

title: Sovereign Refinancing Pressure and Private Credit During Monetary Tightening in Egypt
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: Sovereign Refinancing Pressure and Private Credit During Monetary Tightening in Egypt

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research, authorship, and publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether sovereign refinancing pressure conditions privatecredit dynamics during monetary tightening in Egypt. Refinancing pressure is measured as short-term domestic government debt relative to trailing four-quarter realised fiscal revenue, capturing near-term domestic financing requirements relative to recent fiscal resources. Using quarterly data for 2001Q3-2025Q4 and statedependent local projections with Central Bank of Egypt CBE policy-event surprises, the analysis finds amplification rather than sign reversal: real private credit contracts at both low and high refinancing pressure, but more strongly at the higher state. Moving from the 25th to the 75th percentile on common positive-tightening support is associated with an additional 3.30-log-point decline over quarters two to six. Conventional debt and maturity measures do not reproduce this negative medium-run pattern. The result remains negative across prespecified checks, while sparse policy events and imperfect shock timing limit a structural marginal-shock interpretation.

title: Treasury Absorption, Uncertainty Persistence, and Fiscal Transmission
affiliations: University of Nottingham

detail.title: Treasury Absorption, Uncertainty Persistence, and Fiscal Transmission

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the research, authorship, and publication of this article.
declarations.funderStatement: NA

detail.abstract: This paper studies when the investor base of public debt matters for fiscal transmission. A model links Treasury absorption to domestic intermediary capacity and predicts that external absorption supports private investment more strongly when macroeconomic uncertainty is expected to persist. Prolonged uncertainty raises the value of unused capacity, so Treasury exposure retained on domestic risk-bearing balance sheets competes more strongly with private finance. Government-purchases innovations are identified independently of Treasury-holder composition and traced with local projections across realised absorption and uncertainty environments. During uncertainty build-ups, private investment responds more favourably under relative external than domestic absorption, while output di↵erences become clearer at medium horizons. This contrast survives a specification including monetarypolicy responses, and the external-absorption state ordering remains visible under narrative defence-news identification. The results document a state-dependent investor-base dimension of fiscal transmission centred on private investment.

title: Passive Versus Active Growth: Evidence from Founder Choices and Venture Capital Investment
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Behavioral Policy Science (BPS), Columbia University - Columbia Business School and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) - Sloan School of Management

detail.title: Passive Versus Active Growth: Evidence from Founder Choices and Venture Capital Investment
detail.abstract: This paper develops a novel approach for assessing the role of passive learning versus a proactive growth orientation in the entrepreneurial growth process. We develop a simple model linking early-stage founder choices, venture capital investment and skewed growth outcomes such as the achievement of an IPO or significant acquisition. Using comprehensive business registration data from 34 US states from 1995-2004, we observe that firms that register in Delaware or obtain intellectual property such as a patent or trademark are far more likely to ultimately realize significant equity growth, and these choices also predict early-stage venture capital investment. Moreover, the estimated probability of receiving venture capital as reflected in early-stage founder choices predicts growth even for firms that do not receive venture capital. We use these findings to estimate bounds on the fraction of proactive versus passive firms among firms that ultimately achieve significant equity growth. While nearly half of all firms that achieve modest equity growth (> $10M) are consistent with passive learning (as they neither make early-stage founder choices nor receive venture capital), 78% of firms experiencing an equity growth event greater than $100M are associated with active founder choices and/or venture capital investment, and these firms are concentrated in geographic hubs such as Silicon Valley. Finally, our approach offers a novel approach for estimating the private returns to venture capital, matching on founder choices rather than demographics; consistent with prior studies, venture-backed firms are approximately 5X more likely to grow, with heterogeneity across location and time period.

title: Skill Requirements Across Firms and Labor Markets: Evidence from Job Postings for Professionals
affiliations: Academic Dean, Harvard University - Harvard Kennedy School (HKS) and Yale School of Management

detail.title: Skill Requirements Across Firms and Labor Markets: Evidence from Job Postings for Professionals
detail.abstract: We study variation in skill demands for professionals across firms and labor markets. We categorize a wide range of keywords found in job ads into ten general skills. There is substantial variation in these skill requirements, even within narrowly defined occupations. Focusing particularly on cognitive and social skills, we find positive correlations between each skill and external measures of pay and firm performance. We also find evidence of a cognitive social-skill complementarity for both outcomes. As a whole, the job skills have explanatory power in pay and firm performance regressions, beyond what is available in widely-used labor market data.

title: A Structural Empirical Model of R&D Investment, Firm Heterogeneity, and Industry Evolution
affiliations: University of Toronto - Department of Economics and Duke University

detail.title: A Structural Empirical Model of R&D Investment, Firm Heterogeneity, and Industry Evolution
detail.abstract: This paper develops and estimates an industry equilibrium model of manufacturing plants in the Korean electric motor industry from 1991 to 1996. Plant-level decisions on R&D, physical capital investment, entry, and exit are integrated in a dynamic setting with knowledge spillovers. We use a simulated method of moments estimator and the novel approximation method of Weintraub, Benkard and Van Roy (2008) to estimate the R&D cost, magnitude of knowledge spillovers, adjustment costs of physical investment, and plant scrap value distribution. Knowledge spillovers are essential to explaining the firm-level productivity evolution and the equilibrium market configuration. A counterfactual experiment reveals that a 15% R&D subsidy maximizes industry output and is broadly consistent with a past policy initiative of the Korean government.

title: Monetary Policy Transmission Through Online Banks
affiliations: Ohio State University (OSU) - Department of Finance, University of California, Irvine, University of Chicago and University of Chicago

detail.title: Monetary Policy Transmission Through Online Banks
detail.abstract: Financial technology has the potential to alter the transmission of monetary policy by lowering search costs and expanding banking markets. This paper studies the reaction of online banks to changes in the federal funds rate. We find that a 100 basis points increase in the federal funds rate leads to a 30 basis points larger increase in the deposit rates of online banks relative to traditional banks. Consistent with the rate movements, online bank deposits experience inflows, while traditional banks experience outflows. Results are similar across markets with differing competitiveness and demographics, but vary with the stickiness of depositors.

title: Covariance-Guided Activation Selection with Adaptive Compensation for Efficient Neural Network Pruning
affiliations: Datavid Ltd

detail.title: Covariance-Guided Activation Selection with Adaptive Compensation for Efficient Neural Network Pruning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I declare that there are no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is purely computational and does not involve human participants, animal subjects, or sensitive personal data. All experiments were conducted on standard, publicly available benchmark datasets.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. All computing resources were arranged by Author.

detail.abstract: Structured neural network pruning physically deletes entire channels and intermediate feature projections, delivering immediate memory and computational savings without requiring specialized sparse hardware accelerators. However, dominant channel selection heuristicspredominantly magnitude-based (weight norms) or local activation statistics (mean activation, variance)-treat channels as isolated scalar components, ignoring high-dimensional interchannel covariance structures. Consequently, they either prune channels carrying critical independent task information or retain clusters of mutually redundant features. Furthermore, conventional post-pruning recovery relies either on computationally expensive iterative finetuning or rigid linear weight merging that ignores nonlinear activation dynamics. This paper presents CGAS-NC (Covariance-Guided Activation Selection with Nonlinear Compensation), an end-to-end framework for structural channel pruning and representation recovery. CGAS-NC introduces: (1) a mathematically unified Contribution-Aware Covariance Metric that identifies redundant donor channels by penalizing mutual correlation while explicitly weighting downstream task sensitivity; (2) dynamic layer-budgeting mechanisms based on the participation-ratio Effective Rank (r eff) and layer redundancy mass; and (3) an Adaptive Recovery Hierarchy spanning zero-overhead linear weight folding, orthogonal Chebyshev polynomial compensation, and lightweight basis surrogates. Crucially, CGAS-NC executes true structural pruning by physically contracting weight matrices and eliminating intermediate dimensions, rather than relying on simulated zero-masking. Furthermore, while legacy structural pruning methods (such as Network Slimming) depend fundamentally on Batch Normalization scaling parameters or assume simple piecewise-linear activations (like ReLU), they are intrinsically inapplicable to modern Transformers and Large Language Models (LLMs) that employ LayerNorm or RMSNorm and smooth or gated activations (GELU, SwiGLU, SiLU). In contrast, because CGAS-NC operates strictly on empirical activation covariances and downstream projection sensitivity, it is fundamentally activation-agnostic and normalization-independent. Consequently, CGAS-NC provides a deployable structural pruning mechanism that is also theoretically and practically suitable for integration into LLM training and fine-tuning pipelines. Empirically, this work provides an exhaustive evaluation spanning over 60 distinct configurations across multiple benchmark datasets and architectural paradigms. Across multi-seed training-time structural pruning experiments on feed-forward networks (MNIST and Fashion-MNIST across 5 random seeds), CGAS-NC achieves up to 50% channel reduction with < 0.3% accuracy degradation. On post-training structural pruning of pre-trained Large Language Models (GPT-2 124M on WikiText-2), dynamic Effective-Rank allocation prunes 56% more transformer feed-forward channels than uniform pruning at stable token perplexity, while closed-form ridge projection compensation recovers perplexity from 61.08 to 36.96 (+24.12 PPL). Furthermore, while this paper presents completed empirical benchmarks on multi-layer networks and GPT-2, active investigations are currently underway extending CGAS-NC to deep residual convolutional networks (ResNet-18, ResNet-50) and compact modern foundation language models (such as LLaMA-3.2 and Gemma-2).

title: Windows of Opportunity in Early Childhood: A Dynamic Model of Multidimensional Development
affiliations: Yale University, Universidad de los Andes, Colombia - Department of Economics, University of Naples Federico II and Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey

detail.title: Windows of Opportunity in Early Childhood: A Dynamic Model of Multidimensional Development
detail.abstract:
Using child development data collected during the evaluation of an early childhood education program, this paper estimates a dynamic model of human development from ages 1 to 6. We model three latent factors—health, cognitive skills, and socio-emotional skills—and allow them to interact with each other and with multiple inputs to shape subsequent development. The richness and high-frequency nature of the data permit a flexible specification that (i) allows for complex dynamics, (ii) lets each factor con- tribute to the production of the others, (iii) permits age-varying production technologies, and (iv) treats parental investment as endogenous. We use the estimated model to identify “windows of opportunity” in which parental interventions, or programs that increase investment, are especially effective. Results indicate that developmental dynamics are richer than typically assumed, with important implications for persistence: the impact of inputs can decay or endure in ways that vary across domains and over age. Accounting for endogenous investment is consequential for inference.

title: Timing, Trading Frictions, and the Limits of Subsidy Capture in Livestock Risk Protection
affiliations: North Dakota State University, North Dakota State University, North Dakota State University and North Dakota State University

detail.title: Timing, Trading Frictions, and the Limits of Subsidy Capture in Livestock Risk Protection
detail.abstract:
Publicly subsidized insurance programs can create incentives for subsidy capture when insured products closely resemble privately traded financial instruments. Livestock Risk Protection (LRP) is one such case because it provides price insurance through a contract that closely resembles an exchange-traded put option. Using LRP endorsement records and matched CME options data for 2020–2025, we document that endorsement activity clusters around CME option expiration dates, especially for feeder cattle and lean hogs. Because producer-level derivatives positions are unobserved, however, timing patterns alone cannot identify subsidy capture. We therefore simulate returns to combined LRP-CME strategies using observed contract terms, option prices, and trading frictions, including bid-ask spreads, margin requirements, and financing costs. We find that the subsidy-created premium wedge is observable at purchase, but realized gains are small, commodity-specific, and concentrated in low-volatility environments where realized volatility falls below implied volatility. Even in those favorable cases, combined strategies substantially worsen downside outcomes relative to holding LRP alone. Additional evidence shows that clustering persists across volatility regimes and after the 2025 revisions to the LRP Handbook, suggesting that observed timing patterns may reflect contract alignment and routine hedging practices, instead of widespread economically meaningful subsidy capture.

title: Social Sorting and Political Cleavages: Evidence from 2.5 Million Electoral Candidates
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Banco de España

detail.title: Social Sorting and Political Cleavages: Evidence from 2.5 Million Electoral Candidates
detail.abstract:
How socially distinct are competing political parties' candidate pools? Since names encode cultural milieu, lineage, linguistic origin, and ancestry that standard socioeconomic variables miss, we measure social sorting across parties with names, predicting affiliation out of sample within municipality-years. Across more than 2.5 million local-election candidates, names pick the right-wing candidate in a random within-municipality pair 55.8\% of the time in Spain and 56.5\% in France. Given names alone do most of the work: around 55.0%. Under a stylized model of intergenerational transmission of political orientation, this translates to an implied gap of about 25 p.p. in parental naming propensities. The signal is stable in Spain but doubles in France by 2026. Within ideological families, names separate parties as sharply as across the right--left divide, even more so in France. The Spanish cleavage is linguistic and growing. The French one runs through names of immigrant origin and is strongest in large cities.

title: Quantitative Modeling of Political Decision-Making in Interwar Germany Part 1: Economic and Political Instability, 1919–1933.
affiliations: Kanagawa University

detail.title: Quantitative Modeling of Political Decision-Making in Interwar Germany Part 1: Economic and Political Instability, 1919–1933.
