detail.abstract: The rapid diffusion of unmanned aerial systems (UAS) across African conflicts is transforming the operational dynamics of warfare on the continent. Once the preserve of technologically advanced militaries, drones have become increasingly accessible due to falling costs, expanding commercial drone markets, and growing foreign military assistance. This article examines how the spread of drone technologies is reshaping African battlefields by introducing a new vertical dimension of warfare characterised by persistent aerial surveillance and remote strike capabilities. Drawing on open-source intelligence, conflict reporting, and existing academic literature, the study analyses how both state forces and nonstate armed groups are integrating drones into military operations. Case studies from Libya, Ethiopia, Sudan, the Sahel, and the eastern Democratic Republic of Congo illustrate how drones are altering patterns of reconnaissance, targeting, and force projection. The article argues that drone proliferation represents not merely a tactical innovation but a structural shift in the organisation of violence. As aerial observation becomes cheaper and more widely available, control of the airspace above the battlefield increasingly shapes the outcomes of conflicts on the ground. Understanding this transformation is essential for assessing the future trajectory of warfare in Africa.

title: Artificial Intelligence Exposure and the Premature De-laborization of Africa’s Digital Development Pathways
affiliations: University of Science and Technology Beijing and University of Science and Technology Beijing

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence Exposure and the Premature De-laborization of Africa’s Digital Development Pathways
detail.abstract: Metrics assessing artificial intelligence (AI) exposure currently evaluate existing occupational structures,while development strategies focus on future occupational pathways. This discrepancy results in the largely unquantified technological vulnerability of Africa’s targeted digital-service pathway. We introduce trajectory exposure, a reproducible metric that quantifies AI exposure across occupations targeted by national digital-development strategies, distinguishing it from conventional stock exposure in current employment.Our framework is applied to ten African economies, utilizing AI exposure ratings across 923 O*NET occupations, national employment distributions, Online Labour Index demand and worker data, ICT service exports, and demographic projections. The targeted digital pathway exhibits a mean exposure of 0.656, compared to 0.172 for the existing domestic occupational base, representing a 3.5-4.6-fold differential that remains consistent across alternative specifications. In every economy, trajectory exposure surpasses stock exposure, with trajectory-to-stock ratios ranging from 1.92 to 3.17. Contrary to the assumption thatAI exposure is concentrated in entry-level cognitive work, exposure increases with the level of required occupational preparation. Although ICT service exports grew by 7.2% annually post-2021, online demand systematically shifted away from more AI-exposed categories (Spearman ρ = -1.000, exact p = 0.0002). Furthermore, the export sector could accommodate fewer than 3% of a single annual entrant cohort. These findings suggest that AI may constrain a development pathway before it achieves sufficient scale to absorb demographic labor, necessitating a shift in policy focus from merely skills supply to the ownership anddistribution of complementary productive assets. Complete replication materials are openly available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Premature-De-Laborization-of-supplementary-file-paper-66CD/.

title: AI-Driven Bio-Inspired Energy Management for Photovoltaic-Based Microgrids: A Unified Stochastic Optimization Framework with Theoretical Convergence Guarantees
affiliations: Universiti Teknologi MARA, Shah Alam, Selangor, Malaysia - Solar Research Institute (SRI), National University of Malaysia (UKM) - The National University of Malaysia, Universiti Teknologi MARA, Shah Alam, Selangor, Malaysia - Faculty of Electrical Engineering, Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia, National University of Malaysia (UKM) - The National University of Malaysia and Universiti Kebangsaan Malaysia

detail.title: AI-Driven Bio-Inspired Energy Management for Photovoltaic-Based Microgrids: A Unified Stochastic Optimization Framework with Theoretical Convergence Guarantees
detail.abstract: The photovoltaic (PV)-based microgrid systems suffer from nonlinearities, randomness of the environment, and coupling of operations, making traditional optimization approaches unsuitable for Maximum Power Point Tracker (MPPT), Energy Management System (EMS), and economic dispatch. Despite several success stories using bio-inspired metaheuristic techniques in all these areas, literature review highlights a disorganized state, as far as benchmarking and theory are concerned. The objective of the present paper is to develop a common framework for stochastic optimization that includes a common mechanism for initialization, constraint handling, and fitness evaluation. The theoretical justification of a general model is based on probabilistic convergence, Markov chain ergodicity, Foster-Lyapunov stability conditions, and complexity considerations. The performance of 15 novel bio-inspired optimization algorithms is assessed using the same setup for four applications of renewable energy: MPPT of partial shading condition with multimodality, optimization of the PV tilt angle with maximum annual energy yield, battery management with time-dependent multi-objective constraints, and optimization of fuel cost in hybrid PV-Diesel-battery systems. A comparative study of 30 runs is showed that bio-inspired optimization resulted in 99.0% tracking efficiency of MPPT, 9.3% increment of annual energy generation, 44% saving of battery loss, and 23% saving of diesel fuel costs. A crucial trade-off between accuracy and computation is identified where high-accuracy algorithms yielded superior solutions, whereas low-computation algorithms provided fast solution to be used for real-time embedded control purposes.

title: Cooperation in Repeated Interactions: IQ, Memory, Records, and Attention
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - Department of Economics, UC Berkeley Haas School of Business, UC Berkeley Haas School of Business and University of California, San Diego (UCSD)

detail.title: Cooperation in Repeated Interactions: IQ, Memory, Records, and Attention

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No interest.
declarations.funderStatement: National Science Foundation

detail.abstract: Cooperation in repeated interactions often requires agents to interpret histories and condition current behavior on past outcomes. This creates a role for cognitive traits, but also for institutions that record, organize, and make histories salient. We study these forces in an indefinitely repeated Prisoner's Dilemma with imperfect public monitoring. The experiment measures subjects' IQ and working memory and explores two forms of cognitive infrastructure: access to a history table and an attention aid requiring subjects to record past outcomes. In the baseline environment, where subjects receive neither aid, IQ and working memory predict cooperation, both in the short and long-run. Estimated strategies also differ sharply by cognitive traits. By contrast, these relationships disappear when records or attention aids are available.

title: A Smartphone RTK Positioning Method Based on an XGBoost-Derived Stochastic Model
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: A Smartphone RTK Positioning Method Based on an XGBoost-Derived Stochastic Model
detail.abstract: Smartphones provide a practical platform for low-cost real-time kinematic (RTK) positioning, but their Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) observations are strongly affected by antenna design, receiver hardware and complex surroundings. These factors lead to low carrier-to-noise density ratios (C/N0), large observation noise and unstable data quality, which limit smartphone RTK positioning accuracy. Conventional C/N0 stochastic models weight observations mainly according to signal strength and therefore cannot adequately represent the observation noise of smartphones in complex environments. To address this problem, this study proposes an XGBoost-based stochastic model for smartphone RTK positioning. The model uses raw Android GNSS observations to extract C/N0, satellite elevation angle and Doppler measurements as quality-related features, and uses pseudorange noise as the training target. It learns the mapping between observation features and noise level, allowing observation-noise prediction and adaptive weighting within the RTK solution. Vehicle experiments were conducted on two urban routes using a Huawei Mate 40 and a Xiaomi Mi 8, with a conventional C/N0 stochastic model used as the baseline. The XGBoost stochastic model outperformed the C/N0 model for both devices and both routes. On Route 1, the three-dimensional root mean square (RMS) accuracy improved by 23.47% for the Mi 8 and 28.45% for the Mate 40. On the more obstructed Route 2, the corresponding improvements were 33.78% and 30.74%. These results indicate that the XGBoost-derived stochastic model better represents smartphone GNSS observation noise and improves the accuracy and stability of smartphone RTK positioning in complex urban environments.

title: Tax Enforcement and Mobile Payments
affiliations: Copenhagen Business School and University of Copenhagen

detail.title: Tax Enforcement and Mobile Payments
detail.abstract: We study tax enforcement when third-party transaction data reveal that a payment oc curred but not whether it represents taxable income. We link Danish person-to-person mobile payment records to tax audits of small and medium-sized enterprises and document under-reporting of business income received through private accounts. Following an audit notification, mobile payment inflows fall by 17.4% among taxpayers for whom the subsequent audit detects reporting errors, while taxpayers with no detected errors do not respond. The response emerges only after the tax authority gains systematic access to the underlying trans action data. Yet lower inflows do not translate into higher VAT liabilities, instead, payments partly shift to spouses. Audit notification thus appear to change how noncompliant taxpay ers receive payments rather than inducing tax compliance. The results show how transaction data that cannot be directly matched to taxable income can nevertheless reveal and inform enforcement of noncompliance.

title: Theory for the Coevolution of Cooperation and Conflict
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Theory for the Coevolution of Cooperation and Conflict
detail.abstract: Cooperation and conflict often evolve together within the same interaction. The evolution of cooperation has been understood largely through inclusive fitness theory. A major shortcoming, however, has been that as it’s been used, inclusive fitness theory predicts the evolution of either cooperation or cooperation, as mutually exclusive alternatives. This prediction disagrees with empirical reality, leaving a gap in current theory. Here we extend inclusive fitness theory beyond threshold rules to explain, and predict, the co-evolution of cooperation and conflict within the same interaction, as often observed in nature. Our mathematical approach starts with the ’relatedness ratio’ (R) that has been used informally by previous authors in similar contexts. Using the optimization techniques of differential calculus, we formalize for the first time the intuitions expressed by previous authors about R as a predictor of genetic interests, and prove that R values determine the relative values of quantitative trait optima for different evolving actors influencing the same interaction. Our results show that both cooperation and conflict are likely to evolve in the same interaction under specified conditions, and that genetic conflict is expected as a long-term evolutionary outcome, even between initially cooperating entities. This framework is applicable to interactions among organisms or among sub-elements within an organism, and also to the evolutionary transitions in individuality that produce new kinds of individual.

detail.abstract:
Omai’s August 2026 preliminary economic assessment (PEA) describes a proposed large-scale redevelop‐
ment of a former producing gold district in Guyana. It combines the Wenot open pit and Gilt underground de‐
posit around a 25,000-tonne-per-day carbon-in-leach plant. The company projects 6.327 million payable
ounces over 18 operating years, an after-tax net present value (NPV) of US$3.966 billion at a 5% discount
rate, a 24% after-tax internal rate of return (IRR), and US$1.427 billion in initial capital at an assumed
US$3,600/oz gold price. These are modeled results, not a production forecast with reserve-level confid‐
ence. The PEA explicitly incorporates Inferred Mineral Resources and does not establish a Mineral Reserve.
[S01, pp. 1-5] [S05]
The proposed project has three connected characteristics. First, its physical scale is substantial. The mining
schedule includes 134.1 million tonnes of material from Wenot at 1.08 g/t gold and 22.6 million tonnes from
Gilt at 2.98 g/t. The combined plan reports 156.67 million tonnes of mineralized feed and 788.43 million
tonnes of waste. Second, the schedule depends on two distinct mining systems, high-volume surface mining
and selective underground production, each with different geotechnical, equipment, staffing, ventilation, and
cost exposures. Third, the project uses a brownfield setting with roads, prior workings, a pre-existing tailings
system, and an airstrip, while introducing a much larger new mine footprint and a substantial capital pro‐
gram. [S01, pp. 2-4, 9-13]
The resource inventory provides geological potential but also defines the central qualification.

title: Does Fertility Stabilize At Low Levels? Evidence from Period, Cohort, and Subnational Data
affiliations: Research Institute for Compassionate Economics (r.i.c.e.), University of Texas at Austin, University of Texas at Austin and Hunter College (CUNY)

detail.title: Does Fertility Stabilize At Low Levels? Evidence from Period, Cohort, and Subnational Data
detail.abstract: Many population projections used by international and government agencies assume that, in today's low-fertility societies, future fertility rates will stop declining and roughly stabilize. This paper assesses the evidence for an equilibrium point or rebound from low levels. We show that there is no robust evidence for a systematic fertility rebound, or for a stable equilibrium point at any fertility level conventionally assumed. Instead, where and when fertility has fallen low, it has tended to keep falling. This is true across a range of data sources, time periods, and fertility measures: United Nations data on period total fertility rates for all country-years from 1950 to 2023; Human Fertility Database data on completed fertility for cohorts born between 1935 and 1975 in 31 countries; and fertility rates in subnational geographies in Japan, India, and the United States. We reconcile these results with a prior literature that documented fertility reversals among some low-fertility countries in the early 2000s. Our findings provide an empirical basis for re-examining the equilibrium and rebound assumptions embedded in widely used population projections.

detail.abstract:
Guyana’s Global Biodiversity Alliance, or GBA, has moved quickly from a September 2024 political 
commitment to a formal international platform launched in Georgetown in July 2025. The 
Georgetown Declaration defines the Alliance as open, voluntary, adaptive and non-binding. Its 
stated purposes are to raise awareness, increase ambition and expand access to finance while 
complementing the Convention on Biological Diversity rather than replacing it. [S1][S2]
The Alliance enters its next phase from a position of visible diplomatic reach. On 24 September 
2026, Guyana’s President stated at the United Nations General Assembly that the GBA had 
expanded from 17 to 138 members and that a second conference in October 2026 would begin 
mobilising resources and partnerships. Earlier official announcements documented the World Bank’s 
International Development Association as a formal partner in April 2026 and the United Nations as 
the 97th member in May 2026. [S3][S4][S5]
The central issue is now execution. Membership growth creates reach, but membership alone does 
not prove conservation outcomes, finance mobilisation, improved ecological condition or equitable 
benefit sharing. The revised 2030 Action Plan provides a detailed roadmap organised around six 
pillars: implementation of the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, integration of 
biodiversity into planning, innovative finance, Indigenous and local community leadership, 
monitoring and accountability, and public awareness.

affiliations: Georgetown University Law Center

detail.abstract: This Paper defines performance-based AI governance, a regulatory model that evaluates and permits AI systems based on their technical performance-such as accuracy, fairness, or robustness-rather than their institutional purpose or normative legitimacy. The Paper argues against this model, finding that this regulatory orientation suffers from structural problems: it relies on metrics that rapidly lose relevance, reframes valueladen policy questions as technical ones, and shifts regulatory power to industry actors, eroding democratic oversight in the process. The Paper uses case studies to explore performance-based AI governance: the bans on facial recognition use by law enforcement; the European Union's AI Act; and Large Language Model benchmarks. Two alternatives are offered: governing on principle (identifying and basing regulation on durable societal principles, values and rights), and considering technical invariants of the AI systems. In this vein, the Paper introduces the concept of AI Independence, based on software independence in the voting realm, as a design constraint for important systems so that they do not rely on AI.

detail.abstract:
The energy transition is often presented as a choice between technologies. For decision makers, the more consequential 
choice is how to provide reliable energy service, who finances the infrastructure, who bears the downside risks and how 
the benefits are distributed. A low price for generation does not establish a low delivered cost. A public subsidy does not 
eliminate a cost. An emissions reduction claim does not establish that households have dependable access.
The 2026 evidence strengthens the case for a service-first approach. Global energy investment is estimated at USD 3.4 
trillion in 2026, with about USD 2.2 trillion directed to renewables, nuclear, grids, storage, low-emissions fuels, efficiency 
and electrification [1]. Yet the capital mix is only one part of the transition. IEA estimates that annual grid investment 
must rise by roughly 50% from around USD 400 billion by 2030 to meet expected electricity demand [4]. The gap between 
generation spending and network spending explains why low-cost generation does not automatically produce low-cost, 
reliable electricity at the meter.
The distribution problem is equally material. Tracking SDG7 reports 655 million people without electricity access, 
including more than 560 million in Sub-Saharan Africa [6]. At the same time, the World Bank reports that only about 40% 
of utilities in its developing-country sample cover operating and debt-service costs [14]. A transition that expands 
generation while weakening the utility, raising arrears or leaving vulnerable customers unable to use the service is 
incomplete.

title: From Marriage to Artificial Intimacy: Autonomy, Singleness and the Transformation of Human Relationships
affiliations: Brazilian Bar Association - Primary São Paulo Section / Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil - Seção de São Paulo

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Family law across jurisdictions allocates protection, decisional authority, and economic security primarily through a single proxy: romantic-dyadic status, whether marital, registered, or de facto. This article asks what happens to that architecture as long-term singleness becomes a stable demographic category rather than a transitional stage, and as AI companion systems increasingly perform some of the psychological functions that romantic partnership once supplied without ever becoming legally cognizable as a relationship. Using doctrinal and comparative analysis across the United States (federal marital-status-contingent law and Colorado's Designated Beneficiary Agreement Act), the United Kingdom (stalled cohabitation reform), Brazil (the STJ's anaparental-family jurisprudence), South Korea (the 2023 Act on the Prevention and Management of Solitary Deaths), Japan (an administrative, non-legal response to kodokushi), and the European Union (Italy's Garante enforcement action against the AI companion Replika), the article identifies what it calls the reciprocity requirement: every mechanism that has successfully decoupled legal protection from marriagedesignated-beneficiary statutes, functional-family doctrine, cohabitation reform proposals-still requires a second human party capable of bearing reciprocal legal obligations. AI companionship cannot satisfy that requirement, because it has no legal personality, cannot be sued, cannot inherit obligations, and cannot serve as a decisional surrogate under existing capacity doctrine. The article argues that the growth of stable singleness and the growth of AI companionship, taken together, are producing a widening designee gap between people's actual relational infrastructure and the categories the law uses to allocate protection. It proposes the Chosen Designee Recognition Standard, a modest, registration-based mechanism that decouples selected designee functions from any pre-existing relationship category, while foreclosing any private-ordering attempt to designate an AI system itself as a legal decision-maker or fiduciary.

title: Measuring Dynastic Power: Political Kinship Networks and Local Governance in the Philippines
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Unaffiliated Author, Unaffiliated Author, Unaffiliated Author, Unaffiliated Author and Unaffiliated Author

detail.title: Measuring Dynastic Power: Political Kinship Networks and Local Governance in the Philippines

detail.abstract: We introduce a network-based framework for characterizing political kinship structures. Using Philippine data, we reconstruct co-incumbency kinship networks among local officials across nine election cycles (2001-2025). Surname matching recovers paternal ties, while middle-name matching additionally recovers maternal and marital ties. We develop measures for three features of dynastic structure: the concentration of incumbency among clans, the degree of overlap between the dominant clan and leading party, and inequality in connectedness within kinship networks. Greater dynastic concentration is associated with dimmer night-time lights, weaker own-source revenue mobilization, and lower local-government competitiveness. Greater overlap between the largest clan and plurality party is also associated with worse municipal competitiveness, conditional on the other structural measures and in specifications with province fixed effects. Evidence that network structure matters beyond dynastic presence is strongest for government competitiveness and weaker for development and fiscal outcomes. Results are robust to alternative kinship definitions and samples.

title: What do Standard Measures of Rental Affordability Reveal? A Longitudinal Analysis from 1960-2024
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA), University of California, Irvine - Department of Planning, Policy and Design, University of California, Irvine School of Law and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: What do Standard Measures of Rental Affordability Reveal? A Longitudinal Analysis from 1960-2024

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Affordability is the most salient housing policy issue in the United States. It is also conceptually elusive. The most cited metrics, such as rent burden and rent-to-income ratio, collapse disparate processes into a single outcome, obscuring substantial heterogeneity across people and places. Moreover, these measures are only weakly correlated with rents, meaning that famously expensive metros like San Francisco and San Jose appear just as affordable as Cleveland and Minneapolis. In this article, we assess the analytical value of conventional rental affordability measures by decomposing them into their underlying drivers over time. Using data from 1960 to 2024, we analyze how changes in the renter population, household composition, rents, incomes, and housing supply elasticity across urban areas relate to rental affordability. We focus on rental affordability because most low-income households are renters, and because renters are more vulnerable to eviction and homelessness. Affordability has worsened over the last six decades, primarily because of rent increases. We find that fluctuations in incomes play a large and underappreciated role in changing affordability metrics over shorter time periods. Rents have diverged across metro areas without a corresponding divergence in measured affordability. Housing supply elasticity is more strongly correlated with rents than with rent burdens, suggesting that people adjust to higher rents and lower incomes along multiple non-financial margins. We examine three of these; living with parents, overcrowding, and migration, and find they connect more strongly to rents than to affordability measures. Our findings highlight the importance of multiple measures of housing market problems.

detail.abstract:
This paper presents the PSI Field Lab as a two-stage research methodology for documenting, synchronizing, auditing, and reviewing multimodal field observations in anomalous and paranormal research contexts. Stage I is a synthetic calibration demonstration. Its records were generated computationally with a fixed seed and a documented experimental structure designed to resemble the derived data that a future field study could produce. It tests data integration, quality gates, transparent scoring, unsupervised anomaly detection, site-level repeatability, sensitivity analysis, constrained language-model review, and run-level audit packaging. It does not contain real sensor recordings or evidence about paranormal phenomena.
Stage II is a prospective real-data protocol. It specifies how physiological, EEG, motion, video, audio, environmental, and contextual records would be collected using a Muse 2 headset, a Polar heart-rate system capable of exporting beat-to-beat intervals, body cameras, an independent audio recorder, and environmental instruments. It defines clock synchronization, immutable raw-data retention, transformation into a common ten-second analytical schema, matched target and control sessions, randomized order, blinded review, quality gates, exclusions, and repetition requirements.
Across both stages, the system is restricted to documentation and evidence triage. A high score means unusual under recorded conditions, not paranormal. The methodological contribution is a traceable bridge from synthetic software calibration to preregistered field acquisition, with observation, interpretation, explanation, and causal claims kept separate.

title: Chapter -13 "Robotics in Agriculture Waste Recycling: Intelligent Automation, AI-Driven Sorting and Circular Bioeconomy"

detail.abstract: The recycling of agricultural waste is gaining momentum from traditional, autonomous, laborintensive approaches to robotic, intelligent and circular bio economy-based systems. The use of Artificial Intelligence, robotic manipulators, Internet of Things, computer vision, edge computing, autonomous mobile robots, machine learning, digital twins and intelligent sensing allows for the automated gathering, sorting, transport, processing and conversion of agricultural residues into added-value resources. In this chapter, the new development of using robotics for transforming the crop residues, livestock waste, food-processing by products and biomass into compost, biofertilizers, bio char, animal feeds and bio-based materials. Autonomous vehicles, robotic arms and AI-powered computer vision techniques enable selective picking, segregation, handling and movement of the agricultural waste with reduced human intervention. Edge AI and sensor networks powered by the IoT can help with real-time monitoring of moisture, temperature, biomass quality and processing conditions, while a digital-twin can support optimization of recycling workflows and forecasting of system performance. The advantages of advanced methods such as reinforcement learning, machine vision, collaborative robots, swarm robotics, predictive maintenance and cloud-edge robotics are added to ensure operational efficiency and adaptability. A circular utilization system for agricultural wastes is proposed that can be realized by the integration of waste detection, robotic collection, resource recovery, intelligent sorting, preprocessing, quality assessment and circular utilization in a closed-loop system. The new paradigm of robotics can decrease the amount of open field burning, reduce the cost of waste management, enhance resource recovery, decrease greenhouse-gas emissions and reinforce precision agriculture and sustainable circular farming. The future will see an increase in the development of energy-efficient autonomous robots, multimodal AI, human-robot collaboration, decentralized edge intelligence and scalable Agriculture 5.0 ecosystems.

title: Privacy-Preserving Semantic Deconfliction in Partitioned High-Assurance Environments Architectural Framework, Operational Invariants, and Cross-Border Information Sharing Across Sovereign Legal Boundaries

detail.abstract:
Cross-institutional financial crime intelligence remains structurally paralyzed by the tension between statutory confidentiality (banking secrecy, GDPR, anti-tipping-off provisions) and investigative correlation requirements. Over 90% of actionable intelligence resides in unstructured narrative observations that cannot be shared across sovereign boundaries. Existing paradigms—deterministic hashing (Private Set Intersection), cloud-hosted Trusted Execution Environments, and multi-round Secure Multi-Party Computation—fail to simultaneously satisfy the operational invariants of systemically important institutions: unprivileged local execution, sub-10 ms latency on commodity CPUs, zero cloud dependency, and semantic resolution over free text.
We formalize sovereign semantic deconfliction as a zero-knowledge relation ℛθ enabling independent institutions to verify whether private narrative dossiers share semantic congruence above a calibrated threshold θ without disclosing underlying text. The architecture operates strictly within unprivileged user space (Ring 3, <150 MB RAM, zero kernel extensions). We evaluate proof artifacts against GDPR Recital 26 criteria for non-personal data under the CJEU Breyer doctrine, report empirical benchmarks across an exhaustive all-pairs evaluation matrix of ≈ 106 pairwise determinations (sub-10 ms ingestion latency, empirical false-positive rate bounded at FPR < 3.0 × 10-6 at 95% confidence on baseline commercial traffic), and present an air-gapped retrospective audit methodology enabling supervisory committees to verify protocol precision on historical archives without production exposure.

detail.abstract: Transfer and degree-review decisions routinely rely on grades awarded elsewhere. This paper argues that grades travel farther than the evidence needed to interpret them. Argument-based validity theory holds that validating an interpretation of a result does not validate every use of it, and recent work on assessment in an era of generative AI develops that reasoning for the institution that awards a grade. Historical accounts show how grades became portable by trading local context for forms strangers could read, while credit made courses countable across institutions. Generative AI widens the conditions under which familiar assignments can be completed without making those conditions visible, and courses can now differ in which capability their grades are designed to represent. The paper proposes a division of responsibility. The receiving institution owns the new use and must justify it. The sending institution should state the claim its course grade was designed to support and the AI conditions relevant to that claim. The evidence required should rise with the capability claim the receiving program must make. Before asking a student for more, the program should name that claim and the gap in the record.

title: Trust and Transparency in Online Recruitment: An Exploratory Study of Job Seekers' Perceptions and Experiences in India
affiliations: Independent Researcher

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this study.

detail.abstract: Online recruitment platforms have changed how job seekers access employment opportunities and how employers reach potential applicants. Digital recruitment expands access to vacancies but requires applicants to assess employers and opportunities using limited information presented online. This raises questions concerning trust, transparency, employer verification and platform accountability. This exploratory study examines how job seekers in India perceive suspicious or insufficiently transparent recruitment content and how such experiences relate to trust and expectations regarding platform responsibility. Primary data were collected through an anonymous online survey. An eight-response pilot was conducted before the main survey, and the pilot responses were excluded from the final dataset. The final survey generated 31 valid responses. The study uses descriptive analysis of closed-ended responses and limited qualitative analysis of open-ended responses, supplemented by academic literature and institutional reports. Twenty respondents (64.5%) reported that they or someone they knew had been affected by such recruitment content, while 12 (38.7%) reported direct impact. Commonly reported indicators included requests for payment, missing company information and the absence of an official website. The findings are consistent with information-asymmetry and signalling perspectives and indicate that respondents reported using observable information when evaluating unfamiliar recruitment opportunities. The findings identify areas for further research concerning employer verification, platform transparency, reporting mechanisms and the distribution of responsibility for safer online recruitment.

title: Mercury and Gold Mining in the Amazon
affiliations: Lewis & Clark Law School - Paul L Boley Law Library, The Nature Conservancy and Universidad del Pacifico

detail.title: Mercury and Gold Mining in the Amazon

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Funding for this paper was provided by The Nature Conservancy.

contentType.other: Selected for publication; editing in process

detail.abstract:
This Article addresses one of environmental law’s most daunting challenges: mercury-based gold mining. Across the tropics, such activity threatens human health, ecosystems, and community wellbeing; the problem is nowhere more serious than in the Amazon Basin. Through an examination of five Amazonian countries, we showcase both the potential and limits of environmental law in the world’s most biodiverse region. 

Recognizing the problem of mercury contamination from gold mining and other sources, the global community in 2013 adopted the Minamata Convention. Along with more than 150 others, the five countries studied herein are Parties. Although the treaty does not prescribe a strict set of laws or policies, it requires meaningful steps to reduce mercury emissions from artisanal and small-scale gold mining. 

By documenting approaches in five hot-spot jurisdictions, this Article informs governmental decision-making vis-à-vis mercury-based gold mining. Through our analysis, we present the key elements of effective law and policy, including controls on mercury imports and sales; gold-sector formalization; enforcement, penalties, and restoration; respect for the rights of Indigenous peoples and local communities; and cross-border cooperation.

detail.abstract: We report new data on forecasts, emotional arousal, and risk preferences in experimental asset markets with a constant fundamental value (CFV). Large, sustained bubbles which crash near the terminal value are common, even with higher stakes and experienced participants. Lagged returns and forecasts best predict next-period returns. Electrodermal activity (EDA) measuring arousal adds little. However, EDA is associated with earnings: High earners are most aroused before a crash, while low earners react afterward. Forecasts fail rationality tests yet fit adaptive models. Risk preferences show no association with returns, suggesting bubbles reflect beliefs, not risk tolerance.

title: Is AI Labor-Augmenting? Evidence from Korean Firms

detail.abstract: Does Artificial Intelligence (AI) adoption bias technological change toward labor? We estimate the effect of AI adoption on labor-augmenting and Hicks-neutral productivity for Korean firms from 2017 to 2024. AI adoption raises labor-augmenting productivity by 6.1% and leaves Hicks-neutral productivity indistinguishable from zero, and the adoption effect on output is 1.6%. Manufacturing carries twice the laboraugmenting coefficient of information and communication (ICT). The labor efficiency comes through production processes in manufacturing and through product and service development in ICT. We recover firm markups and find no evidence that AI adoption raises them.

title: Digital Literacy and Access to Public Services among Older Immigrants in the United States Language Dependency Administrative Autonomy and Institutional Design
affiliations: Independent Researcher and Independent Researcher

detail.title: Digital Literacy and Access to Public Services among Older Immigrants in the United States Language Dependency Administrative Autonomy and Institutional Design

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no competing interests.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required because this study did not involve human participants or the collection of original participant data. The research is based on a structured qualitative review of published and institutional sources.

detail.abstract: Public services in the United States increasingly require residents to create accounts, verify identity, upload records, read automated notices, and preserve digital evidence of completed transactions. These requirements can increase convenience while placing a distinctive burden on older immigrants. Age-related differences in technology experience intersect with limited English proficiency, unfamiliar administrative categories, disability, income constraints, and concern about fraud or surveillance. This article examines that intersection through a structured qualitative review of scholarship on digital inequality, aging, immigrant information practices, language access, and public-service delivery. It argues that access should not be measured by connectivity or portal availability alone. A service is accessible only when a person can identify the correct channel, understand its purpose, perform the required transaction, verify the result, and recover from an error without surrendering control over private information. The article develops a sixstage Supported Digital Autonomy Model comprising entry, orientation, interpretation, execution, verification, and recovery. It also distinguishes supportive mediation from administrative dependency. Family members and community organizations often make services usable, yet repeated reliance on intermediaries can weaken privacy, informed choice, and the ability to act when a trusted helper is unavailable. The analysis identifies design principles for agencies, libraries, aging-service organizations, health systems, and community providers. These principles include multilingual task design, assisted pathways, low-risk practice, explicit consent, secure credential handling, alternative channels, and evaluation based on successful and recoverable transactions. The central conclusion is that digital literacy is not solely an individual attribute. It is a relational capacity produced by users, interfaces, institutions, and support networks. Public agencies should therefore treat supported digital autonomy as a service obligation rather than as a remedial program for people who fail to adapt.

detail.abstract: This study examines whether firm-specific trading halts generate short-selling spillovers among economically related firms. Using NYSE and AMEX trading halts from 2005-2006 and transaction-level short-sale data from the Regulation SHO period, we identify related firms based on industry affiliation and market-based characteristics and examine short-selling activity surrounding trading halts. Short-selling activity generally declines in the five-day windows preceding and following a halt, while relative short selling does not change significantly. Intraday analysis likewise provides little evidence of increased short selling in related firms while the halted security is unavailable for trading. Regression and portfolio analyses further show that pre-halt abnormal short selling does not predict subsequent returns. Overall, the findings indicate that trading restrictions on an affected security do not induce substantial migration of short-selling activity to economically related firms, distinguishing information spillovers across related securities from corresponding spillovers in trading activity.

detail.abstract: The impact of climate risk in credit lending is often basic or entirely omitted; the increasing frequency and severity of extreme weather events across the globe are straining this simplification, especially in highly affected sectors such as agriculture. With the institutional implementation of credit risk frameworks such as the Vasicek Credit Risk model, the question of the feasibility and efficacy of adjusting these models to incorporate climate risk is becoming an increasingly prevalent issue in risk management. By using non-performing loan (NPL) data to stand as an observable proxy for loan default probability across Spain, Turkey, and Serbia during the 2022 compound hot-dry event, this paper cross-regime tests the Bank for International Settlements (BIS) climate-extended Vasicek model by comparing baseline NPL rates excluding and then including an added climate component (â = 0 & â > 0) to the model. Having achieved a mean absolute error (MAE) of 3.5641% and root mean square error (RMSE) of 3.6751% the model has proven to be statistically stable in macroeconomic forecasting while crucially having a low variance, signifying that its predictive errors are uniformly distributed rather than having single extreme outliers for the climate event.

detail.abstract: When a practitioner develops a conceptual framework through sustained dialogue with a large language model, what the practitioner remembers building and what the transcript shows can diverge. This paper double-codes every concept unit (N = 107) across eight archived dialogues (84 turns, June 2025 to January 2026) between an independent AI consultant and restaurant owner-operator and Google Gemini, using a five-category origin codebook applied by two independent large-language-model coders and adjudicated where they disagreed (29 of 107 units; exact agreement .73; Cohen's kappa = .63 on the five-category scheme, .58 collapsed to three). The resulting distribution of 15 user-originated, 35 user-seed/model-elaborated, 3 co-constructed, 18 model-originated-and-adopted, and 36 model-originated-and-unused units, against a corrected model-to-user character ratio of 13.98 to 1, shows that the model originated roughly half of all coded units (50.5 percent, whether or not the practitioner used them). A case study of the practitioner's four-book series makes the mechanism concrete: the practitioner asked the model to recall prior themes from its memory of earlier sessions; the model retrieved and sequenced them, including the governing curriculum sentence the practitioner later treated as their own; the practitioner's only substantive input was a one-item correction. No existing authorship-disclosure framework has a category for this pattern, which differs from AI ghostwriting, sycophancy, and cryptomnesia. The paper is reflexive on two fronts: the researcher is the coded subject, and this manuscript was drafted with heavy AI assistance. It closes with a reusable codebook, a disclosure-paragraph template, and a call for replication with human coders.

detail.abstract: Terahertz (THz) technology, operating in the electromagnetic spectrum between microwaves and infrared light (0.1-10 THz), has transitioned from a fundamental physics curiosity to a transformative technology with broad industrial and scientific applications. Historically hindered by the "Terahertz Gap"-the lack of efficient, compact sources and detectors-recent advancements in photonics, semiconductor physics, and metamaterials have propelled THz systems into practical viability. This paper provides a comprehensive review of terahertz technology, detailing its fundamental properties, including non-ionizing radiation and spectral fingerprinting. We explore its critical applications across security screening, non-destructive testing, medical imaging, and next-generation 6G communications. Finally, we discuss the current technical challenges, such as atmospheric attenuation, and outline future research directions, highlighting the integration of artificial intelligence and nanomaterials in advancing THz systems.

detail.abstract: China's economic development challenges simple accounts linking capitalism, economic modernization, and liberal democracy. This paper examines what the Chinese experience reveals about the institutional conditions under which capitalism can generate and sustain economic growth without liberal-democratic convergence. Drawing on research on institutions, democracy and growth, varieties of capitalism, and China's economic reforms, it organizes the institutional foundations of capitalist development around five functions: appropriation, coordination, experimentation, reallocation, and adaptation. China has performed these functions through a distinctive combination of markets, private enterprise, state coordination, decentralized initiative, policy experimentation, and centralized political authority. These mechanisms supported rapid catch-up while also generating distortions in resource allocation, competition, innovation, and policy learning. Their economic significance changes, however, as growth becomes more dependent on productivity, innovation, decentralized information, and selection among uncertain projects. Developments since 2012 further suggest that institutional adaptation need not preserve the mechanisms through which earlier adaptation occurred: greater central strategic direction has altered the balance between coordination, decentralized initiative, and experimentation. The paper therefore identifies institutional adaptability-the capacity to modify how key economic functions are performed as economic conditions change-as central to the sustainability question. China demonstrates that extensive capitalist development and substantial institutional adaptation can occur without liberaldemocratic convergence, while leaving unresolved whether a more centrally steered form of adaptation can sustain productivity growth at higher levels of technological development.

title: When One Window Fits None: Volatility Recency, Correlation Depth, and the Cost of a Common Covariance History

detail.abstract: Volatility and correlation need not benefit from the same amount of historical information. We treat their history lengths as separate empirical quantities and measure the cost of forcing them to coincide. Using daily U.S. equity returns, we first hold information quantity fixed while moving observations further into the past. An equally sized historical block becomes poorly representative of current volatility sooner than it becomes poorly representative of current correlation. We then repeat the same correlation-history comparison as the number of assets rises through fifty nested security sequences. The benefit of deeper correlation history increases at every dimension step, while the penalties associated with long volatility histories remain broadly unchanged. Across two out-of-sample evaluation periods using the same fixed security population, estimators constrained to one history length choose substantially longer histories in the first period. The difference coincides with a much larger cost from using long volatility histories in the second period, even though deeper correlation history remains highly valuable there. A pair of history lengths chosen from the first period continues to improve covariance forecasts when carried into the second, including against a one-decay EWMA selected using the later evaluations. Separating aggregate volatility magnitude from relative cross-sectional dispersion shows that the preference for recent volatility information is not confined to the market-wide level. In the second evaluation period, separate histories do not lower realised global minimum-variance portfolio variance, while deeper correlation history reduces turnover increasingly as the number of assets grows. A common covariance history is therefore a compromise between estimation problems with different responses to information age and dimension, rather than a measure of market memory.

detail.abstract: The processes of economic decision making and market behavior are based on the cognitive function of people. Nevertheless, decision making processes are different at various stages of human development and adolescents demonstrate increased propensity to impulsive behavior as opposed to children and adults. Neuroeconomic theory helps to understand how the brain works in the process of choosing. The imbalance between developing socio-emotional and prefrontal control systems of human brain increases the reward sensitivity. According to Telzer (2016), the increased sensitivity to dopamine does not always lead to risky behavior. "Family and environmental contexts can change the significance and outcomes of VS activity to redirect reward sensitivity in adolescents away from risk taking and toward prosocial and healthy behaviors." Therefore, it is shown that environmental cues and structural limits can affect the behavior of adolescents and influence their ability to choose before the prefrontal system reaches full maturity.

detail.abstract: When should the holder of an American put exercise early if volatility is rough? With time to maturity θ, the BlackScholes exercise boundary sits σ θ ln(1/θ) below the strike in log terms. We show that under rough volatility the boundary is set by the skewness of short-horizon returns. With negative correlation between price and volatility shocks, the upside tail that gives waiting its value is thin, so exercise becomes optimal closer to the strike. In a Gaussian rough volatility model we prove that the distance of the European indierence boundary from the strike is 1 + 1 2 ρηD H θ H ln(1/θ) times its BlackScholes value, where ρ is the spot-volatility correlation, η the volatility of volatility and H the Hurst parameter. The American boundary obeys the same law under a stated hypothesis on an occupation time. With equity-like parameters the European boundary distance is 10% to 18% below its BlackScholes value from a few trading days to a few seconds before expiry. The boundary can also be read o the short-dated smile.

title: Moore's Law Moves to Software: Four Carriers of the AI Exponential and the Human in the Loop as its Pace
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests.

detail.abstract: Exponential growth in computing has been read off the transistor count since 1965. This paper argues that the exponent has changed carrier. Four carriers are distinguished, hardware, resources, algorithms and self-learning, each with its own key performance indicator (KPI) and doubling time from public data. Computations per dollar doubled every 19 months for 84 years and every two to three years since 2005. Frontier training compute doubles every five months, and the capital expenditure of the four largest cloud providers every 17 months. The compute required for a fixed capability halves every five months, and the interval between frontier language-model releases halves every 14 months, from 108 days in 2020 to three days in 2026, across 217 releases from 14 labs. Underneath the four runs a shift from material to logical, and from space to time: Moore's law on silicon measured how many transistors fit on a chip; in software it measures how fast the improvement loop turns. The paper defines the software singularity as the cycle time of that loop reaching zero, and shows that once both sides of the loop are software, the only step that takes time is evaluation. Where the outcome has a test, the human can step out; where it is a judgment, only a human can supply the target. The human in the loop is therefore safeguard and limit at once, the trade-off the public debate argues around without naming; the debate is mapped in three positions. A KPI set in three dimensions, pace, reach and position, is proposed to measure the path, with a first reading to 2030.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the welfare effects of trade transparency in a dynamic adverse-selection market where buyers can acquire costly, noisy private signals about seller quality. Under transparency, buyers observe whether the seller traded in the previous period but not transaction prices. This public history creates two competing forces. A learning effect allows later buyers to economize on costly private information acquisition, but may also discourage private learning that would otherwise support efficient trade. A strategic distortion effect arises because sellers alter current trading decisions to influence future beliefs. The form of this distortion depends on whether trade with the low-quality seller is efficient: transparency can induce overtrading when such trade is inefficient and undertrading when it is efficient. Transparency raises welfare when the informational gains and acquisition-cost savings from public learning dominate these distortions, but lowers welfare when reduced information acquisition and distorted trade generate sufficiently large allocative losses.

detail.abstract: Prompt recipes for learning a new field with AI assistance already converge on a two-move pattern: ask the model to map a field's structure, then ask it to compress the field to its highest-leverage fraction. This practitioner note, built from one author's archived dialogue with an AI system in November 2025, argues that a third move, usually left implicit, should be made explicit and placed first: before mapping a field, the learner should be asked to surface and consciously suspend what they already believe they know, because unexamined prior habits, especially an experienced practitioner's own domain routines, can distort how AI-generated structure and compressed content are absorbed. The Map-Core-Link portion of the resulting four-step sequence is shown operating within the same dialogue across two tracks, learning about AI itself and using AI to learn an unrelated field; the Unlearn step itself is argued for on track-agnostic grounds and is not separately demonstrated on each track. The note states plainly what it does not claim: the Map-Core-Link mechanism is documented prior art in prompt-recipe grey literature and in a peer-reviewed multi-agent system, and one of the dialogue's own turns, which supplied the initial three-step template, was pasted in by the author from a separate AI session and is credited as such rather than as original composition. The note closes with a proposed, unexecuted, within-person evaluation design for testing whether the explicit Unlearn step adds measurable value over skipping directly to Map. No data were collected for this paper.

title: The ESG-Profitability Nexus in the Asia-Pacific Region: An Econometric Analysis of the Value Multiplier Effect

detail.abstract: The traditional finance framework considers ESG spending as a distraction that lowers profit margins of firms. The present work attempts to explore the relationship between Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG) performance and financial returns and unravel how ESG performance is empirically associated with financial returns in the Asia-Pacific (APAC) region. For this purpose, a panel data set of 1,097 firm-years across 220 listed firms in 11 APAC countries (2020-2024) is used in this work. The relationships have been tested through six regression models, along with descriptive statistics and correlation analysis. Our analysis finds the real but small positive correlation between composite ESG score and profitability (r =0.088 with ROE, r = 0.130 with ROA). The relationship is mainly due to the Governance and Environmental aspects of ESG performance while there is no short-run effect of Social spending. This correlation is nonlinear, and firms achieving 75 score or more earn 7.8% more ROE compared to firms with less than 75 ESG score (p=0.007). However, in terms of country context, growing markets like Indonesia and India have higher ROEs although having lower ESG scores than developed countries such as Japan and Australia. Most importantly, once the revenue, cost, and company size are considered in our analysis via Panel Fixed Effect model, the coefficient of ESG becomes statistically insignificant, suggesting that ESG plays its role as an input into the firm's performance rather than an independent factor. In sum, the investment in ESG in APAC is justified but only as an input into firm's performance.

detail.abstract: Complex financial decisions often move across financial planners, lawyers, tax professionals, investment professionals, insurance specialists, and family-office staff. Existing standards already require context, goals, assumptions, rationale, implementation responsibilities, and review, while decision records and structured handoffs are established in adjacent fields. The empirical question is whether a professional handoff can be evaluated by how accurately the receiving specialist reconstructs the originating decision problem, and whether that reconstruction can be improved beyond competent ordinary practice without disproportionate information burden. This pre-field synthetic-case protocol compares a competent conventional brief, a high-quality generic decision record, and an interface-focused handoff against a frozen source case. It further specifies component-removal experiments, context-compression experiments, and a longitudinal reopening study. No participants have been recruited, no empirical results are reported, and no client or family data are used.

title: The Honesty Harness: Expert-Directed, AI-Executed Empirical Research with Frozen Criteria and Asymmetric Verdicts

detail.abstract: By 2026, a domain expert with no programming skill can direct AI agents through an entire empirical research cycle. This delegation loses the expert's scientific authority through four channels: metric pivoting, cheap over-exploration, post-hoc pre-registration prose, and sign-off on conclusions the expert never read at implementation level (preregistration §2). This paper specifies the Honesty Harness, an operational protocol of eight principles — separation of powers, verifiable pre-registration, bias controls as artifacts, multi-level validation, adversarial audit, full traceability, complete publication, bounded scope — in which the agent executes everything and the control lives in cryptographic seals and asymmetric verdicts [4]. Two demonstrations are reported. First, a completed case study in a maximum-temptation domain (retail crypto-perpetuals trading, real money), where each principle's counterfactual is documented from primary artifacts: among them, an annotated metric pivot, the withdrawal of an over-broad cost claim, and an in-sample/out-of-sample selection correlation of +0.598 versus −0.054 that the frozen holdouts made visible (Supplementary Table S1) [2]. Second, a pre-registered, mechanically blinded positive-result challenge: over 600 synthetic worlds, the double-gate verdict detected a planted in-family signal at twice trading costs in 19/20 worlds (Wilson 95% [76%, 99%]), held false positives at 24/500 = 4.80% [3.25%, 7.04%] against a nominal α = 5% (point estimate below α; not conclusive at 95%), and declined an out-of-family signal in 20/20 worlds (S3, §10). Limits are stated up front, including a false-positive rate above its pre-registered expectation band and the protocol's dependence on the expert's own honesty. All materials are public: evidence archive, protocol, and reusable toolkit (DOIs 10.5281/zenodo.21229492, 10.5281/zenodo.21838807, 10.5281/zenodo.22846067).

detail.abstract: How do investors value artificial intelligence (AI) for the firms that run the trading and post trade infrastructure of financial markets? We examine the stock-price reactions of 40 listed firms to 13 frontier AI releases between November 2022 and June 2026. The sample includes 22 exchange and clearing groups in 17 markets, 8 electronic trading and execution platforms, and 10 financial information and analytics providers. For each release, we measure disruption intensity by the abnormal underperformance of the software sector and relate firm-level abnormal returns to it. Inference relies on Kolari-Pynnönen-adjusted tests, event-clustered standard errors, a wild cluster bootstrap, and a placebo distribution of random pseudo-events. Exchange and clearing groups whose revenues come mainly from trading, clearing, and settlement do not respond to disruption intensity (slope -0.05, t = -0.54). Information and analytics providers, by contrast, lose about 0.8 percentage points for each percentage point by which software stocks underperform, and exchange groups with large data businesses (LSEG and Nasdaq) react in the same way. Daily factor regressions show that the exposure of analytics providers to the software factor rose from 0.04 in 2022-2025 to 0.72 in 2026, when agentic AI products for professional workflows appeared, while that of pure infrastructure operators rose only to 0.10. The largest event-window losses were, however, partly reversed within one to two months. We therefore interpret the evidence as a repricing of the risk to information-based revenue, rather than a settled loss of value, that leaves the core functions of matching, clearing, and settlement largely untouched. The results are relevant to exchange strategy, central counterparty (CCP) risk management, and the supervision of AI in capital markets.

detail.abstract: This paper develops an economic growth model with artificial intelligence (AI) and flexible labor supply to analyze how technological accumulation interacts with intertemporal decisions regarding consumption, work, and leisure, thereby contributing to economic growth theory. The central problem is to determine how the accumulation of artificial intelligence and the choice between work and leisure affect the labor supply and long-term economic growth. The study is theoretical and adopts a quantitative methodological approach, using an illustrative calibration based on benchmark parameters from the economics literature. AI is modeled as accumulable software capital produced using finalgood resources; physical capital 𝐾 and the stock of AI 𝐴 are combined into an effective automation capacity Ω(𝐾, 𝐴), which subsequently interacts with human labor 𝐿 through a Constant Elasticity of Substitution (CES) technology to reach equilibrium. The equilibrium is characterized through optimal control, no-arbitrage conditions, reduction of the dynamic system, steady-state analysis, local stability, and comparative statics. In the Cobb-Douglas case, the model exhibits Ramsey-type dynamics with saddle-path stability, where greater efficiency in AI creation 𝜂 , increases the stock of AI software capital 𝐴 ∗ , the stock of physical capital 𝐾 ∗ , steady-state output 𝑌 ∗ , and steady-state consumption 𝐶 ∗ , but does not directly modify steady-state employment 𝐿 ∗ , while a higher valuation of leisure reduces steady-state labor supply. The results show that, under diminishing returns, AI primarily generates permanent level gains, while its growth potential depends on the degree of technological substitution and on households’ endogenous response to the work–leisure choice. In conclusion, AI enables the possibility for an economy to move toward a growth path trajectory.

detail.abstract:
We construct a harmonised longitudinal panel of subjective well-being at local authority level across the United Kingdom, providing 12 annual observations (2011/12-2022/23) for 354 local authorities across four measures: life satisfaction, worthwhile, happiness, and anxiety. The panel addresses three methodological challenges: evolving local government boundaries through population-weighted aggregation for mergers and footprint-preserving combination for county splits; survey measurement uncertainty through inverse-variance weighting derived from published confidence intervals; and the COVID-19 structural break requiring careful temporal specification for policy evaluation. We demonstrate the panel's value through trajectory classification at three hierarchical levels of the ONS 2011 Area Classification. Full-period analysis (2011-2023) shows evaluative wellbeing converging modestly, with diverse metropolitan areas improving from low baselines while anxiety worsens universally. Pre-pandemic sensitivity analysis (2011-2019) reveals these patterns emerged distinctly: broad-based improvement pre-COVID was interrupted by the pandemic, creating differential recovery trajectories that dominate full-period estimates. The substantial clustering of trajectories by area
classification (Kruskal-Wallis p<0.001) validates using these typologies in difference-
in-differences designs, though the COVID structural break requires explicit mod-
elling through year fixed effects or period restrictions. This dataset, with complete
replication code and robustness checks, enables evaluation of post-2020 place-based
interventions while properly accounting for pandemic confounding.

detail.abstract: How do professional forecasters incorporate monetary transmission into their projections? This paper examines the interdependence of Brazilian market expectations using weekly Focus survey medians observed from January 2021 to March 2026, with the main results organized by target years 2022-2026. Bivariate vector autoregressions and Granger tests describe predictive linkages among forecast revisions; multivariate impulse responses characterize the perceived policy response and sectoral adjustment; and initial-to-final forecast comparisons describe cumulative revisions. The reported evidence is more pronounced for inflation and the exchange rate than for aggregate activity and unemployment. Interest-rate and exchange-rate revisions display bidirectional predictive linkages and a correlation of 0.54 for the 2025 target year. Under recursive identification, expected policy rates respond positively to exchange-rate and inflation innovations, whereas responses associated with the output gap and unemployment are less precisely estimated. Sectoral point responses are heterogeneous, although the displayed confidence bands include zero. Expected policy rates are revised upward and unemployment forecasts downward relative to their terminal medians in the reported episodes. These findings distinguish interconnected expectations from accurate calibration of the adjustment path. The paper contributes a joint account of predictive dependence, perceived policy responses, and forecast revision in an emerging-market economy, and develops a complementary framework for investigating time variation in the interest-rate-exchange-rate relationship.

detail.abstract: Using US-wide data from 200M transactions by 11M consumers across 5,000 brands (2020-2022), we document, to the best of our knowledge for the first time, large spatial and industry variation in how consumers maintain the composition of their consumption as inflation rises (inflation resilience). A 1pp increase in local inflation lowers the local high-quality tier spending share by 0.68pp on average but with large variation across counties (SD = 1.6pp) and industries (SD = 1.4pp). Leveraging unique mappings of brands, transactions, and retailers, we show that retail market structure matters: keeping income constant, lower brand variety and higher retail concentration lead to lower resilience at all inflation levels. Contrary to standard economic intuition, consumers are resentful about inflation only if it is paired with quality downgrading, which instead should protect their consumption quantity. We use county-level shifts from Biden to Trump in the 2024 Presidential election as a proxy for consumers' dissatisfaction: it is not higher local inflation but lower inflation resilience conditional on inflation levels that predicts the shifts.

title: CEO Narcissism and Corporate Risk-taking: The Contingent Moderating Role of Governance Mechanisms across Developed and Emerging Markets

detail.abstract: This study examines whether observed CEO narcissism is associated with corporate strategic risk-taking, and whether governance mechanisms attenuate this association differently across developed and emerging markets. To address the theoretical fragmentation surrounding these relationships, we develop the Institutional-Contingent Narcissistic Risk-Governance (ICNRG) framework, which integrates Upper Echelons Theory, Agency Theory, Institutional Theory, and-as a central pillar-the theory of Managerial Discretion. Perceptual data from 452 financial analysts, institutional investors, and fund managers across 14 countries (7 developed, 7 emerging) were analysed using hierarchical moderated regression with heteroskedasticity-robust HC3 standard errors and multi-group structural analyses. Results indicate that CEO narcissism, as observed by external market participants, is positively associated with corporate risk-taking. Governance quality is negatively related to risk in both markets, but a Chow test of coefficient equality (F = 23.30, p < .001) confirms that the strength of these associations differs sharply across institutional contexts: the governance-risk association is markedly stronger in emerging markets than in developed markets. A CFA marker-variable procedure and a comprehensive measurement-model assessment suggest that common method bias does not meaningfully inflate the observed associations. We frame these findings as an advance-rather than a resolution-of the debate on how institutions shape the boundary conditions of executive personality effects. The study offers implications for corporate governance policy in institutionalvoid contexts and outlines a longitudinal agenda for causal identification.

detail.abstract: Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) structures knowledge of equipment failure, yet its conventional risk priority number often remains fixed between review cycles. Predictive maintenance models update estimates from operating signals but frequently provide an alert without an explicit link to failure consequences, detection controls or feasible maintenance actions. This paper develops a conceptual integration of the two approaches for mechanical equipment. A focused, illustrative synthesis of published FMEA, prognostics and maintenance decision research informs a failure-mode-centred framework. A governed register links each failure mode to measurable signals, a prediction horizon, conditional failure probability, severity, detection capability, uncertainty and action constraints. The proposed decision rule retains safety and statutory escalation as hard controls; other modes can be compared using expected consequence and a separately reported confidence assessment. A feedback loop records decisions and observed outcomes to revise mappings and recalibrate models. The analysis explains why a probability forecast cannot simply replace the ordinal occurrence score in a conventional FMEA product, why rare failures and changing operating regimes challenge model reliability, and how human review and data provenance support accountable use. Three comparative tables and two original conceptual figures specify the inputs, interfaces and implementation sequence. The contribution is a testable architecture and validation agenda, rather than an empirically demonstrated improvement. Industrial adoption should be judged against static FMEA and alert-only baselines using prospective, time-aware evaluation of calibration, missed severe failures, maintenance burden and decision lead time.

title: Puroḍāśa and the Meatless Foundations of Vedic Sacrifice Chapter 3 -The Textual Antiquity, Preparation Method, and Ritual Centrality of the Grain Offering

detail.abstract: Modern discourse on Vedic sacrifice has given greater visibility to animal offerings, while the antiquity and ritual centrality of plant- and dairy-based offerings such as grain, flour, dhānā, karambha, apūpa, parivāpa, and payasyā have remained comparatively neglected. This study conducts a context-based examination of Ṛgveda 3.52, Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa 1.6.2.5 and 1.2.3.5–9, Aitareya Brāhmaṇa 2.23, Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 1.5.2, Pāṇini 4.3.148, the Pāraskara Gṛhyasūtra, and the Āpastamba and Baudhāyana Śrautasūtras. The evidence shows that puroḷāśa/puroḍāśa was not merely a later nonviolent reform; from the Ṛgvedic savana through Brāhmaṇical interpretation and the Sūtra-period method of preparation, it remained continuously present, deity-specific, regulated by the number of kapālas, and a principal grain offering sustaining the structure of sacrifice. The Śatapatha narrative of the “fivefold animal” does not make grain a simple negation of the animal; rather, by locating sacrificial potency in rice and barley, it constructs an alternative metaphysics of ritual efficacy. The article concludes that the food system of Vedic sacrifice was diverse from the outset; meatless offerings were not peripheral to it, but foundational.

detail.abstract: Producing countries in Africa, Latin America and Asia increasingly seek to capture the processing of the critical minerals they extract, and a large literature holds that institutional quality is the key to doing so. This monograph tests that proposition. It constructs a producer-side value-chain capture gap, the difference between a country's share of world mine production and its share of world processing, for 15 countries, four minerals (copper, nickel, cobalt and lithium) and the years 2000–2024, using British Geological Survey production statistics, UN Comtrade trade data reconstructed with mirror statistics, and the 2025 revision of the Worldwide Governance Indicators. The gap is large, persistent and concentrated: in 2023 the DR Congo mined 69% of the world's cobalt and refined none of it, Australia mined 44% of the world's lithium, and China refined 80% of the world's cobalt and 47% of its copper. In fixed-effects panel models, institutional readiness does not narrow the gap in any of seven specifications, and an apparent interaction between export bans and readiness disappears under a wild cluster bootstrap. Indonesia's nickel ore bans coincided with a rise in its share of world refining from 1% to 45%, but with a lag and with mixed formal evidence. Capture depends on leverage over supply, persistence of policy and the availability of processor capital rather than on general institutional readiness.

title: Banks versus Private Credit: How Capital Requirements Shape Tailored Lending

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have nothing to declare.

detail.abstract: The rise of private credit is typically attributed either to regulatory arbitrage or to a distinctive lending technology. We argue that the key force is their interaction, as capital requirements affect not only how much banks lend but also the contracts they offer. We formalize this insight in a model where banks and private credit funds compete to finance heterogeneous firms with endogenous contract tailoring. Tailoring relaxes borrowing frictions but makes loans harder to distribute. Capital requirements therefore act as a tax on tailored loans, pushing banks to easily distributable loans and widening private credit's comparative advantage in tailored financing for riskier firms. Consistent with the model, more tailored bank loans are less likely to be distributed, while lower-quality firms sort toward private credit and more tailored financing. Exploiting tighter leverage requirements for systemic banks, we show that affected banks reduce hard-to-distribute tailored contract features, while distribution rises. Quantitatively, this channel is important: absent bank capital requirements, private credit lending falls by 25 percent and bank tailoring more than doubles.

title: The Hours-of-Work Burden Across U.S. States, Nations, and Centuries: An Empirical Application of a Universal Affordability Metric
