detail.abstract: This paper extends the hours-of-work affordability framework developed in the first two parts of this trilogy by applying it empirically across U.S. states, peer nations, and seven centuries of European economic history. The metric expresses economic burden as the number of labor hours required each month to meet a standardized set of basic needs, allowing comparisons that are independent of currency, inflation, and purchasing-power distortions. Using contemporary data for single adults, married couples, and families of four at both minimum and median wages, the analysis shows that no U.S. state permits minimum-wage survival within a standard full-time schedule, and that median-wage households supporting children often require 150-200 hours per month. International comparisons place the United States as a high-burden outlier relative to Europe, Oceania, and Canada, while historical wage and cost series reveal that modern European workers experience the lowest survival burden in recorded history. In contrast, U.S. minimum-wage workers face burdens comparable to those of medieval laborers. These results demonstrate the empirical power of a time-based metric and highlight structural pressures that monetary measures routinely obscure, completing the trilogy by situating modern economic burden within a broad geographic and historical context.

detail.abstract: The universality, ratification, and enforcement of the Singapore Convention on Mediation (SCM) are significantly lower than those of the New York Convention on Arbitration (NYC), due to factors such as the European Union deadlock and fragmented standards for mediators. However, no study has quantitatively examined its relationship with international businesses. Using the World Bank's Business Ready (B-Ready) data, this study finds only weak evidence that ratifying, not merely signing, the SCM is associated with better conditions for international trade. Nevertheless, socioeconomic factors are more strongly associated with international businesses than either convention, and policymakers should prioritise them.

title: Does Free Speech Discipline Corporate Tone Management? Evidence from Anti-SLAPP Laws

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether state-level anti-SLAPP (Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation) laws affect the tone of firms' Management's Discussion and Analysis (MD&A) disclosures. Anti-SLAPP laws limit firms' ability to use costly litigation to deter critics, plausibly reducing managers' ability to conceal adverse information from external stakeholders. Using a stacked-cohort difference-indifferences design and textual measures constructed from the full population of 10-K filings from 1993 to 2025, we find that MD&A tone becomes significantly more negative following the enactment of an anti-SLAPP law in a firm's headquarters state. The effect is concentrated in the most negative tail of the tone distribution and among firms with greater ex ante incentives to conceal adverse information. It is also stronger in states with more expansive statutory protections and where anti-SLAPP laws have had the greatest impact on litigation activity. Finally, we find that investors respond less favorably to optimistic MD&A tone at the 10-K filing date following anti-SLAPP adoption.

title: Urbanization, Changing Values, and the Politics of Environmental Protection
affiliations: Paris School of Economics (PSE), Univ. Rennes, CNRS, CREM - UMR 6211, F-35000 Rennes, France. and University of Birmingham - Birmingham Business School

detail.title: Urbanization, Changing Values, and the Politics of Environmental Protection

detail.abstract: How will urban growth affect the long-run environment? This paper focuses on an overlooked channel: how urbanization shapes environmental values and, with them, political support for environmental protection. Our theory combines two mechanisms: the extinction of experience documented by conservation science, whereby reduced contact with nature erodes attachment to it, and a cultural transmission process involving rational socialization decisions. Both are embedded in an overlapping-generations model with rural-urban migration and voting over environmental policy. When the extinction of experience dominates, urbanization erodes support for environmental protection. However, when socialization is effective, the picture reverses: the interaction between location and socialization choices gives rise to a process of cultural dissemination through which urbanization raises environmental values. Our main theoretical predictions are consistent with a set of stylized facts on environmental preferences, residential location, and policy support that we document using data from the International Social Survey Programme.

title: Does Exposing Misconduct Improve Politician Performance? Evidence from the UK Parliamentary Expenses Scandal

detail.abstract: We leverage the 2009 UK parliamentary expenses scandal to study whether exposing politician misconduct improves subsequent performance. Our empirical strategy combines the exogenous timing of the scandal with cross-constituency variation in misuse of public funds by Members of Parliament (MPs). We find that legislative performance improved across several dimensions in heavily implicated constituencies during the following parliamentary term. Political turnover drives these gains: implicated incumbents were much less likely to run in the 2010 election and the performance effect attenuates substantially when we compare the same MP over time. Performance gains are also larger where misconduct received greater press coverage. Sitting incumbents did respond immediately, but only by reducing claims for living expenses, the margin directly exposed by the scandal. Our results show that revealing misconduct can improve politician performance beyond the behavior disclosed, with the broad performance gains operating primarily through changes in who holds office rather than within-incumbent adjustment.

title: The Price of Procurement Access
affiliations: Jinan University, Guangdong University of Foreign Studies, Jinan University - College of Economics and Guangdong University of Foreign Studies

detail.abstract: We link 5,171 firms identified in bribery cases to 10.8 million Chinese public procurement contracts to study the value and pricing of procurement access. Procurement gains persist for about three years, including among firms with only one recorded bribery year, and are concentrated among firms whose payments were made for procurement-related purposes. Larger firms and firms in more competitive industries obtain greater procurement gains, but these differences are only weakly reflected in recorded bribe payments. Instead, payment amounts vary substantially across other characteristics, such as localities and the administrative level of recipients' departments. Together, these findings suggest that bribery purchases durable, purpose-specific access whose price is only coarsely differentiated across firms. In a financial subsample of about 1,000 firms, however, we find no detectable improvement in returns on assets or equity following bribery.

title: Human Finitude in an Age of Increasing Capability
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Human Finitude in an Age of Increasing Capability

declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is a conceptual and theological monograph based on analysis of published literature and biblical and theological sources. detail.abstract: This monograph develops a Christian theology of human finitude for an era in which scientific and technological capabilities increasingly alter the conditions under which human beings know, act, heal, communicate, reproduce, calculate, predict, and intervene in the world. It argues that finitude is not merely a temporary shortage of power, information, longevity, or control. Finitude is a constitutive dimension of creaturehood: human beings are mortal, embodied, temporally located, epistemically partial, dependent upon God and others, vulnerable to uncertainty, and unable to foresee or govern all consequences of their action. Technological achievement can genuinely relieve suffering, extend agency, enlarge knowledge, and improve human life; none of those goods requires a theology hostile to invention. Yet capability can also generate a practical illusion of transcendence when the ability to do more is interpreted as evidence that creaturely limits have ceased to matter. The resulting error is not simply optimism. It is a category mistake in which increased instrumental power is confused with sovereignty, information with omniscience, prediction with providence, extension with immortality, connectivity with communion, and control with wisdom. Drawing on biblical texts, classical and modern Christian theology, and philosophy of technology, this study analyzes eight dimensions of finitude: mortality, incomplete knowledge, uncertainty, dependence, embodiment, time, unintended consequences, and moral limitation. It then proposes a constructive ethic of finite agency organized around humility, precaution, reversibility, distributed responsibility, Sabbath, embodied presence, intergenerational accountability, and hope. The argument concludes that a mature theology of technology neither demonizes capability nor sacralizes it. It receives human ingenuity as a genuine creaturely good while insisting that the more consequential human power becomes, the more urgently power must be disciplined by the truth that human beings remain creatures rather than gods.

title: Impact of Adults’ College Completion on their Parents’ Mortality: Evidence from the 1993 Korean Higher Education Reform
affiliations: University of Southern California, University of California, Berkeley and University of California, San Francisco (UCSF) - Department of Epidemiology and Biostatistics

detail.title: Impact of Adults’ College Completion on their Parents’ Mortality: Evidence from the 1993 Korean Higher Education Reform
detail.abstract: A large literature examines the economic and health returns to college education. We extend this literature by studying the upward intergenerational effects of children’s education on parental mortality. We exploit Korea’s 1993 Higher Education Reform, which we estimate raised college completion by 13 percentage points among eldest children in the 1974–1983 birth cohorts relative to the prior 10-year cohort. Using data from the Korean Longitudinal Study of Aging, reduced-form estimates indicate a 27% (s.e.=10%) reduction in mortality among parents whose oldest child was in the reform-affected cohort. Because the reform affected college completion but not other education levels or quality, we use it as an instrumental variable (IV) for child college completion. IV estimates indicate a 20% (s.e.=7%) reduction in parental mortality for children induced to complete college by the reform. These parents received greater financial support and contact from their children and had lower smoking and higher physical activity, although these mechanisms explain only a small share of the mortality benefit. Effects were larger for parents of daughters in reduced-form analyses, although IV estimates did not differ significantly by child gender. Future research should further investigate the mechanisms through which children’s college education affects parental mortality.

title: Decomposing First-mover Advantage: A Decision-making Perspective
affiliations: Erasmus Univeristy Rotterdam School of Management, Erasmus University Rotterdam (EUR) - Erasmus School of Economics (ESE) and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) - Faculty of Business Administration (Munich School of Management)

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflicts of interest
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: We develop a theory of first-mover advantage (FMA) grounded in decision-making ability and error propensity. Our simulation model demonstrates how small initial advantages compound through systematic differences in error rates between first-and secondmovers. We show that FMA amplifies when both competitors have higher decisionmaking ability and when abilities are closely matched, whereas FMA increases for low complexity of the decision-making environment but decreases for higher complexity. To test these predictions, we analyze 3.66 million chess games, exploiting quasi-random assignment of move order and objective ability measures. Results strongly support our theory: FMA increases from 3.5% for low-ability players to 11% for high-ability players, peaks when competitors are evenly matched, and strengthens in complex decision environments. Move-level analysis reveals second-movers make larger errors when operating from disadvantageous positions under complexity, explaining FMA persistence through compounding mistakes rather than resource advantages.

detail.abstract:
n April 2025 Pittsylvania County, Virginia refused to rezone 763 acres for a private gas plant and data centers. Nine months later the same Board of Supervisors made data centers by right on 3,500 acres at the Berry Hill megasite that already permitted private power plants, in a district whose text says the county's own data center standard does not apply there. Within eight weeks the county's regional industrial authority had approved a sale contract defining the buyer's project as no less than 3,300 megawatts of data center capacity with onsite gas generation.

The case study follows both decisions through the primary record: county packets, minutes and ordinances, the regional industrial facility authority's resolutions, purchase agreement form and executed performance agreement, Danville's council and utility commission minutes, State Corporation Commission dockets, and meeting video. It sets the district's substitute standard against the county's 2024 data center section and against the refused applicant's proffers, including noise (52 dBA offered, 77 dBA adopted, and that only beside residential zoning), and documents the August 2026 site assessment for large electricity users that exempts the megasite district from most of its requirements. On the utility side it traces the Berry Hill loop and substation, built by Appalachian Power under the business park pilot statute that deems need met once the state's economic development agency approves a park; the company's flat forecasts against 24,881 megawatts of load in inquiry; and the four utilities whose territories divide the county's two sites. It closes by placing the sequence, refusal and then entitlement by ordinance on the county's own motion, against the five-posture typology of Governing the Demand Shock.

title: Critical Mass for Panic Contagion: Dispersion, Coupling, and Symmetry Breaking in a Spin Model of Coupled Trading Agents
affiliations: Fairmont Preparatory Academy and Independent

detail.abstract: As a growing share of order flow is generated by automated agents that share architectures and signals, the possibility that many agents fail in the same direction at the same moment becomes a structural concern rather than a hypothetical one. Existing accounts of cascading market failure establish that such events can occur, but none measures how much simultaneous panic is actually required to trigger one. We address that question in a deliberately minimal setting: a two-dimensional Ising-type spin market in which agents hold a binary position, are coupled ferromagnetically to their neighbours, and experience the crowding penalty of BORNHOLDT (2001). A market prepared in a stable consensus is perturbed by forcing a fraction f of agents to sell simultaneously, and we measure the probability that the whole market follows. We find a sharp threshold at f c ≈ 0.06 under baseline coupling, whose transition narrows from a width of 0.0140 to 0.0109 as the system grows from L = 24 to L = 64. Two pre-registered hypotheses are refuted. First, f c rises monotonically with herding strength, from 0.041 to 0.101 across our coupling range, because stronger herding stabilises the prevailing consensus rather than making it easier to overturn. Second, and more strikingly, spatially concentrated panic is far less dangerous than dispersed panic: compact seeds require f c = 0.44 against 0.059 for scattered seeds, a factor of 7.4. The mechanism is not droplet nucleation but disorder-induced melting, since n scattered agents disrupt O(n) neighbours while n contiguous agents disrupt only O(√ n). In a narrow window near threshold the market loses its consensus almost every time, with tightly concentrated timing (15 ± 3 sweeps), yet reforms downward only 46-59% of the time, reproducing the pattern of determined timing and random direction reported by Bayraktar and Munk (2018) in an entirely different framework.

detail.abstract:
Background: Physical climate risks increasingly affect UK homes, yet recognition does not necessarily mean households understand risks to their own property or feel able to act. We examined how homespecific awareness, perceived protection and practical readiness align for flooding and overheating.

Methods: We analysed an online survey of 907 UK adults using descriptive statistics, paired and subgroup comparisons, and multivariable logistic regression.

Results: Three patterns emerged. Only 11.6% reported awareness of extreme-weather risks affecting their own home, while 50.3% recognised that flooding or overheating could affect mortgage or borrowing outcomes. Perceived protection was lower for overheating than flooding: 23.9% rated their home fairly or very well protected against overheating, compared with 42.7% for flooding. Although 87.0% expressed willingness to improve their home, only 42.7% had acted or planned to act. Uncertainty about what to do, lack of trusted advice and affordability were prominent barriers. Readiness was associated with prior experience, perceived timing, personal responsibility, trust in mortgage providers and perceived overheating protection.

Conclusions: Generic awareness-raising may be insufficient for climate-resilient housing. Priorities include property-specific information, feasible actions, trusted advice and practical or financial support. Housing intermediaries may support practical action and link risk reduction to comfort, health and lower bills.

title: Does Crypto Trading Activity Follow New York Time? Cross-Venue and New York-London Evidence from Clock Changes

detail.abstract: Cryptocurrency markets trade continuously, but continuous access need not make liquidity and information processing temporally uniform. We test whether Bitcoin and Ether trading activity is anchored to fixed Coordinated Universal Time (UTC) or to the local operating hours of a traditional financial center. U.S. daylight-saving transitions move the 9:30 a.m. New York equity-market open by one hour in UTC, causing two fixed thirty-minute UTC windows to exchange local-time alignment while retaining their UTC identities. Using five-minute Binance and Coinbase spot data from 2018 through spring 2026, the calendar-year-aggregated estimate implies 36.3% greater activity in the aligned window (exact year-level sign-randomization p = 0.0078). The effect appears on both venues and for both assets, remains positive in a twentytrading-day local-trend design (p = 0.0117), and is positive in all 56 documented activity specifications. It weakens when U.S. institutions are closed, survives scheduled-announcement exclusions and same-season placebo transitions, and is not mirrored at the London open. A paired New York-versus-London triple difference supports geographic specificity. Realized variance moves in the same direction but is less precisely estimated. The contribution is to identify cross-venue transaction-activity re-anchoring at the exact New York open and its geographic specificity, complementing contemporaneous evidence that longer-run Bitcoin volatility has migrated toward U.S. trading hours.

title: The Rich Get Gas, the Poor Go Back to Firewood: Transition Incidence and the Liquidity of the Clean Energy Escape in Nigeria's 2023 Fuel Subsidy Reform
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Rich Get Gas, the Poor Go Back to Firewood: Transition Incidence and the Liquidity of the Clean Energy Escape in Nigeria's 2023 Fuel Subsidy Reform

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests that could have influenced the work reported in this paper. The research was conducted independently, and no party with an interest in its findings had any role in the paper's design, analysis, or conclusions.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This paper did not involve human participants, animals, or the collection of new primary data. It relies solely on secondary analysis of publicly available, de-identified survey data (the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel and official statistics from the National Bureau of Statistics and related public sources). Ethics approval was therefore not required.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant from any funding agency in the public, commercial, or non-profit sectors. It was carried out by the author on an independent, self funded basis.

detail.abstract:
“The subsidy is gone.” With those four words on the 29th of May 2023, Nigeria ended the cheap petrol that two generations had treated as a birthright, and within a year the pump price had climbed from under ₦200 per litre to more than ₦1,000. Every study of a reform like this asks this one question; who pays more at the pump? This paper asks a more revealing one; when the price of energy rises, who can indeed change how they live, and who is stuck?

Following a balanced panel of 4,682 households, weighted to 25.2 million through the Nigeria General Household Survey Panel, before and after the reform, this paper watches each family's cooking fire and light switch. The escape ran through a single fuel; cooking gas. Among the richest fifth of households, clean LPG cooking jumped 21.8 percentage points; among the poorest two-fifths, just 2.3. That 20.4 points gap (95% CI 14.9 - 25.6) is the heart of this paper. Kerosene vanished and split its users in two directions at once with half climbed to gas, while three in ten slid back to firewood. The petrol generator was abandoned across the whole distribution. And the poorest households, already about 94% dependent on wood and charcoal, almost did not move.

This paper is deliberately careful about cause. Two survey waves five years apart, with a currency float bundled in, cannot prove the reform did this, and a pre-reform placebo shows the rich were already pulling ahead before 2023. But the policy lesson does not need a causal claim. The burden of the reform; who paid more at the pump was broadly progressive, yet the chance to escape upward was hoarded at the top. Nigeria's compensation was cash. However, cash pays a bill; it does not buy a gas cylinder. So, when a fossil fuel price shock hits a poor economy, what the poor cannot afford is not only the higher price but the way out. A reform that ignores this widens the very gap it was meant to close, one gas cylinder and one bundle of firewood at a time.

title: From Nominal Capacity to Operational Coherence: A Conceptual and Descriptive Analysis of Hospital Readiness and Nursing Capacity in Lebanon

detail.abstract: Background. Counts of hospitals, beds and health workers are the usual measures of health-system capacity. In Lebanon they overstate the care the system can deliver. The country has 153 hospitals and about 13,000 beds, yet public sources report bed closures, reduced operating capacity, nurse emigration and conflict-related hospital closures. Objective. To examine the gap between nominal and operational capacity, and to propose a four-layer capacity model interpreted through the RUISA™ framework (Roles, Users, Information, Situation, Actions). Method. Conceptual and descriptive analysis of public sources from WHO, the Lebanese Ministry of Public Health, UN agencies and peer-reviewed studies. Sources differ in period and definition and are read as complementary signals, not a time series. RUISA™ is used as an interpretive lens and is not tested. Findings. WHO reported in 2022 that most hospitals were working at about 50% of capacity, more than 30% of private beds had closed, and only 27 public hospitals, with about 2,000 beds, were operational. About 20% of the nursing workforce had emigrated. Twelve North Lebanon hospitals lost a net 10.24% of their nurses in 2020-2023 despite replacement hiring. Conflict had closed or disabled 15 of 153 hospitals by November 2024, and six hospitals were fully closed by April 2026. Contribution. The paper distinguishes nominal, functional, staffed and coherent capacity. It argues that the last-staffed resources aligned with roles, information, situational awareness and action-best represents readiness. Conclusion. Future research could test whether shift-level readiness measures explain effective capacity beyond conventional infrastructure indicators.

title: Computational Framework for the Dynamic Simulation of a Radial- Access Percutaneous Coronary Intervention using Judkins Catheters
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, Polytechnic University of Valencia, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Computational Framework for the Dynamic Simulation of a Radial- Access Percutaneous Coronary Intervention using Judkins Catheters
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Transradial percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) has been associated with reduced access-site complications compared to transfemoral approaches; however, catheter engagement and backup support may be suboptimal in certain aortic anatomies. This study presents a patient- specific finite element framework to evaluate the mechanical behavior of Judkins catheters during transradial coronary cannulation.Methods: A three-dimensional aortic geometry reconstructed from magnetic resonance imaging was combined with computer-aided design (CAD) models of Judkins left (JL) and right (JR) catheters (3.5, 4.0, and 4.5) and a 0.36 mm (0.014-in) coronary guidewire. Explicit dynamic simulations were performed to analyze two procedural stages: guidewire advancement toward a distal coronary target and catheter deformation until aortic wall support was achieved. The ap- plied force conditions were defined within a range of 1.5–2 N to induce sufficient catheter deformation for ensuring stable mechanical support.Results: Maximum contact forces obtained ranged from 0.13 N to 1.7 N, while equivalent Von Mises stresses in the aortic wall varied between 5.25 MPa and 41.6 MPa depending on the catheter geometry and trajectory. JL configura- tions showed a more homogeneous redistribution of stresses on the wall along the aortic arch, while JR catheters produced higher and more spatially localized stress concentrations. These differences highlight the fundamental role of the catheter curvature and of the access trajectory in determining coaxial alignment and modulating the catheter-wall contact patterns.Conclusion: This study evaluates device–artery contact, catheter deformation, and force transmission, providing a mechanistic framework to assess support conditions during transradial PCI.

title: Critical Minerals Are the New Energy Security
affiliations: Independent Research and Policy Analysis

detail.title: Critical Minerals Are the New Energy Security

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is employed by Aurora Gold Mines Inc., a company operating in Guyana's mining sector. This independent research examines critical-mineral markets, mining, supply chains and industrial policy. The manuscript was prepared in a personal capacity from public sources and does not represent an official position or endorsement of the employer or any institution cited.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Not applicable. This study is secondary research based on published and publicly available sources. No human participants were recruited and no confidential or personally identifiable data were collected.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was personally funded by the author, Ragunauth Ramsaroop. No employer, institution, external sponsor or grant provided financial support.

detail.abstract: Critical minerals now sit at the intersection of energy security, industrial competitiveness, digital infrastructure, defence capability, climate policy and development strategy. The shift does not mean minerals function like oil. Fossil fuels are consumed continuously, while most minerals are embodied in long-lived assets. Mineral disruption therefore acts mainly through the cost, timing and location of new industrial capacity, replacement equipment and manufacturing output. That distinction changes the logic of security policy. The central finding of this monograph is that geological abundance is a weak proxy for secure supply. Security depends on the entire chain between a resource and a qualified industrial input. Exploration, financing, permitting, mine construction, water and power, beneficiation, refining, chemical conversion, specialised equipment, process knowledge, logistics, trade rules, customer qualification, social legitimacy, recycling and substitution all shape the final outcome. The International Energy Agency reports that critical-mineral demand continues to grow strongly across all scenarios. Under its 2026 Stated Policies Scenario, aggregate demand approaches twice current levels by 2040. Lithium rises more than threefold. Copper adds about seven million tonnes of demand. Refining concentration is even more consequential. Excluding rare earths, the average share held by the top refining country reached 72 percent in 2025, up from 70 percent in 2023. (International Energy Agency, 2026b, 2026f) Trade intervention has moved from theoretical risk to observed disruption. OECD analysis finds that export restrictions on critical raw materials increased fivefold from 2009 to 2024. About 16 percent of global critical-raw-material trade faced at least one export restriction during 2022 to 2024. Exposure was far higher for cobalt, manganese, graphite and rare earths. (Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development, 2026) The IEA reports that the number of mineral tariff codes subject to Chinese export controls tripled since 2023. Policy actions by other producers, including the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Zimbabwe and Mozambique, have also altered supply expectations. (International Energy Agency, 2026b) This study develops three contributions. First, it synthesises current market evidence and peerreviewed criticality research into an eight-domain Mineral Security System Framework covering geology, project execution, processing, logistics and trade, technology and knowledge, finance and markets, environmental and social legitimacy, and circularity and adaptation. Second, it presents a structured scenario architecture for 2026 to 2040 that separates demand shocks, supply shocks, policy shocks, technological change, environmental disruption and compound events. Third, it proposes a research agenda and testable propositions for universities, policy institutes, mining companies and industrial researchers. The report does not treat a single scenario as a prediction. It treats scenarios as stress tests. It also does not assume that the fastest route to more supply is always the most resilient route. Low-cost supply, geographically diverse supply, environmentally credible supply and politically stable supply are related goals, yet they are not identical. The practical research challenge is to determine where redundancy, inventory, substitution, recycling, local processing, long-term contracts and public risk sharing produce the largest resilience gain relative to economic cost.

detail.abstract: Guyana is entering a period in which resource abundance, capital availability and geopolitical relevance are expanding faster than the institutions and productive capabilities required to convert them into durable national advantage. This white paper proposes a Strategic Asset Conversion Framework for linking petroleum, minerals, energy, forests, geography and rapid growth to permanent financial, productive, human, institutional and natural capital. Its central policy standard is resource multiplication: major national assets should be judged by the capabilities they leave behind after the immediate revenue, commodity premium or construction phase ends.

title: Multi-Currency Risk Modeling and Volatility Targeting: Empirical Evidence from an EGARCH-Student Model on the MASI 20
affiliations: Université Mohamed VI Polytechnique (UM6P)

detail.title: Multi-Currency Risk Modeling and Volatility Targeting: Empirical Evidence from an EGARCH-Student Model on the MASI 20

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflict of interest and no competing financial or personal relationships that could have influenced this research.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding or financial support. It was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how volatility and tail risk evolve on the Casablanca Stock Exchange (CSE) using the MASI 20 index from 2021 to 2026. By applying an EGARCH(1,1) model with a Student-t distribution, this study captures the volatility clustering and asymmetric leverage effects common in frontier markets. The research also estimates dynamic Value-at-Risk (VaR) across three investor currencies: the Moroccan Dirham (MAD), Euro (EUR), and US Dollar (USD). Backtesting demonstrates that while the model performs robustly for domestic and Euro investors, USD investors face significantly higher, often underestimated tail risk due to the Dirham's fixed-basket peg. Finally, a dynamic Volatility Targeting strategy is tested, improving the portfolio's Sharpe ratio from 0.07 to 0.25, while highlighting the real-world trading costs and liquidity constraints of executing this quantitative approach on the CSE.

title: (Un)intended Consequences of Extreme Heatwaves for Air Pollution and Its Social Cost: Evidence from the Power Sector in China
affiliations: Renmin University of China - School of Applied Economics, Renmin University of China, National Climate Center, Renmin University of China, National Climate Center, Renmin University of China - School of Applied Economics and National Climate Center

detail.title: (Un)intended Consequences of Extreme Heatwaves for Air Pollution and Its Social Cost: Evidence from the Power Sector in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No conflict of interest
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: We gratefully acknowledge financial support from the National Key Research and Development Program of China (Grant No. 2024YFF0809202 for Q.C., Y.W., and C.W.), the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 72203218 for B.G. and Grant No. 72503244 for P.S.), the Fundamental Research Funds for the Central Universities, and the Research Funds of Renmin University of China (Grant No. 25XNN063 for B.G. and No. 24XNF059 for P.S.).

detail.abstract: Extreme heatwaves can undermine the efficiency of fossil-fuel power generation, amplifying air pollution and health risks. Using plant-level operational data and high-resolution weather data from China, we find that during the 2022 extreme heatwave in Guangdong Province, exposed plants experienced approximately 21.4% higher PM 2.5 emission intensity relative to unexposed plants, an increase attributable to heatwave-induced efficiency losses. Coal-fired plants exhibited an additional 12.3% increase relative to gas-fired plants. Similar patterns are observed for other combustion-related pollutants. We estimate that heatwave-induced pollution from power-sector efficiency losses imposes an annual social cost of USD 4.21 billion in China, which could be reduced by USD 1.42 billion under a complete coal-togas substitution scenario. Looking ahead, under the high-emissions SSP5-8.5 scenario, which is associated with approximately 4.4 Celsius of warming by 2100, annual costs in China could rise to USD 20.41 billion. The impacts are highly uneven across provinces, with coal-dependent and industrial coastal regions disproportionately affected. Our findings highlight how extreme heatwaves can amplify air pollution and health damages through an overlooked energy-sector efficiency channel, underscoring the broader societal costs of continued fossil-fuel dependence in a warming world.

title: The Forum Problem: A Structural Map of India's Judicial Ecosystem
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: The Forum Problem: A Structural Map of India's Judicial Ecosystem

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing financial or personal interests. The Judiciary Entity Map (JEM), the dataset underlying this paper, is a project the author created and maintains; it is released as a public good under a CC0 (data) and MIT (code) licence, is personally funded, and is not operated for commercial gain. The author has no financial relationship with, and received no support from, any of the institutions analysed in the paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external, institutional, or grant funding. The Judiciary Entity Map and the work reported here were personally funded by the author.

detail.abstract:
India's judicial-reform debate is organised around the queue: pendency counts, disposal rates, judge-topopulation ratios. This paper argues that the queue is the second question. The first is whether the room exists-whether the forum a statute promises has been constituted, staffed, and given an unambiguous place in the appellate lattice. That is a question about state capacity, and it is one emerging markets share wherever legislated institutions outrun the administrative capacity to build them.

I introduce the Judiciary Entity Map (JEM), an open, source-linked structural dataset of India’s judicial and quasi-judicial ecosystem. Release v1.0.1 holds 1,145 entities and 1,800 relationships, and those entities are not courts. They are the whole administrative graph: the adjudicatory forums together with the appointers, funders, complaint-recipients, and office-holders that wire them, plus role archetypes and generic scaffolds held apart from the substantive counts. Any forum-level sub-count is an approximation, not a census. Every relationship is grounded, where possible, in constitutional text, statute, gazette notification, or official report, with explicit data-quality flags where it is not.

From the dataset I derive a four-part typology of carrying-capacity failure: forums delayed (GSTAT, eight years from statute to seated members), forums never built (the Arbitration Council of India, the Mediation Council of India, seven state and Union Territory Lokayuktas), forums hollowed (APTEL’s technical-member vacancy filled only after judicial prompting; the Allahabad High Court at roughly half strength), and forums ambiguous (Debts Recovery Tribunal appeals from Hyderabad and Visakhapatnam rerouted to an appellate tribunal some 1,500 kilometres away, generating writ litigation in two High Courts about where to litigate). Each mode redirects disputes rather than resolving them, and the redirection lands, predictably, on the constitutional courts.

The account has become newly concrete. In August 2026 Parliament passed the Tribunals Reforms Act, 2026 (Act 17 of 2026, in force from 25 August 2026), establishing a National Tribunals Commission and a National Tribunals Data Grid for sixteen central tribunals. It is an appointments reform, and it leaves three of the four failure modes, and the wider ecosystem, outside its reach. The paper’s finding is not the dataset but the absence the dataset fills: no official, public, current map of India’s judicial forums exists.


JEM is offered as an imperfect, automation-built, community-reviewed starting point — an existence- proof that such a map can be built — and the recommendation follows from it. India needs an official, live dashboard of every judicial entity and its status, and a standing authority to institutionalise carrying capacity across the whole ecosystem, not sixteen tribunals alone.

title: Is the Auto Industry on Track? : Examining auto sector compliance pathways for achieving the 2030 vehicle emissions target
affiliations: Pembina Institute for Appropriate Development

detail.title: Is the Auto Industry on Track? : Examining auto sector compliance pathways for achieving the 2030 vehicle emissions target

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Not Applicable
declarations.funderStatement: Not Applicable

detail.abstract:
In early 2026, Canada announced its plan to amend the vehicle emissions standard (VES) regulation, which sets annual fleet-wide greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions targets for automakers. The proposed Canadian emission targets under the amended VES start at 170 grams of carbon dioxide equivalent per mile travelled (g/mile) in 2027 and decline to 74 g/mile by 2035, with an interim 2030 target of 120 g/mile. The regulation aims to put Canada on track to achieve 75% electric vehicle (EV) sales by 2035. Relatedly, Canada has committed itself to reducing its greenhouse emissions by 45–50% below 2005 levels by 2035. Our earlier modelling shows that  a stronger VES trajectory, including an interim 2030 target of 100 to 105 g/mile would be needed to achieve Canada's emissions and EV sales targets. 
In this analysis we examine whether Canada’s auto industry can comply with the emissions trajectory described in early VES reports (120g/mile by 2030) and whether a stronger emissions trajectory (100 to 105 g/mile by 2030), consistent with Canada’s 2035 EV sales goal and emissions reduction target, is achievable through available compliance pathways.
We find that under a business-as-usual case, the Canadian auto industry could realistically achieve a 2030 VES target of 120 g/mile. Moreover, with a modest increase in EV share, and shifting the sales mix toward more car sales (vs. light trucks), the stronger vehicle emissions target of 100 to 105 g/mile can also be achieved by 2030. We also  discuss the compliance pathways automakers may use to achieve these emissions targets.

title: OCT-RAFT: A Weakly Supervised Deep Learning Framework for Optical Flow Estimation in Embryonic OCT Imaging
affiliations: Koç University, affiliation not provided to SSRN, Koç University and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: OCT-RAFT: A Weakly Supervised Deep Learning Framework for Optical Flow Estimation in Embryonic OCT Imaging
detail.abstract: Background and Objective: Quantifying blood flow in embryonic vasculature from optical coherence tomography (OCT) images is hindered by severe speckle noise, low contrast and the absence of ground-truth motion labels. Particle image velocimetry and generic deep learning optical flow models are sensitive to speckle, suffer from domain mismatch and depend on dataset-specific preprocessing. This study aimed to develop a weakly supervised deep learning framework for dense flow estimation in noisy embryonic OCT image sequences.,Methods: We propose OCT-RAFT, which couples a pretrained Recurrent All-Pairs Field Transforms (RAFT) backbone with a lightweight U-Net refinement module. Because annotated flow data are unavailable, the model is trained with Farneback-derived optical flow as a weak supervisory signal and a center-weighted spatial loss mask that emphasizes high-motion vascular regions; the loss combines masked L1 flow, relative angle and spatial smoothness terms. The model was trained on seven OCT sequences from seven chick embryos using a single standardized preprocessing pipeline. It was evaluated on an in vitro microfluidic phantom with a known flow rate and on 15 independently acquired in vivo chick embryos at Hamburger–Hamilton stages 18, 20 and 22 (n = 5 per stage), and compared with particle image velocimetry, Farneback dense optical flow, SPyNet, pretrained RAFT and fine-tuned RAFT. Results were analyzed descriptively using means, standard deviations and 95% confidence intervals.,Results: In vitro, OCT-RAFT velocities agreed with continuity-based theoretical predictions within 8.1% at the channel inlet and 8.3% at the widest section, with inter-run coefficients of variation of 2.1% and 6.0% for the inlet and channel-averaged velocities. In vivo, OCT-RAFT yielded mean velocity magnitudes of 0.11 ± 0.06, 0.19 ± 0.11 and 0.48 ± 0.15 mm/s at stages 18, 20 and 22, compared with 0.32 ± 0.30, 0.81 ± 0.44 and 3.30 ± 1.70 mm/s for particle image velocimetry, and produced spatially coherent flow fields with fewer background artifacts than the baseline methods.,Conclusions: OCT-RAFT provides a weakly supervised framework for quantitative blood flow analysis in embryonic OCT imaging without dataset-specific tuning, and its design may transfer to other speckle-rich biomedical imaging modalities.

title: Uneven Persistence: Historical Population Patterns and Modern Prosperity in China
affiliations: Lanzhou University of Finance and Economics and Lanzhou University of Finance and Economics

detail.title: Uneven Persistence: Historical Population Patterns and Modern Prosperity in China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors have no relevant financial or non-financial interests to disclose.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for conducting this study.

detail.abstract: How does the relationship between historical population patterns and modern prosperity differ between northern and southern China, and does it depend on the historical benchmark? We use four population reconstructions produced within a common framework, spanning 2–1820 CE, to examine the conditional association between historical population density and city-level gross domestic product (GDP) per capita in 2019. Across the Han, Tang, Song and Qing benchmarks, southern point estimates exceed their northern counterparts; the statistical evidence for this difference is clearest for the Qing benchmark. We directly compare Tang (742 CE) and Qing (1820 CE) population patterns in a common sample of 233 cities. We find a larger South–North association gap for Qing than for Tang patterns, with statistical support in both the baseline and land-area-control specifications. The widening mainly reflects a stronger positive southern association, with no comparable strengthening detected in the North. Repeating the Tang–Qing comparison using modern population density, GDP density or nighttime lights, we do not detect a corresponding widening of the South–North association gap. These findings show that understanding the long-run relationship between historical population patterns and modern prosperity requires distinguishing regions and historical benchmarks, as well as output per capita from the spatial concentration of population and economic activity.

title: What do Property Tax Experts Actually Agree on? Evidence from the ABFM Expert Panel Survey
affiliations: Arkansas State University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We declare no interest.

contentType.other: paper is currently under review with a journal

detail.abstract: At least thirteen states are weighing proposals to eliminate or restrict the property tax (Pew Charitable Trusts, 2026). This Field Note reports an Association for Budgeting and Financial Management 2025 expert panel in which nine public finance scholars rated fourteen property tax propositions, reporting their confidence and written reasoning. Using the Tastle-Wierman agreement index descriptively, the panel reaches strong consensus on six propositions, including that eliminating the tax would impair local governments and that it is more transparent, not less, than its alternatives, and divides on four propositions, including whether the tax is regressive and whether burdens have grown too quickly. A companion federal budgeting panel agrees less, suggesting the local evidence base is comparatively settled. For legislators, the panel counsels caution about replacing a hard-to-replace tax; for local officials, it flags assessment quality as the main lever over fairness.

title: Emissions Abatement Under a Rate-Based Emissions Trading System: Facility-Level Evidence from China
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS) - Lee Kuan Yew School of Public Policy, National University of Singapore (NUS) - Institute for Environment and Sustainability, Tsinghua University - Institute of Energy, Environment, and Economy and Chinese Academy for Environmental Planning

detail.title: Emissions Abatement Under a Rate-Based Emissions Trading System: Facility-Level Evidence from China

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: This research is supported by the National Social Science Fund of China (Project 18ZDA107).

detail.abstract: As the world's largest emissions trading system (ETS) by covered emissions, China's national ETS uses an unconventional rate-based design to allocate allowances, which inherently creates "winners" (surplus units) and "losers" (deficit units). Utilizing a unique facility-level dataset and a continuous difference-indifferences framework, we show that the national ETS reduces CO2 emissions from regulated power units by 2.3%. Crucially, this abatement is mainly driven by reallocating output from deficit to surplus units instead of within-unit efficiency gains or fuel switching. Moreover, such output substitution is more pronounced among units within the same regional grids or parent companies. This policy also delivers substantial co-benefits by reducing air pollution from regulated plants. Our findings contribute ex-post evidence on the effectiveness of rate-based ETSs and offer insights for policymakers seeking to mitigate emissions on a broad scale while maintaining production levels.

title: The Economic Costs of Nepal's Open Border with India: A Case Study on Smuggling
affiliations: Tribhuvan University

detail.title: The Economic Costs of Nepal's Open Border with India: A Case Study on Smuggling

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors. The analysis and conclusions presented are based solely on the interpretation of secondary data from the cited sources.
declarations.funderStatement: This research was conducted independently and did not receive any specific grant from funding agencies in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract: The border between Nepal and India, which was opened in 1950 by the Treaty of Peace and Friendship, has created unique conditions for developing cultural and social ties between the countries. However, the open border has also led to negative consequences for the national economy of Nepal. This research aims to discuss the effects of smuggling through the 1,880 km border and analyze the situation in the context of the foreign trade deficit and the deteriorating economic situation in the country. Based on the data presented by the study, it is possible to draw the conclusion that smuggling contributes significantly to the trade deficit between Nepal and India. Smuggling of gold, drugs, agricultural products, and people constitutes a substantial part of trade between the countries. It is reported that 42.5% of the officially recorded trade between Nepal and India is smuggling, which results in a loss of 33.5 billion rupees for the Nepalese economy. In addition to the loss from unofficial trade, the state loses 3.58 billion rupees in duty and 3.71 billion rupees in value-added tax. The article also reports that the trade deficit in Nepal this year amounts to NPR 180 billion, of which a considerable part is caused by smuggling. Thus, the current situation in which Nepal allows free trade between the countries is extremely disadvantageous for the national economy. The study provides multiple examples that prove the large scale of the problem, including the cases of Badhaiyatal and Bardibas, where the largest captures of marijuana, gold, and peas in recent years were registered. According to official data, 30,000 people are trafficked illegally into Nepal every year, resulting in significant losses for the economy. The causes of the problem include the policy of open borders, insufficient control mechanisms, corruption, and taxation issues. However, the authors of the article believe that a smart border is necessary to ensure the prosperity of the Nepalese economy through trade with India.

title: Household Food Insecurity And Third-Trimester Maternal Anaemia In Cali, Colombia: An Analytical Cross-Sectional Study
affiliations: Pontificia Universidad Javeriana, Universidad Libre, Universidad Libre, Fundación Universitaria San Martín and Universidad Libre

detail.abstract:
Background:Household food insecurity is common during pregnancy, but evidence linking it to maternal anaemia is limited and inconsistent in Latin America and the Caribbean. We examined this association in a Colombian obstetric population. 

Methods: We conducted an analytical cross-sectional study of consecutively enrolled women aged ≥18 years at a tertiary obstetric centre in Cali, Colombia (March–August 2026). Eligibility required written consent, ability to participate in the postpartum interview, and a third-trimester complete blood count; 332 women were analysed. Interview data covered sociodemographic and food-security variables; clinical data came from medical records. ELCSA was administered postpartum before investigators knew the haemoglobin result and referred to the preceding 3 months. Anaemia was haemoglobin <11·0 g/dL. Robust Poisson regression adjusted for maternal age, number of pregnancies, household income, and education; marginal prevalences were standardised.  

Findings: Among 332 women, 73 (22·0%) had anaemia. Food insecurity affected 121/317 (38·2%); anaemia occurred in 42/121 food-insecure women (34·7%) and 28/196 food-secure women (14·3%). The adjusted prevalence ratio was 2·44 (95% CI 1·53–3·88). Adjusted marginal prevalence was 34·8% versus 14·3%, an absolute difference of 20·5 percentage points (95% CI 9·3–31·7). Binary food-insecurity estimates were similar across alternative adjustment and missing-data analyses.  

Interpretation: Household food insecurity was associated with substantially higher third-trimester anaemia prevalence after accounting for measured maternal and socioeconomic characteristics. Because ELCSA was administered postpartum over a recall period overlapping late pregnancy, temporal ordering and residual confounding cannot be resolved; causal or dose–response interpretation is not warranted.

detail.abstract: This paper studies the endogenous informational evolution of dynamic economic systems. Building on Hurwicz's conceptual framework, such a system is defined as a dynamic joint adjustment process of resource and information allocation linked by recursive feedback. Economic theory gains precision by isolating particular margins, but when information production, disclosure, learning, incentives, actions, and future feasibility interact across these two processes, conclusions obtained by holding other margins fixed need not survive their joint determination. The paper develops a system-level dynamic equilibrium framework for this interaction. Holding particular links fixed yields familiar environments in dynamic mechanism design, information design, experimentation and learning, feedback and disclosure, and information acquisition. The analysis establishes three central failures relative to fixed or partially exogenous informational environments: informational efficiency under exogenous feasibility is generally incompatible with endogenous dynamic feasibility; incentive and disclosure design cannot generally be separated; and informational monotonicity can fail without implementation replicability. It also identifies the corresponding positive boundaries. Optimal disclosure may be interior or extreme; bang-bang disclosure arises under additional conditions, and a further specialization generates an endogenous transition from opacity to transparency. Information may therefore be optimally withheld even when its direct decision value is strictly positive. Extensions to private payoff-relevant information and limited commitment preserve the recursive structure.

title: Social Media Exposure and Herding Behavior Among Retail Investors: A Survey-Based Analysis of Self-Reported Trading Decisions Across Age Groups

detail.title: Social Media Exposure and Herding Behavior Among Retail Investors: A Survey-Based Analysis of Self-Reported Trading Decisions Across Age Groups

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing personal or financial interests that could have influenced this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study collected fully anonymous survey data from voluntary adult participants. No identifying information was collected, and participants were informed of the study's purpose before beginning the survey. No formal institutional ethics board review was sought, as this was an independent, non-institutional research project.

detail.abstract: Does scrolling through TikTok or Reddit before placing a trade change how retail investors behave, and is this something that fades with age or cuts across generations? This exploratory study tests whether consumption of finance-related social media content predicts self-reported herding behavior among retail investors, controlling for financial literacy and risk tolerance, and asks directly whether the relationship differs by age. Drawing on informational cascade theory and recent evidence of attention-induced trading, 104 retail investors aged 18 to over 30 were surveyed using an adapted herding scale, the Lusardi-Mitchell financial literacy questions, and a risk tolerance item. A reliability check showed that a reverse-scored item was undermining the original herding scale, so results are reported using a corrected three-item index (Cronbach's α = .71). Social media exposure showed a positive but statistically non-significant association with herding (r(102) = .18, 95% CI [-.02, .36], p = .076), and the relationship remained directionally positive but non-significant after controlling for literacy and risk tolerance (F(3, 100) = 1.59, p = .197). Platform type did not significantly predict herding (F(3, 100) = 2.16, p = .098), although long-form YouTube users, rather than short-form video users as hypothesized, reported the highest herding scores, a pattern consistent with parasocial trust in individual creators. Age did not moderate the relationship (p = .889), which runs against the common assumption that social-media-driven herding is mainly a young investor's problem. A post-hoc power analysis indicates the study had roughly 43% power to detect the observed effect, with about 254 respondents needed for 80% power. The results point toward a real but modest effect that this sample was too small to establish conclusively, and the paper offers a tested survey instrument and a concrete sample-size target for confirmatory work.

title: What Firms Sell: Product Exposure to Generative AI *

detail.abstract: Generative AI can now produce the products certain firms sell. Based on whether customers can obtain substitutes for the firms' main products directly from generative AI, we construct the AI Product Exposure measure from firms' business descriptions. The measure captures product substitution rather than task automation and has little correlation with existing labor AI exposure measures. Using a differencein-differences design around ChatGPT's launch, we find declines in exposed firms' revenue, cost of goods sold, and gross profit, with no statistically significant change in gross margin. Exposed firms adjust their workforce mainly by hiring less, with no evidence of increased separations. The results are robust after controlling for labor AI exposure. Supplementing research on AI exposure through the labor channel, these findings highlight how generative AI affects firms and the workforce via the product channel.

detail.abstract: Australia's Payment Systems and Netting Act 1998 (Cth) was enacted for a payment systems environment that has changed significantly over the past three decades. The development of distributed ledger technology (DLT), tokenised money and the increasing interlinking of domestic and foreign payment systems raise new questions about whether its settlement finality protections remain adequate for the next generation of payment infrastructure. This article examines whether the PSNA remains fit for purpose and what reforms may be required. It argues that the Act's technology-neutral language is capable of accommodating properly governed DLT-based systems, although some clarification may be desirable. Cross-border interlinking presents a more significant challenge because the Act lacks a general framework for recognising qualifying foreign payment systems. Drawing on the European Union's proposed Settlement Finality Regulation as a comparative model, the article proposes targeted modernisation of the PSNA to preserve its existing strengths while extending legal certainty and protection against systemic risk to new technologies and increasingly interconnected payment systems.

title: The Externality of Learning: Adaptive AI and Market Resilience
affiliations: GARCH INSTITUTE

detail.title: The Externality of Learning: Adaptive AI and Market Resilience

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Adaptive financial AI creates a system-level question that single-model evaluation cannot answer: what happens when multiple agents learn from the same experience? I identify this externality with a marginal-preserving experiment that varies exact cross-agent overlap in sequential learning histories while holding each agent's marginal learning problem fixed. Learned policies enter matched limit-orderbook markets under Deep/Thin liquidity and Shock/No-shock counterfactuals. In a pre-specified 240block architecture screen, KNN5 produces a +12.25 bp-round market-resilience effect and remains significant after family-wise correction across Ridge, CART, and KNN5 (max-T adjusted p = 0.023), while Ridge and CART remain near zero. KNN5 is then frozen and run on a fresh 240-block seed domain; the second estimate has the same sign and is statistically compatible with the first. Pooling the two independent KNN samples yields +9.32 bp-rounds [2.74, 15.91], and the result survives exclusion of the shock round itself. Shared histories increase policy dependence without materially changing heldout loss, while KNN converts that dependence into common local reference sets. Common learning therefore creates joint dependence; the architecture and locality with which experience is reused determine its market pass-through under stress.

title: Does Borrowing Make a Company Cheaper to Fund? Debt, Beta, and Ten Years of Indian Companies
affiliations: Savitribai Phule Pune University (SPPU) - Savitribai Phule Pune University (SPPU), Students

detail.title: Does Borrowing Make a Company Cheaper to Fund? Debt, Beta, and Ten Years of Indian Companies

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no conflicts of interest.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract:
Every discounted cash flow valuation assumes that a company's equity becomes riskier when the company takes on more debt. The standard formula used for this is the Hamada relation, which is applied whenever an analyst removes the effect of debt from a beta and then adds it back. Modigliani and Miller's theory is based on the same idea: the additional risk taken by shareholders offsets the benefit of using cheaper debt. Whether Indian share prices actually behave in this way has not been directly tested. 
This paper tests the relationship using 127 non-financial Nifty 500 companies with meaningful debt, covering 1,266 company-years of balance-sheet data from FY2017 to FY2026. The approach is simple: follow the same companies over time and check whether their equity beta increases when their debt increases. 
It barely does. Compared with what the Hamada relation predicts, only about 8% of the expected increase in beta is actually observed (θ = 0.079, 95% interval 0.002 to 0.160). For example, if a company’s debt-to-equity ratio increases from 0.3 to 0.6, the Hamada formula predicts that its beta should increase by about 0.24. The actual increase is only about 0.02.
The result is similar whether leverage increases because the company takes on more debt or because its share price falls. Across all the different specifications tested, θ ranges from -0.06 to 0.13. This is far below the theoretical value of 1 and also below the estimate of about 0.45 reported for US banks.
Because the cost of equity changes very little when debt increases, WACC falls steadily as leverage increases. It falls by about 0.8 percentage points for every 10 percentage point increase in the share of debt in the capital structure, with no increase in WACC anywhere in the data. 
This result is largely a mathematical consequence of the first finding. It means that, using the inputs normally used by practitioners, WACC never shows that a company has taken on too much debt. Among the most highly indebted companies, beta actually falls as debt increases. 
This suggests that CAPM beta does not capture the additional risk associated with financial distress.

title: Across the Capital Structure: Bond Signals and Equity Returns *
affiliations: Yonsei University - School of Business and Yonsei University

detail.title: Across the Capital Structure: Bond Signals and Equity Returns *

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: A firm's bonds and stocks are claims on the same business, but their prices need not incorporate information at the same speed. We extract common return variation from 24 characteristic-sorted corporate bond portfolios and map the resulting signal to the equities of the same issuers. In rolling out-of-sample tests, the bond-implied equity portfolio earns an average excess return of 0.54% per month and a monthly alpha of 0.65% relative to the Fama-French five factors and momentum. A one-standard-deviation increase in the issuer-level signal predicts approximately 21 basis points higher next-month stock returns after controlling for stock characteristics. Predictability survives conditional stock-factor models and established return-spillover strategies, is stronger among smaller firms and issuers with intermediate credit ratings, and attenuates at longer horizons. These findings are consistent with gradual incorporation of bond-market information into equity prices and show that jointly extracted bond signals predict equity returns beyond established spillover benchmarks.

title: Ten Years Hence: Business Angel Tax Credits, the Absent Employment Lift, and a Decade of Convergent Evidence
affiliations: Saint Louis University

detail.title: Ten Years Hence: Business Angel Tax Credits, the Absent Employment Lift, and a Decade of Convergent Evidence

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author is the founder and editor of Undeterred Press, the journal in which this article was published; the article was not subject to independent external review. The article revisits and extends the author's own 2016 doctoral dissertation. The author is a former angel investor in early-stage companies and, as such, belongs to the class of investors that angel tax credit programs are designed to benefit. The article's conclusion, that these credits do not produce their intended employment effects, runs contrary to that interest. The author has no other financial relationships relevant to this work.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding.

detail.abstract: A 2016 doctoral dissertation employed a Campbell and Stanley dual-pair quasi-experimental design across matched state pairs to examine whether US state business angel tax credits produce the technology employment lift that constitutes their principal legislative intent. Across three independent treatmentcontrol configurations (Kansas-Minnesota, LMM F = .026, p = .794; Wisconsin-Tennessee, F = .023, p = .879; and Wisconsin-Minnesota, p = .797), the null hypothesis of no employment effect was accepted at 95% confidence. Ten years later, the evidence base has grown decisively and convergently. Denes, Howell, Mezzanotti, Wang, and Xu (2023), publishing in the Journal of Finance across 31 US states using difference-indifferences methodology, confirm the null employment finding while identifying the mechanism: angel tax credits increase angel investment by approximately 18% but attract nonprofessional, inexperienced investors who provide capital without managerial support, producing crowding-out rather than net job creation. International evidence from the United Kingdom, Ireland, Germany, and Sweden sharpens the mechanism further: outcomes track the managerial engagement investors actually provide, and investor subsidies that attract inexperienced, unengaged investors produce the mal-investment signature predicted by Austrian Business Cycle Theory in 2016. Lerche (2025), in the American Economic Review, demonstrates that direct firm subsidies, bypassing the investor intermediary entirely, produce robust employment gains, completing the evidentiary picture. Meanwhile, the federal Angel Tax Credit Act has been introduced in Congress five times since 2014 without enactment, and over 30 states have collectively allocated more than $8.1 billion to these programs since 1989 (Denes et al., 2023), a decade of compounding null evidence notwithstanding. This article argues that the persistence is structural, not accidental.

title: Why a Pre-distribution Sovereign Wealth Fund Needs the Same Multi-metric Discipline as Private Equity -The Case of Danantara Indonesia
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Why a Pre-distribution Sovereign Wealth Fund Needs the Same Multi-metric Discipline as Private Equity -The Case of Danantara Indonesia

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Danantara, Indonesia's newly consolidated sovereign wealth fund, has been placed under an explicit performance mandate by President Prabowo Subianto: a minimum 5 percent return on assets (ROA) applied to more than US$900 billion in state assets, translating into a minimum remittance of US$50 billion to the state each year, rising toward a long-term target of 10-15 percent ROA. This mandate functions, structurally, as a hurdle rate imposed on a fund's general partner. Yet Danantara, launched in February 2025, is barely nineteen months into what, in private-equity terms, is a multi-year J-curve. This paper extends the multi-metric framework proposed in "Beyond IRR" (Pratama, 2026)-pairing KS-PME as a measure of benchmarkrelative alpha with TVPI and DPI as an anchor for absolute economic scale-to a sovereign wealth fund evaluated at a stage where almost none of its reported value has been realized. It argues that a single-metric, single-point-in-time ROA figure is acutely vulnerable to the same mark-to-market timing sensitivity this author previously identified in institutional private equity, compounded here by a documented 2026 contraction in Indonesia's domestic equity market in which Danantara was simultaneously an affected holder and an active participant. Using publicly disclosed capital-deployment figures, this paper constructs an illustrative-not definitive-demonstration of this sensitivity, and proposes that Danantara adopt, as it works toward its first Santiago Principles self-assessment as an Associate Member of the International Forum of Sovereign Wealth Funds (IFSWF), the same multi-metric disclosure standard this author previously proposed to the Institutional Limited Partners Association (ILPA) for private equity.

detail.abstract: In a pre-registered experiment, rare outcomes made cooperation in a randomly matched Prisoner's Dilemma pay more nine times in ten at unchanged expected payoffs. When payoffs were learned from experience, cooperation rose from 10 to 67 percent; in a companion game where cooperation is dominant, it fell from 96 to 41. With lotteries displayed, effects were about half and a quarter as large and majorities chose the expected-value action, yet dilemma cooperation stayed five times its baseline. Reliance on small samples predicts all four effects; prospect theory with calibrated weights, loss aversion and inequity aversion predict none or the opposite.
