detail.abstract: Value-weighted industry returns can carry the own shocks of their largest firms. The standard variance decomposition then counts those shocks as industry rather than firm risk, even though its components still add up. We derive the bias and correct it without assuming equal firm volatilities. In US stocks from 1996 to 2025, the bias was about one-third of the measured industry share for two decades and roughly half in 2024. Tesla, Apple, and Nvidia accounted for 63.5 percent of the 2024 bias. The corrected industry share shows no comparable recent increase. The change is concentrated in a few industries dominated by one firm.

title: Reversing Digital Dollarisation in Europe
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Reversing Digital Dollarisation in Europe

declarations.declarationOfInterest: James Wyatt previously worked for the New York State Department of Financial Services, a US government body.
declarations.funderStatement: Self-funded.

detail.abstract:
European institutions conduct approximately €50 billion annually in dollar-denominated stablecoin transactions, while the euro-denominated stablecoin market accounts for less than 0.3 per cent of global supply. This paper argues that digital dollarisation in Europe persists not because of a failure of regulation or settlement infrastructure, but because the Eurosystem has not issued a transferable euro-denominated token for wholesale tokenised markets. The retail digital euro settles in central bank money through TARGET Instant Payment Settlement (TIPS), but its account-based architecture cannot function as collateral or settlement asset on distributed ledgers. The European Central Bank's (ECB) Pontes project, launching in Q3 2026, will provide wholesale settlement for distributed-ledger transactions through TIPS, yet its initial phase does not create a transferable central bank liability that circulates natively on those ledgers. Private euro stablecoins such as EURC and EURR have not achieved institutional scale. 

Until the ECB issues a wholesale digital euro that is natively transferable on distributed ledgers, i.e. a bearer instrument with no redemption fee, no private counterparty risk, and universal collateral acceptance, European firms, treasuries, and protocols will continue to convert euros into dollars and settle in USDC. The United States is prohibited from issuing a CBDC until at least 2030. The EU has a window to establish the euro as a tokenised settlement currency and reverse the dollarisation that is occurring, but only if the wholesale layer of the digital euro is designed as a transferable token rather than as an account-based settlement overlay.

title: Politicians' Green Incentives and External Auditing
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, Singapore Management University - Singapore Management University - School of Accountancy and Fudan University-the School of Management

detail.title: Politicians' Green Incentives and External Auditing

declarations.declarationOfInterest: We have no personal or other interests
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract: This paper examines whether and how politicians' green incentives affect external auditing. Specifically, we investigate the effects of China's Green Audit of Outgoing Officials (GAOO) policy, which directly links environmental performance to public officials' promotions. Employing a DID approach, we observe a significant reduction in audit fees for high-polluting firms after the implementation of GAOO. The decrease is stronger when firms are located in regions with departing officials, contribute less to the local economy, or have lower levels of state ownership. We explore two channels driving this trend: (1) Auditors rely on environmental information generated from intensified governmental efforts, thereby economizing on their efforts (i.e., a substitution effect); (2) High-polluting firms improve their environmental performance, thus reducing client risk. Additional analyses show that GAOO is not associated with a deterioration in audit quality or the switch to lower-ranked audit firms.

title: The Influence of Power on Trust in Buyer-Supplier Relationships: An Actor-Partner Interdependence Approach
affiliations: Tilburg University, University of Arizona, HKU Business School, The University of Hong Kong and Tianjin University

detail.title: The Influence of Power on Trust in Buyer-Supplier Relationships: An Actor-Partner Interdependence Approach

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA
declarations.funderStatement: This research was supported by funding from the National Natural Science Foundation of China (#72432009, #72091210/72091214, and #71525005) to the last author. Research support was also provided by a National Science Foundation CAREER Award (#1943688) granted to the second author.

detail.abstract: Trust is among the most critical factors in buyer-supplier relationships. In an effort to understand the origins of trust, power has become the focus of a burgeoning body of literature. However, research on the association between power and trust has been plagued by inconsistencies in terms of whose power and trust are being examined, which has led to confusion and hindered cumulative progress. We address this issue by disentangling the effect of the focal organization (actor effect) from the effect specific to its partner (partner effect) and accounting for both simultaneously. We further theorize and show that the partner's level of self-promotion communication about his or her own achievements and credentials moderates both actor and partner effects, thus adding knowledge about a contingency that accounts for a considerable degree of variation in the linkage between power and trust. Using multi-informant, dyadic survey data paired with archival information scraped from firms' webpages, we find that (i) actors low (vs. high) in power tend to place more trust (ii) while simultaneously eliciting higher levels of trust from their partners; however, (iii) these effects differ markedly depending on the partner's level of self-promotion communication. Our study offers a novel, integrative perspective on power and trust, and we elaborate on its important implications for understanding buyer-supplier relationships.

keywords: asset pricing tests. JEL classification: G12

detail.abstract: Option-implied factors are largely, but not entirely, spanned by the equity factor zoo. We construct 137 option-implied characteristics for optionable U.S. stocks from 2004 to 2023, screen them to 20 representative long-short factors, and test each against 160 equity factors with the double-selection LASSO of Feng, Giglio, and Xiu (2020). In-sample, the equity factors account for about 91% of the option factors' variance, and adding the option factors does not significantly raise the maximum Sharpe ratio. Individually, however, 8 of the 20 option factors, mainly measures of jump tails, kurtosis, and implied-volatility convexity, have non-zero SDF loadings after controlling for the equity zoo, and 4 remain significant after a Bonferroni correction. Options thus add a few pricing-relevant dimensions rather than a new factor zoo.

title: Ecological Stewardship and Human Development
affiliations: Independent Researcher

detail.title: Ecological Stewardship and Human Development

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no known financial, professional, institutional, or personal relationships that could have influenced, or reasonably be perceived to have influenced, the research, analysis, interpretation, or conclusions presented in this study.
declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval was not required for this study because it is a theological and conceptual research monograph based on analysis of biblical texts and published scholarly literature. The study did not involve human participants, patients, identifiable personal data, clinical interventions, surveys, interviews, or animal subjects.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding. The study was independently conceived, conducted, and prepared by the author without financial support from any government agency, academic institution, commercial entity, nonprofit organization, religious organization, or other external funder.

detail.abstract:
Contemporary ecological discourse often oscillates between two errors: an unrestricted model of human exploitation in which nature is treated as raw material without intrinsic limits, and an anti-development model in which human cultivation, technological expansion, resource use, or economic growth are regarded as presumptively suspect. This monograph develops a biblical theology that rejects both extremes. Scripture presents humanity as neither sovereign owner nor ecological intruder, but as a commissioned creature whose vocation is to cultivate, guard, name, order, develop, conserve, and transmit the fruitfulness of creation under the prior ownership and moral authority of God. The biblical pattern therefore affirms productive human agency while subjecting it to covenantal restraint, neighbor-love, justice, Sabbath, animal care, land limits, protection of the vulnerable, and accountability for long-term consequences. 

The study traces this framework from Genesis through Torah, wisdom literature, the prophets, the teaching of Jesus, Pauline creation theology, and the eschatological vision of renewed creation. Particular attention is given to the paired commands to "work" and "keep" the garden, the dominion mandate, Sabbath and sabbatical institutions, gleaning, animal welfare, land tenure, resource use, abundance, waste, intergenerational obligation, and the moral meaning of technological capability. The argument distinguishes use from abuse, abundance from excess, conservation from paralysis, and development from idolatrous mastery. It proposes "responsible abundance" as a constructive category: the disciplined development of created goods so that human communities may flourish without treating ecosystems, animals, or future persons as expendable. 

The monograph concludes that ecological stewardship is not a retreat from human development but its moral ordering. Biblically faithful development is productive, bounded, restorative, distributive, prudent, and accountable. It should seek sufficient and resilient abundance, especially for the poor and vulnerable, while preserving the regenerative capacities of the created order on which present and future life depend.

title: The Wealth of Nations: Origins of Prosperity and Seeds of Inequality
affiliations: Brown University - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Wealth of Nations: Origins of Prosperity and Seeds of Inequality
detail.abstract:
What ignited humanity’s momentous ascent from millennia of stagnation to an era of sustained economic growth? And what are the roots of the vast disparities in the wealth of nations? These enduring mysteries, which have preoccupied scholars across generations, lie at the core of Unified Growth Theory. This encompassing framework captures the evolution of societies over the entire course of human history and identifies the universal wheels of change that governed humanity’s long journey, propelled the growth process, and shaped inequality across the globe. The theory uncovers the forces underlying the dramatic transformation in living standards over the past two centuries, emerging from an economic ice age of near stagnation, while highlighting the enduring historical roots of the immense divergence in the prosperity of nations. It suggests that forces set in motion in the distant past played a pivotal role in shaping development across the globe and remain essential for the design of effective policies that foster economic progress and mitigate inequality in the wealth of nations.

Institutional subscribers to the NBER working paper series, and residents of developing countries may download this paper without additional charge at www.nber.org.

reference: Evaluating ATL Zoning 2.0, Report Delivered to the City of Atlanta (2026).
title: Evaluating ATL Zoning 2.0
affiliations: George Washington University -Law School

detail.title: Evaluating ATL Zoning 2.0

declarations.declarationOfInterest: This report was commissioned by the City of Atlanta.
declarations.funderStatement: This report was commissioned by the City of Atlanta.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Evaluating ATL Zoning 2.0, Report Delivered to the City of Atlanta (2026).

detail.abstract:
A zoning code is a blueprint for a community’s future, impacting people for generations.  Revising and adopting a new zoning code presents a significant opportunity to shape economic, social, environmental, and public-health outcomes for the better.  

 

Recognizing the importance of zoning, the City of Atlanta embarked several years ago on a comprehensive rewrite of its zoning code.  This report evaluates the draft code released in December 2025 (the “Draft Code”) with regard to whether it would enhance upward economic mobility.  It focuses on three strategies through which the Draft Code might improve economic mobility: streamlining the entitlement process for housing and related development; expanding the availability of diverse housing options; and reducing the cost of creating new housing.  

 

The report finds that the Draft Code fails to advance the economic mobility goals of the City, instead creating a confusing permitting system that could have worse outcomes than the current zoning code.  First, while appearing on the surface to streamline the entitlement process, the Draft Code creates a complex regulatory framework that undermines predictability and flexibility at key junctures.  Second, while the Draft Code modestly facilitates diverse housing options, the Draft Code does not go far enough to ensure such housing will actually be built.  Third, the Draft Code reduces costs in some ways (notably by lifting many parking mandates), but it increases costs in other ways. 

 

This memo proceeds in several parts.  The first Part affirms the City’s push to replace Atlanta’s current zoning code given the City’s economic mobility challenges and given the current code’s relatively poor approach to housing.  The second Part evaluates the extent to which the Draft Code advances the city’s three economic mobility strategies.  The third Part offers recommendations for changes to the structure and content of the Draft Code so the next draft better promotes economic mobility.

title: Injury, Workload, and the Strategic Response of Coaches in the NBA
affiliations: Pennsylvania State University - Department of Economics, Central European University and Analysis Group

detail.title: Injury, Workload, and the Strategic Response of Coaches in the NBA
detail.abstract:
Worker effort increases contemporaneous output but may result in injury or burnout. Directing effort away from the workers most exposed to injury would reduce this risk, but information on the exposure is often hidden. We ask whether managers act on such private information, studying the NBA as a data-rich workplace. Instrumenting workload with teammate absence, we find that work causally raises injury risk, which contrasts with the spurious negative correlation commonly found in sports medicine studies. We also show that coaches rest players in response to injury risk shocks. By acting on this private information, coaches can raise player productivity.

title: Climate Concern Is Not Consensus: Labour Market Informality, Job Quality, And The Political Economy Of Green Transitions
affiliations: Azim Premji University Bangalore - Azim Premji University and Colorado State University

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: How people participate in the labour market shapes their perceptions of collective problems, including climate change. Whether a worker holds a formal or informal job determines their exposure to institutions, their material conditions, and ultimately the lens through which they evaluate policy. This chapter takes that premise seriously and asks what it implies for the political economy of green transitions. We revisit three major global surveys covering up to 1.2 million respondents across more than 140 countries. By disaggregating climate attitudes by intensity, we show that claims of an emerging consensus among the general public on climate change and the need to address it reflect considerable overoptimism. In most parts of the world, public support for ambitious climate action is weaker and more uneven than aggregate figures suggest. We then interact this intensitybased reading with a crosscountry measure of labour market informality, a defining feature of job quality in developing economies. High-informality economies are not uniformly less concerned about climate change, nor are low-informality ones reliably greener in attitudes. These findings carry a practical implication. Heterogeneity in job quality and in climate attitudes jointly constrains both the fiscal capacity of states and the political feasibility of environmental policy.

title: Beveridgean Phillips Curve
affiliations: University of California, Santa Cruz and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Beveridgean Phillips Curve
detail.abstract:
This paper develops a Beveridgean model of the Phillips curve. While the New Keynesian Phillips curve is based on monopolistic pricing under price-adjustment costs, the Beveridgean Phillips curve is based on directed-search pricing under price-adjustment costs. Under directed search, prices respond to slack instead of marginal costs. The resulting Phillips curve has three properties that match recent US evidence. First, it delivers the divine coincidence: inflation is on target whenever unemployment is at its efficient level—the full-employment rate of unemployment (FERU), the geometric mean of the unemployment and vacancy rates. Second, it is decreasing and convex in the unemployment-inflation plane: inflation responds more strongly to unemployment when the labor market is inefficiently tight than when it is inefficiently slack. The convexity is inherited from the Beveridge curve, which makes unemployment a decreasing and convex function of tightness. Third, shifts of the Beveridge curve move the FERU and therefore shift the unemployment-inflation Phillips curve. The model also implies that the Fed's dual mandate is internally consistent, that a soft landing from an inefficiently tight labor market is possible, and that the zero lower bound is not topsy-turvy.

title: Property Rights Uncertainty, Prices, and Speculation: Evidence from China's Housing Market
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics, Tsinghua University - Hang Lung Center for Real Estate and Georgia State University - J. Mack Robinson College of Business

detail.title: Property Rights Uncertainty, Prices, and Speculation: Evidence from China's Housing Market
detail.abstract:
We examine the causal effect of uncertainty in property rights on housing prices and speculative behavior. We take advantage of a distinctive setting in Shenzhen, China, where neighboring residential units that are otherwise similar differ in the strength of their property rights protections. Some units have full property rights (FPR) with a 70-year leasehold, whereas others have only limited property rights (LPR) protections. Using detailed listing data, we find that the sales market prices these protections, while the rental market does not. Our estimates imply that the perceived probability that FPR rights could be questioned at the end of the 70-year term is between 7% and 21%, and that the probability the LPR receives no legal protection in any future year exceeds 50%. We further show that LPR units are more susceptible to speculation, as reflected in higher turnover and greater price volatility. Lastly, we show that the public release of new urban planning codes raises listing prices and lowers turnover and price volatility for LPR properties relative to matched FPR units.

title: Deep Learning as a Projection Method for Solving Economic Models
affiliations: Stanford University - The Hoover Institution on War, Revolution and Peace and IMD

detail.title: Deep Learning as a Projection Method for Solving Economic Models
detail.abstract:
Deep learning is increasingly presented in economics as a new paradigm for solving dynamic models, superseding the classical projection methods of numerical economics. We argue that this dichotomy rests on a misclassification. The neural-network solvers emphasized in this literature are least-squares projection methods with an adaptive nonlinear parameterization. Placing deep learning inside the projection family reorients the agenda. The issue is not a contest between paradigms, but suggests a single toolkit using a variety of approximation methods, residual criteria, and evaluation designs to be chosen on the merits for the model at hand. In low and moderate dimensions, linear-basis and sparsegrid methods are often more accurate, faster, and easier to verify than a trained neural network. In high dimensions, an appropriate choice for the space of permissible functions will often avoid the curse of dimensionality.

title: Network General Equilibrium as a Threat to Identification: The Failure of Time Fixed Effects
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Finance Area and University of North Carolina (UNC) at Chapel Hill - Finance Area

detail.title: Network General Equilibrium as a Threat to Identification: The Failure of Time Fixed Effects
detail.abstract:
Time fixed effects are not a general-equilibrium control. In network economies, aggregate shocks do not enter firm outcomes uniformly: they propagate through equilibrium prices, costs, and demand, leaving a residual network gradient after time demeaning. When an instrument, treatment, or exposure design even partially aligns with this gradient, standard panel estimators recover the direct effect plus an endogenous network-leakage component. We develop a tractable framework that signs and quantifies this Network-SUTVA bias in closed form, showing how network topology governs its magnitude. Weak instruments magnify the leakage. Difference-in-differences designs are similarly contaminated because controls can be untreated by assignment but treated in equilibrium. Calibrated to the U.S. production network, the distortion can exceed 130% of the true direct effect. We propose observed- and hidden-network diagnostics and remedies, and test them on canonical difference-in-differences designs, showing that standard estimators can confound direct policy responses with systemic network leakage.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes that inflation dynamics follow a law of motion analogous to Newtonian mechanics, driven by a "repulsive force" between the government and households. While the government attempts to manipulate the real interest rate toward its preferred level, households resist to maintain their own, resulting in a strategic tug-ofwar. The study demonstrates how this force-based inflationary motion mirrors Newtonian laws-specifically inertia, acceleration, and action-reaction. Additionally, the concept of kinetic energy is employed to analyze central bank strategies for achieving price stability.

detail.abstract: Public transaction records are the raw material of empirical work on distressed-debt markets, yet they are the last link of a chain that begins with an event and passes through a disclosure obligation, a publication rule, an archive, a source document and a machine-extraction step before anything becomes a research variable. This paper treats that chain as the object of measurement, using China's regulator-designated pilot platform for non-performing loan (NPL) transfers, the Banking Credit Asset Registration and Transfer Center (Yindeng Center), 2021-2026. We build a record-by-field observability panel covering 44,508 measurement cells (3,709 parsed announcements × 12 fields), benchmark the recoverable archive against the venue's own official statistics, and run a controlled optical-character-recognition (OCR) recovery experiment on pre-2023 scanned attachments. Three results stand out. First, archive coverage is asymmetric: across five non-overlapping benchmark windows, public listing announcements average 1.216 per officially reported listed project (range 1.189-1.238, sd 0.0202), while public result announcements recover 58.2%, 68.8%, 57.7% and 67.6% of officially confirmed transactions in 2021-2024. The transaction ratio is not robust to the timing convention: across three equal-length 12-month alignments it ranges from 57.7% to 100.5%, because the official series counts at confirmation while the public record counts at announcement. Second, field observability is jointly structured by document format and announcement templates. The share of records with text-free scans falls from 89.2% in 2021-2022 to 1.9% from 2024 onward, while buyer capture rises from 14.6% to 98.4%. A comparison across the 2022/2023 boundary supports stability at the template-field level: all five fields of the result-announcement template are present in the source on both sides. What changed is whether those fields can be read without OCR; the test does not rule out changes in realized content, timing or completeness. Third, the OCR corpus contains 270 scanned result announcements; across 261 unique result announcements the pre-OCR record supplies a usable buyer for 14.9%. Re-extracting the originals at 300 dpi under a geometry-corrected rule raises candidate extraction to 100%, validated accuracy to 98.9% and the effective usable yield to 98.9% (258 of 261); the extraction rule actually shipped in the previous version reaches 97.7% on the candidate measure but only 93.9% once every candidate is checked against the document it came from. The gap between those two numbers is the paper's central methodological point: a non-empty field is not a measured variable. Amount fields in scanned listing notices still require visual or layout-aware reconstruction, and transaction price is not published by the platform at all. Throughout, every recordby-field cell carries an explicit four-state source status rather than a binary observed/missing flag, and presence claims rest on field-level evidence rather than on the mere existence of a scan.

title: The Political Foundations of Industrial Policy: Emergence, Endurance, and Exhaustion
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley, University of British Columbia (UBC) and London School of Economics & Political Science (LSE)

detail.title: The Political Foundations of Industrial Policy: Emergence, Endurance, and Exhaustion
detail.abstract:
We study how politics shapes industrial policy through two paradigmatic twentieth-century cases: the Cassa per il Mezzogiorno in Italy (1950–1984) and Kennedy's Moonshot in the United States (1961–1972). Drawing on historical and primary political sources, we show that each policy originated in a broader political project rather than in an economic diagnosis: the Christian Democrats' pursuit of national integration and democratic consolidation, and Kennedy's New Frontier. We introduce the concept of industrial policy vision - a publicly articulated, transformational objective that political leaders attach to a set of ideals and pursue through state-led intervention in the economy - and develop a five-component definition that makes it empirically tractable. We then trace each vision through decades of newspaper coverage, combining topic modeling and sentiment analysis with systematic close reading. In both cases, public debate proceeded largely within the frame the vision set, granting the policies tolerance for setbacks and expense. The cases diverge in their fates: the Moonshot's bounded vision was redeemed on schedule, while the Cassa's open-ended vision was exhausted by accumulated failure and the policy outlived it only briefly. This divergence points to our central conclusion: while a vision holds, it sets the terms on which an industrial policy's performance is judged, including what counts as failure and how much time the policy is given to deliver.

detail.abstract: The universality, ratification, and enforcement of the Singapore Convention on Mediation (SCM) are significantly lower than those of the New York Convention on Arbitration (NYC), due to factors such as the European Union deadlock and fragmented standards for mediators. However, no study has quantitatively examined its relationship with international businesses. Using the World Bank's Business Ready (B-Ready) data, this study finds only weak evidence that ratifying, not merely signing, the SCM is associated with better conditions for international trade. Nevertheless, socioeconomic factors are more strongly associated with international businesses than either convention, and policymakers should prioritise them.

detail.abstract: We study how publicly posted floors change when distressed-debt claims are listed repeatedly after an unsuccessful offering. The selected panel contains 223 repeatedly listed assets or claim packages, 608 listing rounds, and 230 continuous disposal episodes on Chinese online trading venues between 2022 and 2026. After excluding one pre-specified unitinconsistency record by asset and round identifier rather than by price direction, 375 adjacent within-episode comparisons remain: 127 repeat the preceding floor exactly, 248 reduce it, and none increase it. The positive-markdown distribution is lumpy: 154 of 248 markdowns lie within 20% +/-0.5 percentage points, while recurrent four-decimal ratio cells also occur at 0.70, 0.8333, 0.85, 0.8571, 0.875, 0.90, and 0.95. Path-level evidence is stronger than one-step bunching: among 121 episodes with at least three rounds, 20 follow a ratio that rounds to 0.8000 at every adjacent step and 35 keep every adjacent markdown within 20% +/-0.5 percentage points. A forward validation exercise does not show that a seller's earlier behavior predicts held-out assets materially better than a fixed 0.8 rule: with at least two prior transitions from at least two other assets, mean absolute error is 0.07092 for the seller-history rule versus 0.07099 for the fixed rule, and the result is dominated by one seller. Exploratory sequence evidence instead reveals a synchronized cohort: ten Guangxi Liujiang paths show two near-20% reductions followed by an unchanged relisting; nine share the same first three listing dates and the same fourth date. We interpret this as case evidence of batch-like public repricing, not as a general seller rule. The paper contributes descriptive evidence on discrete public repricing and an event-state architecture for repeated listings, while leaving causal effects, internal pricing rules, and claim-package composition changes unidentified.

title: Shipping to America
affiliations: Tsinghua University, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics, University of International Business and Economics, University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and University of Oxford

detail.title: Shipping to America
detail.abstract:
We study the macroeconomic and trade-policy implications of disruptions to U.S.-bound shipping routes. Standard models treat them as iceberg-cost shocks, conflating the shock with the response to it. Using satellite vessel-tracking data, we construct route-level measures of potential and effective capacity for all U.S.-bound container ships from 2016 to 2025. Utilization losses in recent disruptions ran 20 to 40 percentage points, and began months before port congestion became visible. We embed these measures in a general equilibrium model in which firms reallocate a common fleet without internalizing the congestion they create and price above marginal cost, while importers' sourcing responds to route profitability. The reallocation triggered by a disruption then has first-order welfare effects, and the route's Domar weight is not a sufficient statistic for its welfare cost. The 2021 West Coast crisis and the 2023-2024 Red Sea attacks cost 0.69% and 0.35% of output. Naval protection of Red Sea shipping generated benefits of 0.04-0.08% of output at a fiscal cost of 0.02%. Tariffs decongest the routes they tax, offsetting or even reversing their conventional welfare cost.

title: Foreign Tax Advantages after the U.S. Tax Reform of 2017
affiliations: University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - Department of Economics and University of Minnesota - Minneapolis

detail.title: Foreign Tax Advantages after the U.S. Tax Reform of 2017
detail.abstract:
We construct a firm-year panel of income-tax rate reconciliations from annual 10-K filings of public companies to study the effects of the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) on U.S. multinational profit shifting. These reconciliations decompose the gap between company-level effective tax rates and the federal statutory corporate tax rate, allowing us to isolate the contribution of foreign tax advantages before and after the reform. We find that TCJA significantly reduced the tax rate gap and increased effective tax rates for companies most exposed to pre-TCJA international tax benefits. This resulted in an onshoring of profits with foreign profit shares falling 1.3 percentage points per percentage point of tax increase. Among more exposed companies, we find no differential change in investment, employment, or the geographic distribution of sales and installed capital. A neoclassical model of a multinational that chooses where to book its income rationalizes this pattern: the reform raised the average tax on income booked abroad relative to income booked at home, which governs where profits are reported, while the marginal tax on capital, which governs investment, changed by an amount common to all firms. Controlling for deferred-tax windfall gains leaves our main results unchanged.

title: Like a Good Neighbor: Childhood Neighbors Influence Occupation Choice
affiliations: University of Maryland Baltimore County, Kellogg School of Management, Brigham Young University and Brigham Young University

detail.title: Like a Good Neighbor: Childhood Neighbors Influence Occupation Choice
detail.abstract:
Occupation choice is a key determinant of economic mobility. This paper studies how childhood neighbors influence occupational choices and later-life earnings. Using linked historical U.S. census records for over six million boys and four million girls, we reconstruct neighborhood microgeography to identify childhood neighbors and their occupations. We find that living next door to someone in a given occupation increases the probability of working in that same occupation 30 years later by about 10 percent relative to other children on the same street. The transmission effect is higher with more intense exposure, in more connected neighborhoods, and when neighboring families are more similar. Exposure to high-income or highly educated neighbors has lasting economic effects, leading to significant gains in adult income and education even compared to other children from the same street. These findings suggest that neighborhood networks play an important role in shaping intergenerational economic mobility.

title: Evaluating the Spatial Consequences of a Climate Tipping Point
affiliations: Federal Reserve Banks - Federal Reserve Bank of New York, Southern Methodist University (SMU) and University of Chicago

detail.title: Evaluating the Spatial Consequences of a Climate Tipping Point
detail.abstract:
The Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation (AMOC) is a system of ocean currents that plays a key role in regulating global climate, including moderating temperatures in Europe and the North Atlantic. Its potential collapse due to global warming is widely considered one of the more likely climate tipping points. This paper examines the economic implications of such a collapse using a dynamic spatially integrated assessment model (S-IAM) of the world economy. Scandinavia and parts of Russia are predicted to experience significant losses in GDP and welfare, while southern Europe, northern Africa, and Brazil benefit from slightly colder temperatures. S-IAMs generally predict that global warming is especially harmful to low-income regions, but an AMOC collapse could mitigate some of these negative impacts in parts of the developing world while instead harming some of the more advanced economies. This lowers spatial inequality, but global welfare drops by 1.9% by 2200 under an intermediate-emissions scenario.

title: Transportation Bottlenecks and Aggregate Shocks
affiliations: New York University (NYU) - New York University, Harvard University - Department of Economics, Boston College and Harvard University

detail.title: Transportation Bottlenecks and Aggregate Shocks
detail.abstract:
Do transportation disruptions affect aggregate outcomes? We develop a tractable model of the transportation sector to study its impact on prices and international trade. By casting maritime transportation as a queueing network, the model identifies where the transportation bottlenecks lie and delivers a simple and easy-to compute measure of transportation capacity over time. We calibrate the model using shipping and trade data and use it to evaluate the resilience of the shipping sector during the last 20 years. During the Great Supply Chain Disruption, port bottlenecks raised commodity prices and caused shortages, but a contemporaneous contraction in commodity supply reduced shipping demand and thereby dampened these effects. By contrast, insufficient shipping capacity was a key driver of price increases during the 2000s Commodity Supercycle.

detail.abstract: Does policy uncertainty drive inflation, or does inflation drive policy uncertainty? Using monthly U.S. data from 1985 to 2026 and a quantile-on-quantile frequency connectedness approach, we examine spillovers between headline inflation and economic, monetary, and trade policy uncertainty. The answer depends on the horizon. In the short run, policy uncertainty is a net transmitter to inflation; in the long run, the direction reverses and inflation becomes the net transmitter. This pattern holds for all three uncertainty measures. Connectedness is concentrated in the tails of the joint distribution and is close to zero around the median of inflation, and transmission linked to trade policy uncertainty concentrates in its upper tail.

title: The Dynamics of Development in a Zero-Sum World

detail.title: The Dynamics of Development in a Zero-Sum World
detail.abstract:
This chapter examines the consequences of zero-sum environments for cultural change, innovation, and long-term economic growth. We introduce innovation into the framework developed by Bergeron et al. (forthcoming), in which zero-sum environments give rise to demotivating beliefs. Although demotivating beliefs improve static efficiency by limiting excessive competition in zero-sum environments, we show that they can also impede long-term growth. Because demotivating beliefs suppress effort, they can also reduce learning-by-doing and other production spillovers. Hence, they can inhibit innovation and act as a cultural evolutionary kludge. We apply the model to explain the cultural changes associated with Western Europe's economic rise after 1500.

title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics and Northwestern University

detail.title: Terra Incognita: The Economics of a Shrinking World
detail.abstract:
As of 2026, humanity is likely below replacement fertility. That has never happened before, not in wars or pandemics. But the real surprise is that the fall has been concentrated in low- and middle-income countries and among poorer and less educated women. We fit a single-factor model to 236 countries since 1950: the common component peaked in 1978, and what drives fertility down today are country-specific trends, 219 of them negative and not one leveling off. None of the commonly cited mechanisms can account for this pattern, so we offer a conjecture: modernity itself, which makes a third child expensive and childlessness cheap. Children come in integers, so it takes very little to move a cohort’s fertility rate from 1.8 to 1.3. And nothing in an economy pushes fertility back to 2.1. We close with the main economic consequences, in particular slow growth.

detail.abstract: The expanded auditor's report presumes that the auditor's account of what mattered most informs investors. Standards require a fresh judgment each year but not a rewritten description. Using 14,917 firm-years of Japanese non-financial listed firms with March fiscal year-ends (2019-2025), we pair updating with market reaction. In pooled estimation, key audit matter (KAM) count and length show no significant association with filing-date absolute abnormal returns, and equivalence tests rule out effects of 0.50% or more per KAM and per log-length unit. Japanese KAMs are firm-specific (the median cross-firm similarity within a year is 0.044-0.045) yet barely rewritten. Median year-over-year similarity is 0.860, and 47.3% of firm-years repeat the same items with near-identical wording. Even among firms swinging to a loss, two-thirds do not substantively revise their descriptions. Where descriptions are rewritten, no filing-date reaction is detected, so the null extends to the updating dimension.

detail.abstract: We study buyer sorting in China's Yin-Deng-registered market for corporate non-performing loan (NPL) transfers. After a buyeridentity audit, the completed-transfer sample contains 636 projects through 25 September 2026: 274 acquired by national financial asset management companies (AMCs) and 362 by licensed local AMCs; principal is observed for 606. National-AMC share rises monotonically from 18.4% in the smallest principal quartile to 73.7% in the largest. The association survives seller fixed effects, debtorprovince-by-year fixed effects, two-way clustering by seller and buyer parent, a true within-seller sample of 49 sellers trading with both buyer tiers, alternative size measurement, and deletion of the extreme right tail. detail.abstract: We ask whether Key Audit Matter (KAM) disclosure moves investors' required returns, exploiting Japan's two-stage introduction (voluntary 2020, mandatory 2021). Using 29 early adopters within 10,519 firm-years (2019-2025), we estimate four implied-cost-of-capital (ICC) models and their average. The multi-model average rises more for early adopters. Yet the model that barely loads on earnings forecasts shows no increase, a well-powered null (0.76-percentage-point minimum detectable effect), and decomposing the ICC into inputs localizes the increase in the two-yearahead forecast growth spread, not the price. It is not investor repricing; what moved the forecasts, and whether they were borne out, remain open. The mandate does not widen the early adopters' gap. Even from a credible source, KAM does not detectably reprice equity in this large, mature market, as preemption of largely known risks predicts. A post-implementation review reading investor benefit off a forecast-sensitive measure would mistake forecast movements for repricing.

detail.title: Early Results from the RESET Demonstration Project: Inflation in Food at Home
detail.abstract:
This paper presents early results from the RESET Demonstration Project, an initiative that constructs price and sales indices using item-level transactions data. The project’s overarching goal is to demonstrate the feasibility and advantages of leveraging modern transactions data for economic measurement by pointing toward a future in which official economic statistics are rebuilt on 21st-century data and technology. The paper introduces new inflation measures for Food at Home and evaluates them on two fronts: how they compare to current official statistics and what they offer as novel measures that capture more accurately the dynamics of consumer choice. The paper also addresses the challenges of producing reliable and credible official statistics from item-level transactions data and reports findings on recent Food at Home inflation trends.

detail.abstract: We assemble a daily, 234-year (1792-2026) synthetic total-return dataset for U.S. equities and Treasuries and deliver with it the yield-curve construction, the bond-return mathematics, the leverage engine and the estimators, so that each result and its construction form one object. Every value carries a quality tier (observed, reconstructed, analogized or synthesized), and every headline is reported on the full sample and on clean sub-samples. A calendar-time clock removes the annualization bias of a trading week that shortens from six days to five. Each return is carried gross of dividend withholding (GTR), net of the 15% treaty rate (NTR Half) and net of the 30% statutory rate that the official S&P 500 Net Total Return index applies (NTR Full). Results are stated as signs that hold across 1,000 plausible reconstructions, and each headline is then tested against a block bootstrap of the one observed history, the removal of single crises, other start dates and higher costs. Two demonstrations illustrate what the dataset supports. First, a permanently levered 3× equity position is driven to near-total loss (maximum drawdown ≈-99.9%) and ranks below 2× on Calmar in every reconstruction and in 61-87% of resampled histories. Whether it also compounds below 1× depends on the window and the tax track. On gross returns it does over the full 234 years (median CAGR 4.5% against 8.0%), a span that includes the synthesized pre-1885 path. Over 1885-2026 and 1926-2026 it does not, and the CAGR peaks at 2× on the observed path but in only about half of the resampled histories. Net of the 30% withholding, its full-sample CAGR has a median of about zero and is negative in 53% of the reconstructions. Second, net-of-fee, daily-reset equity ETFs peak at 2× over 1926-2026, a shape that rests chiefly on 1929-32. A 3× equity fund ends 0.4 pp above 1× from 1926 (10.8% against 10.4%) and 0.1 pp below it from 1928, the first year of the daily S&P Composite. An extra 19 bp a year per borrowed unit turns the first gap, and financing 1926-33 at the Treasury rate instead of commercial paper turns the second, so the sign of the gap between 3× and 1× is not identified. The 2× fund keeps a cost cushion of 1.4-1.6 pp a year over 1×. A levered long bond only deteriorates, and every inverse equity fund loses heavily. Rolling 10to 30-year windows show that whether 3× beats 1× depends on the window (it does in 47-61% of them), while 1× keeps the better Calmar in 84-100%, shares that rest on few non-overlapping windows. An independent 226-year reconstruction corroborates the equity total-return level (7.79% against 7.59%). The series is illustrative and directional. It should not be used for path-dependent daily statistics before 1885 (equity) or 1962 (bonds), for bond-level precision before 1940, or for frictions finer than the fund fees its ETFs carry.

title: Economics of Demand-Side and Supply-Side Climate Policies
affiliations: University of Chicago

detail.title: Economics of Demand-Side and Supply-Side Climate Policies
detail.abstract:
Should a jurisdiction seeking to cut greenhouse gas emissions use demand-side climate policies that target fossil fuel consumption? Or should it introduce supply-side policies that target extraction? My analysis points to a policy portfolio rather than an either/or choice. ``Leakage'' of emissions to unregulated jurisdictions can be mitigated by combining standard demand-side carbon emissions pricing with supply-side pricing of carbon extraction. Emissions pricing drives leakage by lowering fossil fuel prices abroad; extraction pricing counteracts this effect. Supply-side climate policies in practice, however, do not broadly price extraction but instead narrowly foreclose investments in fossil fuel infrastructure and are thus inefficient. To reduce carbon demand, an alternative to emissions pricing is support for clean energy. I emphasize reforms to transmission planning and utility governance as crucial for unlocking clean energy resources' potential, and I highlight the case for publicly supporting clean energy R&D, including green industrial policy, to reduce carbon emissions not just at home but also abroad. I close by discussing distributional consequences. Domestically, carbon pricing and clean energy subsidies have sharply different distributional profiles. Globally, carbon extraction pricing would harm low-income countries that are also fossil fuel importers, though there also exist low-income fossil fuel exporters that would benefit.

title: Foreign Opportunity and Regional Revival: Evidence from the French Rust Belt
affiliations: University of California, Berkeley and University of California, Berkeley

detail.title: Foreign Opportunity and Regional Revival: Evidence from the French Rust Belt
detail.abstract:
This paper studies whether and how distressed regions can recover from industrial decline. We exploit differences in access to an increasingly thriving Luxembourg labor market for neighboring residents of the French “Rust Belt.” We document a three-phase expansion of treated local labor markets, driven by an initial workplace substitution of incumbent residents towards cross-border job opportunities, a medium-term rise in local labor force utilization, and a long-run sustained increase in population via net domestic in-migration. A broader process of local revitalization follows, with higher incomes, reduced reliance on transfers, and resilience to social dislocation, although it is partially offset by rising housing costs and unequal congestion. This leads to a net decrease in far-right and anti- EU vote shares, muting the rise of populism visible elsewhere in former industrial regions of France. Our findings suggest that former industrial regions are not inherently rigid nor doomed to fall to anti-globalization backlash, but can and do adjust – given sufficiently large-scale reversals in local labor demand.

title: The Commoditization of Labor
affiliations: Boston University, Columbia University - Columbia Business School, Finance and Columbia University

detail.title: The Commoditization of Labor
detail.abstract:
Technical change often simplifies jobs. This increases productivity, but it also makes workers more substitutable–or more "commoditized." Commoditization of labor drives down worker bargaining power: anyone can do the job, implying workers are disposable, which improves the outside option of firms and can lower worker wages. We develop a model that captures both the productivity enhancing and wage depressing effects of commoditizing technical change. Commoditizing technical change involves firms standardizing tasks. This reduces the sensitivity of output to worker quality. Firms benefit because they can more easily fill vacancies for their durable jobs. We show that our model can help explain the divergence between productivity and wages in the service sector, increasing wage markdowns despite falling local concentration, and the decline of the large-firm wage premium.

title: Global Temperature and Global Mortality
affiliations: Harvard University, Northwestern University and Stanford University

detail.title: Global Temperature and Global Mortality
detail.abstract:
This paper documents large indirect mortality impacts of climate change. Exploiting natural global temperature variability, we find that 1°C of warming increases annual mortality by 2.5 deaths per 1,000 individuals, compared to 0.1 deaths per 1,000 due to the associated local heat exposure. Using external estimates of the impact of global income on mortality, we show that the macroeconomic effects of global temperature changes explain two thirds of the gap between these estimates. We use this evidence to estimate damage functions in a neoclassical growth model that links mortality and economic activity and accounts for adaptation to mortality impacts. Mortality contributes $400 per ton of CO2 to the Social Cost of Carbon, or one quarter of total climate damages. These results suggest that economic adaptation has a double dividend by also reducing climate-related mortality.

title: A Non-Asymptotic Class of Dense Precision Matrix Estimators: Complexity, Signal, and Double Descent
affiliations: North Carolina State University - Poole College of Management, Columbia University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research, ETH Zürich - KOF Swiss Economic Institute and Columbia University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Operations Research

detail.title: A Non-Asymptotic Class of Dense Precision Matrix Estimators: Complexity, Signal, and Double Descent

declarations.declarationOfInterest: none
declarations.funderStatement: none

detail.abstract: Precision matrix estimation is a cornerstone problem in statistics, economics, and finance. Estimators that are dense, high-dimensionally consistent, and free of latent factor estimation have so far been available only separately. We introduce a general class achieving all three jointly, extending the projection-based linear predictors developed for a single regression coefficient in a hidden factor model (Bing et al., 2021; Bunea et al., 2022) to the full precision matrix, while establishing error bounds that hold uniformly across all p rows rather than pointwise for one outcome. We solve the main difficulty of estimating the diagonal term, which does not extend by tools of Bing et al. (2021) Bunea et al. (2022). Our analysis isolates three random quantities, complexity, retained signal magnitude, and projection bias, that jointly govern the estimation error under a signal-to-noise-ratio condition. A tuning-free special case, the ridgeless regression estimator, exhibits potential double descent in estimation error as the number of outcomes increases relative to the sample size, a matrix-valued counterpart to the phenomenon known from linear regression. An S&P 500 portfolio application illustrates an analogous, doubly ascending pattern in realized Sharpe ratios as portfolio size grows.

title: The Great Accretion and the Great Depression
affiliations: University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics, University of Pennsylvania and University of Pennsylvania - Department of Economics

detail.title: The Great Accretion and the Great Depression
detail.abstract:
The Second Industrial Revolution sparked a wave of new products and industrial processes, fueling an optimistic Roaring Twenties. But did excitement about technological progress contribute to an over accumulation of investment, despite a slowdown in new product development and satiated demand during the 1920s? And, was this over investment worsened by continuous process innovation? Could these factors have played a role in triggering the Great Depression? To explore these questions, a macroeconomic model that incorporates both process and product innovation is proposed. Proof-of-concept simulations are performed to assess whether these factors can help explain the Great Depression. The answer is yes.

title: Subjective Models of the Macroeconomy and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
affiliations: Georgetown University, European Central Bank (ECB) - Directorate General Research, European Central Bank (ECB) and National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER)

detail.title: Subjective Models of the Macroeconomy and the Transmission of Monetary Policy
detail.abstract:
Standard macroeconomic theories assume that representative or heterogeneous agents share a common model of how the economy operates. Yet evidence shows that households hold heterogeneous subjective models---distinct beliefs about how macroeconomic variables interact. As a result, identical shocks or policies may elicit different responses from otherwise similar households. We test this hypothesis by measuring subjective models and investigating their role in the transmission of monetary policy to consumption embedding randomized controlled experiment in a large-scale, multi-country survey. Consumers who believe that monetary tightening primarily operates through its effects on borrowing or savings rates plan to reduce consumption more in response to randomly assigned rate increase scenarios. By contrast, those who think about inflation or general equilibrium effects adjust consumption less. These differences are not explained by demographics, financial characteristics, including mortgage holdings and mortgage type, or country-level factors. Households' actual consumption responses to endogenous policy-rate changes exhibit broadly similar patterns. Our findings stress that heterogeneity in subjective models is an overlooked determinant of monetary policy transmission.

title: The Authority of What Was Never Examined: Borrowed Credentials, Legislative Facts, and the Limits of Evidential Correction
affiliations: Independent Scholar

detail.title: The Authority of What Was Never Examined: Borrowed Credentials, Legislative Facts, and the Limits of Evidential Correction

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares no competing interests. No person or organization had any role in the research, analysis, or writing of this Article, and the author received no compensation for it.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific grant or funding from any agency, institution, or organization in the public, commercial, or not-for-profit sectors.

detail.abstract:
Every legal order acts on premises about whole peoples, and two of the most durable hold that nations can be ranked by measured intelligence and that certain civilizations built nothing of their own. Each carries the authority of a science, a number in the one case and a historical period in the other. Each has been refuted for decades by the discipline competent to refute it, and neither has lost circulation, as their appearance as common knowledge at the World Economic Forum in January 2026 attests. Law is among the principal institutions through which such propositions acquire operative force, converting an assertion about a population into a quota, a sterilization order, or a condition of entry. Law is also the institution that has built the most elaborate machinery anywhere for screening unreliable knowledge before acting on it. The conjunction is what makes the case worth a lawyer’s attention, because in both instances examined here the machinery did not engage.

This Article is the first to read three literatures together. Psychometric critics from Gould to Wicherts, Hassall and Sherratt, Sear, and Warne have shown the national-IQ rankings rest on unrepresentative samples, imputed values, and correlations that dissolve under spatial analysis. Historians from Haskins to Burnett, d’Alverny, Saliba, Gutas, and Lindberg have documented the passage of algebra, optics, medicine, and philosophy into Latin Europe during the very interval that Petrarch and Baronio taught Europe to call dark. Legal scholars from Davis and Karst to Monahan and Walker, Faigman, and Larsen have shown that legislative facts reach courts through channels no rule of evidence governs. Drawing on Omi and Winant’s theory of racial projects, the Article reconstructs each claim from its primary sources and finds in each the constitutive operation was never performed. No representative population resident in Somalia was ever tested, and no user of the term Dark Ages ever inventoried the interval it names. Ten figures measure the defects from the literature’s own data.

The failures share a four-part architecture, a borrowed credential, an absence rendered authoritative, insulation from the competent discipline, and routing toward institutions that act, and the architecture explains why further evidence has almost no corrective effect. The legal consequence follows directly. Claims of this kind enter law as legislative facts, which the law of evidence does not screen, and the screens it does possess are calibrated to other defects. Buck v. Bell, which sustained compulsory sterilization on a hereditary claim about a woman the deposing expert never examined, is the demonstration. The Article offers courts, legislatures, and agencies a three-question verification protocol, answerable from public materials in an afternoon, and shows that calling either claim merely controversial misstates the record in the direction that serves the claims.

title: Upstreamness of Digital Product Imports and Corporate Green Low-Carbon Technology Innovation
affiliations: Hunan University, Hunan University, Hunan University and Hunan University

detail.title: Upstreamness of Digital Product Imports and Corporate Green Low-Carbon Technology Innovation
detail.abstract: Firms’ advances in green and low-carbon technology, together with faster progress toward peak carbon emissions and carbon neutrality, provide an important foundation for high-quality development. By combining Customs import records with data on China’s A-share listed companies from 2000 to 2016, we develop a firm-level measure of upstreamness for imported digital products and assess its causal influence on corporate green and low-carbon innovation. Estimation results indicate that a more upstream position in these imports has a significant positive influence on such innovation. This association is especially salient for companies in digitally advanced regions, industries characterized by intense competition, high-technology enterprises, and importers of ICT goods. Mechanism tests indicate that digital transformation, product upgrading, and cost savings are important channels. Further analysis shows that absorptive capacity strengthens the positive effect of import upstreamness, which also expands the technological frontier of green low-carbon innovation.

detail.abstract: This paper studies a public-data U.S.-equity research pipeline in which security identity, filing availability, source transitions, transaction costs, and temporal validation are specified before performance is interpreted. The released sample screens 822 securities and admits 487 equities. It contains 715,447 daily market observations and 37,273 point-in-time fundamental observations. Forty-seven of 48 factor definitions are estimable. Five asset-pricing families show higher mean in-sample adjusted R-squared for multifactor specifications (0.259–0.301) than for CAPM (0.063). Eight long-only portfolio methods are evaluated under ex-ante one-way costs of 5, 10, and 20 basis points over a 32-month factor-portfolio window. Eight prediction models are assessed in 17 purged monthly test folds using two characteristics. Every non-constant model’s bootstrap interval for mean rank correlation includes zero, and stable after-cost incremental value is not established. The contribution is a connected empirical design that preserves negative and inconclusive findings while making the sample’s public-data and short-window limitations explicit.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence increasingly shapes routing, dispatch, dynamic pricing, fleet allocation, service planning, infrastructure prioritisation, and automated mobility. Yet distributional harms are frequently identified only after implementation, when disadvantaged communities may already have experienced reduced affordability, accessibility, service availability, reliability, or practical access to healthcare, employment, education, care, and other essential opportunities. This article introduces EQUIMOS AI for Predictive Mobility Justice, a humangoverned research framework for anticipating, comparing, preventing, and subsequently auditing inequitable mobility outcomes. It integrates Mobility Justice Digital Twins, an Essential Opportunity Access Graph, a Mobility Justice Impact Engine, a Justice Constraint Compiler, an Equity Counterfactual Optimiser, Federated Justice Transfer, and Prediction-to-Outcome Accountability. The framework is grounded in mobility justice, transport justice and accessibility, sociotechnical AI governance, procedural justice, and responsive regulation. Its conceptual framework specifies the constructs, evidence inputs, relationships, policy profiles, counterfactual requirements, human-review pathways, and accountability outcomes to be validated. UK, EU, and US requirements are represented through jurisdiction-specific policy profiles rather than false regulatory harmonisation. Its distinctive contribution is a Policy-to-Constraint-to-Outcome Accountability Chain that translates authorised policy requirements into traceable, machine-testable conditions while preserving legal interpretation, democratic authority, professional judgment, community voice, and final human responsibility. EQUIMOS AI currently comprises a developed research framework, a prospectively registered comprehensive validation protocol, and a confidential technical implementation plan for a proposed modular cloud-based platform. The validation protocol was prospectively registered on the Open Science Framework on 26 September 2026 at osf.io/p5stg and is presently under embargo. It governs independent multidisciplinary expert appraisal, stakeholder validation, standardised synthetic mobility-intervention vignette assessment, inter-reviewer reproducibility, qualitative analysis, mixed-method integration, framework refinement, and the determination of readiness for technical implementation-plan refinement. The technical implementation plan provides the engineering, data, model-governance, security, human-review, assurance, testing, monitoring, and controlleddeployment blueprint for translating the validation-informed framework into a future cloud-based platform. The proposed platform itself has not yet been developed, validated, tested, deployed, or approved for institutional use. Neither the validation protocol nor the technical implementation paper establishes empirical validity, predictive performance, policy accuracy, cybersecurity, institutional endorsement, regulatory approval, deployment readiness, effectiveness, or scalability; and neither is included in, attached to, or offered for publication with this article.

title: Trading Regulation: Markets for Regulatory Attributes in Banking
affiliations: Yeshiva University - Sy Syms School of Business and New York University (NYU) - Leonard N. Stern School of Business

detail.title: Trading Regulation: Markets for Regulatory Attributes in Banking

declarations.declarationOfInterest: No Declaration of Interest
declarations.funderStatement: No Funding Received

detail.abstract: Can tradable regulatory claims undermine the activity regulation is designed to promote? We study India’s Priority Sector Lending Certificate market, where banks can satisfy lending mandates by purchasing regulatory credit without acquiring the underlying loans. Trading allows banks to separate regulatory attributes from balance-sheet lending and reallocates compliance toward institutions with comparative advantage. This lowers the real cost of meeting regulatory targets, but it also reduces incentives to originate qualifying credit. The results reveal a fundamental policy tradeoff: markets for regulatory claims improve compliance efficiency while potentially weakening the real activity that regulation seeks to encourage.

title: Human Frontier Models: AI, the Common Model, and Disagreement
affiliations: University of Utah

detail.title: Human Frontier Models: AI, the Common Model, and Disagreement

declarations.declarationOfInterest: None
declarations.funderStatement: None

detail.abstract: Economists and strategy scholars have made strong arguments about AI’s ability to not just augment but replace humans when it comes to expertise, scientific discovery, and the production of knowledge. I argue that most accounts of AI—including the jagged frontier—build on what might be called a “common model”: a model that is suited for settled domains but not the knowledge frontier. The common model treats knowledge as a stock that can be codified, transferred, recombined, aggregated—and benchmarked against a criterion of correctness that is given in advance and is the same for every actor (a version of the modeler’s rabbit-hat problem). This paper emphasizes the unsettled nature of any knowledge frontier—whether scientific, economic or technological—characterized by disagreement. Frontiers are constituted by heterogeneous, competing lines of attack. Progress at the frontier is driven by “human frontier models”: forward-looking, actor-specific causal theories that generate these lines of attack and that cannot be retrieved from an existing corpus or adjudicated in advance by experts, consensus, data, or AI. This heterogeneity—in the form of competing theories and lines of attack—raises fundamental questions about claims of autonomous AI knowledge production, including questions of provenance or priority, and how we conceptualize the frontier itself.

title: Spillovers in Space: Does Geography Matter?
affiliations: Central European University (CEU), Pennsylvania State University, College of the Liberal Arts - Department of Economic, University of Warwick - Department of Economics and London School of Economics - Centre for Economic Performance (CEP)

detail.title: Spillovers in Space: Does Geography Matter?
detail.abstract: We simultaneously assess the contributions to productivity of three sources of research and development spillovers: geographic, technology and product-market proximity. To do this, we construct a new measure of geographic proximity that is based on the distribution of a firm's inventor locations rather than its headquarters, and we report both parametric and semiparametric estimates of our geographic- distance functions. We find that: i) Geographic space matters even after conditioning on horizontal and technological spillovers; ii) Technological proximity matters; iii) Product-market proximity is less important; iv) Locations of researchers are more important than headquarters but both have explanatory power; and v) Geographic markets are very local.

title: Sales Taxes and Internet Commerce
affiliations: Stanford University - Department of Economics, Uber Technologies Inc., Stanford Graduate School of Business and eBay Research Labs

detail.title: Sales Taxes and Internet Commerce
detail.abstract: We estimate the sensitivity of Internet retail purchasing to sales taxes using data from the eBay marketplace. Our first approach exploits the fact that seller locations are revealed only after buyers have expressed interest in an item by clicking on its listing. We use millions of location "surprises" to estimate price elasticities with respect to the effective sales tax. We then use aggregated data to estimate cross-state substitution parameters, and substitution between offline and online purchases, relying on the variation in state and local sales taxes, and on changes in these rates over time. We find substantial sensitivity to sales taxes. Using our item-level approach, we find a price elasticity of around -2 for interested buyers. Using our aggregate approach, we find that a one percentage point increase in a state's sales tax increases online purchases by state residents by just under two percent, but decreases their online purchases from home-state retailers by 3-4 percent.

title: Asset Pricing with Endogenously Uninsurable Tail Risk
affiliations: University of Wisconsin-Madison and University of Minnesota - Minneapolis - Department of Economics

detail.title: Asset Pricing with Endogenously Uninsurable Tail Risk
detail.abstract: This paper studies asset pricing and labor market dynamics in a setting in which idiosyncratic risk in human capital is not fully insurable. Firms use long-term contracts to provide insurance to workers, but neither side can fully commit; furthermore, owing to costly and unobservable retention effort, worker-firm relationships have endogenous durations. Uninsured tail risk in labor earnings arises as a part of an optimal risk-sharing scheme. In equilibrium, exposure to the tail risk generates higher aggregate risk premia and higher return volatility. Consistent with data, firm-level labor share predicts both future returns and pass-throughs of firm-level shocks to labor compensation.

title: The Disintermediation of Financial Markets: Direct Investing in Private Equity
affiliations: INSEAD - Finance, Harvard University and Harvard Business School - Finance Unit

detail.title: The Disintermediation of Financial Markets: Direct Investing in Private Equity
detail.abstract: One of the important issues in corporate finance is the rationale for and role of financial intermediaries. In the private equity setting, institutional investors are increasingly eschewing intermediaries in favor of direct investments. To understand the trade-offs in this setting, we compile a proprietary dataset of direct investments from seven large institutional investors. We find that solo investments by institutions outperform co-investments and a wide range of benchmarks for traditional private equity partnership investments. The outperformance is driven by deals where informational problems are not too severe, such as more proximate transactions to the investor and later-stage deals, and by an ability to avoid the deleterious effects on returns often seen in periods with large inflows into the private equity market. The poor performance of co-investments, on the other hand, appears to result from fund managers' selective offering of large deals to institutions for co-investing.

title: When Selling Becomes Viral: Disruptions in Debt Markets in the COVID-19 Crisis and the Fed’s Response
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management, University of Rochester - Simon Business School and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Anderson School of Management

detail.title: When Selling Becomes Viral: Disruptions in Debt Markets in the COVID-19 Crisis and the Fed’s Response
detail.abstract: We study disruptions in debt markets during the COVID-19 crisis. The safer end of the credit spectrum experienced significant losses that are hard to fully reconcile with standard default or risk premium channels. Corporate bonds traded at a large discount to their corresponding CDS, and this basis widened most for safer bonds. Liquid bond ETFs traded at a large discount to their NAV, more so for Treasuries, municipal bonds, and investment-grade corporate than high-yield corporate. These facts suggest investors tried to sell safer, more liquid securities to raise cash. These disruptions disappeared nearly as fast as they appeared. We trace this recovery back to the unprecedented actions the Fed took to purchase corporate bonds rather than its interventions in extending credit. The March 23rd announcement to buy investment-grade debt boosted prices and lowered bond spreads (particularly at shorter maturities and the safer end of investment-grade) while having virtually no effect on high-yield debt. April 9th, in contrast, had a large effect on both investment-grade and high-yield, even for the riskier end of high yield which would only indirectly benefit from the policy. These facts highlight the importance of financial frictions early on in the crisis, but also challenge existing theories of these frictions.

detail.abstract: The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) is rejected empirically because market beta is weakly related to average returns. Using idiosyncratic news from the Dow Jones Newswire and institutional attention measures from Bloomberg search activity, I isolate states in which market-wide attention is focused on publicly available idiosyncratic news. In these states, the CAPM prices risk. Market betas explain the cross section of stock returns, and the security market line is steep and positive. In contrast, when attention is elevated but not well explained by idiosyncratic news, the beta-return relation flattens. To rationalize these findings, I develop a noisy rational expectations model in which investors choose between concentrating limited attention on noisy idiosyncratic signals or dispersing it towards broader market level learning. Because attention to idiosyncratic news crowds out private learning about systematic conditions, greater attention to idiosyncratic information increases posterior factor uncertainty. Investors require compensation for bearing this uncertainty, generating a higher equilibrium factor risk premium and a steeper security market line.

detail.abstract: We show that US monetary policy affects the cost of trading equities worldwide. Using tick data from 37 markets over 2010-2022, we estimate liquidity responses to highfrequency policy surprises decomposed into federal funds rate, forward guidance, and asset purchase shocks. Only funds-rate shocks matter: spreads widen for up to two months, while equally sized surprises to longer-maturity yields reprice equities but leave liquidity unchanged. Effects are strongest where local policy rates closely track the federal funds rate and where foreign ownership is high. Trading costs are thus a distinct channel through which US policy shapes global financial conditions.

detail.abstract: Can the enhanced mobility created by transportation infrastructure investments help people to avoid environmental extremes? We use transaction records from China’s card payment system to measure experienced pollution exposure (EPE)—that is, exposure based on the pollution levels at travelers’ actual locations—and evaluate how EPE was affected by the country’s high-speed railway network, even while holding pollution itself constant. Our estimates imply a reduction in EPE that corresponds to a mortality benefit of 21.3 million life-years saved, primarily due to travelers changing their destinations towards locations with predictably cleaner air.

detail.title: Human Capitalists
detail.abstract: The widespread and growing use of equity-based compensation has transformed high-skilled labor from a pure labor input to a class of “human capitalists.” High-skilled labor earns substantial income in the form of equity claims to firms’ future dividends and capital gains. Equity-based compensation has increased substantially since the 1980s, representing thirty-six percent of total compensation to high-skilled labor in US manufacturing in recent years. Ignoring equity income causes incorrect measurement of the returns to high-skilled labor, with substantial effects on macroeconomic trends. In manufacturing, the inclusion of equity-based compensation almost eliminates the decline in the high-skilled labor share, and reduces the total decline in the labor share by about one-third. Only by including equity pay does our structural estimation support complementarity between high-skilled labor and physical capital greater than that of Cobb and Douglas (1928). We also provide additional regression evidence of such complementarity.

title: Multivariate uncertainty and distributional transmission
