detail.abstract: Buyers increasingly delegate supplier discovery and evaluation to autonomous AI agents that retrieve, interpret, and recommend on their behalf. Marketing theory has not yet specified the firm-level capability that determines outcomes under this arrangement, and the vocabulary that has emerged to fill the vacuum is unstable: a single recent article defines the relevant capability three incompatible ways, and the label it uses was already claimed for an unrelated construct in research on language model simulation. This article proposes Agentic Discoverability, defined as a firm's capability to be retrieved, accurately reconstructed, and credibly evaluated by AI systems acting on a buyer's behalf. Following Jaakkola's (2020) theory adaptation template, the article adapts network gatekeeping theory to a gatekeeper class that selects through retrieval and generation, specifying the gated party's information production ability for that case. The construct's dimensional structure is derived from the three independent points at which the pathway from a published claim to an agent recommendation can fail, each grounded in an established theory: scent clarity in information foraging theory, structural parsability in research on machine-directed disclosure, and signal verifiability in signalling theory. The article argues that signalling theory does not transfer intact to an algorithmic receiver, proposing that machine-resolvable verifiability substitutes for perceived signal cost as the separating mechanism. Six propositions and a measurement development path are advanced.

detail.title: Multi-Purchase Assortment Optimization with Heterogeneous Baskets: Overcoming the Curse of Dimensionality

declarations.declarationOfInterest: NA

detail.abstract: We study multi-purchase assortment optimization with heterogeneous basket capacities and general utilityshock distributions. In the multi-purchase random utility model (MP-RUM), a customer with random capacity B selects up to B offered products with the highest realized utilities, provided they are preferred to an outside option. Assortment optimization under MP-RUM is computationally challenging because computing purchase probabilities requires joint ranking of offered products, while capacity heterogeneity introduces a curse of dimensionality. We develop a two-step approximation framework to address these challenges. First, we replace the random rank threshold with a deterministic counterpart for each capacity level and assortment, defining a surrogate choice model and its associated surrogate assortment problem (SP). Under regularity conditions on utilities and shock tails, optimizing SP incurs an additive O(1) revenue loss under MP-RUM, independent of catalog size and the basket-capacity distribution. Without these conditions, we establish a distribution-free bound of square-root order in mean capacity and show that this order is tight. Second, to address the curse of dimensionality, we compress the capacity distribution into a small set of representative values and bound the loss in surrogate revenue by the mean absolute compression error. This reduction yields a polynomial-time approximation scheme for SP under mild conditions on capacity variability and inner-problem tractability. We also identify conditions under which replacing the distribution by its mean incurs a controlled loss in surrogate revenue. Our numerical experiments show near-optimal revenues across utility-shock distributions. Moreover, linear relaxation and basket-capacity compression preserve this accuracy while reducing solution times, enabling large-scale optimization.

detail.abstract: This monograph examines the structural and psychological drivers underpinning contemporary Turkish foreign policy toward Greece, challenging conventional neorealist frameworks that treat bilateral friction merely as tactical competition over maritime boundaries and energy assets. Grounded in the theoretical framework of State Ontological Security and Geopolitics, this study demonstrates that the Republic of Türkiye perceives Greece not simply as a regional adversary, but as a foundational, existential counterweight. The analysis investigates four interconnected structural drivers: (1) The Anatolian territorial substrate, whereby the modern Turkish state resides upon territories steeped in millennia of continuous Hellenic civilization; (2) The archaeogenetic and demographic paradox, highlighting that the modern Anatolian gene pool is overwhelmingly derived from indigenous Aegean and Byzantine populations assimilated via linguistic and religious conversion rather than Central Asian population displacement; (3) The historical trauma of the 1821 Greek War of Independence as the catalyst that fractured Ottoman imperial cohesion and institutionalized the enduring "Sèvres Complex"; and (4) The strategic insular geography of the Aegean Sea, where the Greek island chain legally constrains Turkish regional expansionism under the United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS 1982), rendering doctrines such as the "Blue Homeland" (Mavi Vatan) structurally revisionist. The paper concludes that lasting regional stability cannot be achieved through diplomatic appeasement of ontological anxieties, but through robust multidimensional deterrence and unyielding adherence to international legal norms.

detail.abstract: Respecting another person's difference does not require tolerating every factual error they hold. Once a belief has been separated from mere preference and classified as objectively wrong, a further practical question remains for anyone who must share space with the person who holds it: correct the error, or let it stand? This practitioner note develops a three-tier harm-radius rule for that decision in a previously unaddressed setting: a single practitioner, face to face, with no research time and no triage queue, such as an owner-operator in a small workplace. The rule directs the practitioner to act when the error's potential harm is immediate or direct, to weigh intervention when the harm is potential or social, and to refrain when the error is local and harmless. A six-item checklist operationalizes each tier, drawing on the harm principle, error-management research, face-work and politeness theory, psychological safety, correction-efficacy findings, and epistemic paternalism. The note makes two contributions: it treats the decision to correct as analytically separable from the prior question of whether a belief is wrong at all, a distinction the wrong/different test itself does not draw, and it translates existing harm-weighting logic to this practitioner niche, a setting existing frameworks were not built to address. That second, larger move translates harm-weighting logic already present in institutional, media-scale fact-checking frameworks; it is not a new taxonomy of harm. The rule and checklist are illustrated with clearly labeled constructed scenarios; no empirical validation is claimed or reported.

detail.abstract: Manufacturing equipment does not require one universal maintenance policy. Corrective, scheduled preventive, condition-based and predictive approaches differ in their cost, information needs, intervention burden and ability to control consequential failure. Choosing among them is a multiple-criteria decision problem, yet a simple weighted ranking can suggest an unsafe or infeasible option and can hide sensitivity to disputed weights. This conceptual paper develops a staged framework for selecting maintenance strategies for defined asset groups within a manufacturing system. A focused, non-exhaustive synthesis of maintenance policy and decision-analysis research informs a procedure that first defines functions and failure modes, then screens out alternatives that breach safety, technical or resource constraints. Eligible policies are evaluated on distinct criteria for safety and environmental exposure, availability, lifecycle cost, quality, implementation readiness and operational flexibility. A transparent weighting and outranking or distance-based comparison can support deliberation, while sensitivity and scenario analysis test whether the preferred policy survives plausible changes in assumptions. A second portfolio stage checks interactions among assets, outage windows, labour and spare-parts budgets. Three tables and two original diagrams translate the framework into a reviewable decision process. No plant data, numerical ranking or empirical improvement is claimed. The paper contributes a decision architecture that separates eligibility, preference and portfolio feasibility and specifies how future manufacturing case studies should test its usefulness against current policy selection practice.

detail.abstract: Existing finite support theory for online linear programming gives regret bounds independent of the number of requests but typically polynomial in the reward support size. On the other hand, continuous support theory establishes that the regret is logarithmic in the number of requests. Given the quite different regret behaviors in these two settings, it is natural to study the intermediate regime, where both the number of requests n and the reward-support size S are large but finite. This regime is also important at a practical level, as it describes settings in which the number of customer types and number of requests are both large. We consider the single resource problem with independent and identically distributed requests from a known distribution. Under appropriate regularity conditions, we prove an O(log(min{n, S^2 }) + 1/π_{min}) regret bound for the Fluid Bayes Selector algorithm, where π_{min} denotes the smallest point mass in the marginal distribution of resource consumption. This bound requires no nondegeneracy assumption on the finite support fluid LP. Under additional conditions, every feasible policy incurs Ω(log(min{n, S^2 })) regret. We construct two sequences of instances to show that the 1/π_{min} term is necessary in the worst case but not for every instance. For the multisecretary problem, exact asymptotics under additional smoothness and polynomial support growth establish \sqrt{n} as the exact support size scale at which continuous support theory correctly predicts the leading order term of regret of the large support regime. These results quantify the transition between finite and continuous support regret behavior, and clarify the impact of support size on regret.

detail.abstract: The pervasive failure of digital transformation initiatives with industry and scholarly benchmarks reporting collapse rates between 70% and 80% stems fundamentally from a structural paradigm misattribution rather than isolated technological or execution inadequacies. Traditional management doctrines, rooted in classical Newtonian-Cartesian paradigms, persist in conceptualizing business enterprises as predictable, linear, mechanical systems. Consequently, contemporary artificial intelligence interventions are routinely misapplied as mechanistic automation instruments overlaid upon antiquated commandand-control hierarchies. To resolve this persistent productivity paradox, this study develops a pioneering, non-reductive theoretical paradigm termed Augmented Business Administration (ABA). Positioned at the intersection of Complex Adaptive Systems theory, Dynamic Capabilities View, and Distributed Cognition, ABA redefines the enterprise as a living, autopoietic, complex adaptive organism and elevates the managerial archetype from an operational controller to a systemic decision architect. Methodologically grounded in conceptual synthesis and abductive theory-building, the framework establishes a rigorous Three-Layer Architecture: the Worldview Layer (ontological grounding in organizational cybernetics and autopoiesis), the Execution System Layer (driven by the triadic pillars of Smart Seeing, Tech-Enabled Transformation, and Agile Human Execution), and the Application Layer (operationalized through a recursive Eight-Stage Execution Cycle and the Augmented Business Administration Maturity Model). The systemic capability function is formalized through non-linear mathematical relations, and four foundational, testable theoretical propositions (𝑃 1 through 𝑃 4) are formulated to delineate the conditions of dynamic equilibrium, cognitive load mitigation, and non-reductive synergy. By overcoming the institutional silos separating human agency from algorithmic capability, the ABA framework resolves the mechanistic crisis of legacy governance. This work shifts the paradigm of enterprise administration from brittle computational control toward resilient socio-technical orchestration, providing a structured conceptual foundation and an empirical agenda for scholars and strategic leaders navigating the frontiers of human-machine coexistence.

title: Transformative agency in peer group mentoring: Enacted and envisioned change
affiliations: University of Oslo

detail.title: Transformative agency in peer group mentoring: Enacted and envisioned change
detail.abstract: This article investigates thesis supervisors’ reported practice changes after engaging in peer group mentoring (PGM). PGM denotes structured group conversations in which peers discuss practice-related problems. Organized as a semester-long course, PGM was implemented by faculty leadership at the University of Oslo as a professional development measure to bring supervisors together to share experiences and solve problems. By thematically analyzing three group-interviews among 11 supervisors following their participation in PGM, the study reveals how they connect specific enacted or envisioned changes in practice to different aspects of the PGM experience. The changes consisted of accounts of implementing new practices or planning for future changes, understood through the lens of transformative agency, which concerns intentional and profound change through breaking with existing practices (Virkkunen, 2006; Lund & Vestøl, 2020). Transformative agency is operationalized by identifying the problem situations and the artifacts employed when taking action for change, following the principle known as double stimulation. Findings show how change was inspired by both immediate discussions, cumulative reflection over time, and the mediating structure of the PGM model itself. This study's contributions include the development of three analytical categories of practice change—pragmatic, dialogic, and conceptual—constructed from participants' accounts. Methodologically, it operationalizes double stimulation to connect reported changes back to PGM, and conceptually, it expands understandings of how transformative agency may manifest in collegial conversations for faculty development.

detail.abstract: Power systems are being reshaped by distributed renewable generation, electrified transport, pervasive sensing, and growing exposure to extreme weather and cyber threats. These pressures have made machine learning (ML) an attractive tool for forecasting, control, and security in smart grids. The literature, however, is fragmented. Studies of load and renewable forecasting, reinforcement learning for dispatch and demand response, and ML-based intrusion detection are usually developed and evaluated independently, and resilience is often treated as a by-product of routine optimization rather than as a design objective. This paper presents a narrative review of peer-reviewed work across four themes: probabilistic forecasting, learning-based optimization and control, cyber-physical security, and resilience analytics. It then identifies four gaps: the lack of resilience-aware learning objectives, weak robustness under distribution shift and adversarial conditions, limited interpretability and operator trust, and the absence of integrated evaluation across normal and stressed conditions. To address these gaps, the paper proposes a conceptual, layered framework that links data assurance, probabilistic forecasting, constrained decision-making, security monitoring, and human oversight through a shared uncertainty representation. The framework is presented as a research agenda and has not been experimentally validated. The paper closes with practical implications for utilities and a set of future research directions, including synthetic scenario generation, federated learning, and benchmark development.

detail.abstract: This monograph examines a fundamental eschatological question: what becomes of human culture when God makes all things new? Christian teaching sometimes oscillates between two inadequate pictures. In one, salvation culminates in the abandonment of ordinary creaturely existence, as though art, knowledge, work, architecture, sociality, memory, nations, and civilization were temporary scaffolding destined simply to disappear. In the other, the biblical promise of new creation is assimilated to a theology of uninterrupted cultural progress, as though humanity could gradually construct the kingdom through education, technology, political development, or civilizational achievement. This study argues for a more discriminating account. The biblical horizon is neither the negation of creation nor the canonization of history. It is resurrection, judgment, purification, liberation, and consummation. Romans 8 depicts creation itself as awaiting liberation rather than disposal; Isaiah 60 portrays the wealth and glory of the nations entering Zion while violence, oppression, and defilement are excluded; Revelation 21-22 presents the holy city descending to a renewed creation, with the glory and honor of the nations brought into it, even as nothing unclean enters. Resurrection theology likewise insists on continuity of identity through radical transformation: what is raised is genuinely the creature God made, yet glorified beyond corruption. These patterns support a theology of cultural continuity-with-judgment. Human cultural goods can possess real creaturely value, but no historical achievement carries an automatic title to eschatological permanence. What is truthful, beautiful, just, loving, creaturely, and rightly ordered may be understood as capable of fulfillment in God's new world; what depends upon idolatry, domination, exploitation, deception, violence, or death belongs to the order that is judged. The final hope is therefore not cultural extinction, nor civilizational self-redemption, but the transfiguration of creaturely life under the unmediated reign of God and the Lamb.

detail.abstract:
This practitioner portfolio case study examines how enterprise operating systems were diagnosed, redesigned, and implemented across a multi-sector body of executive operating work conducted from 2024 through 2026. The cases span businesses, professional practices, institutions, community organizations, construction-related enterprises, health and behavioral health services, education environments, and organizations preparing for growth. Although presenting problems varied, the underlying operating conditions repeatedly involved executive dependency, undefined roles and processes, insufficient organizational capacity, disconnected financial and operating decisions, premature automation, fragmented accountability, and growth ambitions unsupported by the infrastructure required to execute them.

Using a practitioner-based portfolio case study method, the analysis examines interventions involving organizational restructuring, work and role architecture, process standardization, institutional procurement, financial operations, workforce design, technology and automation, project capacity, market architecture, and organizational scaling. Across engagements, operating interventions were evaluated not simply by whether processes changed, but by whether organizations developed greater capacity to acquire, accept, deliver, retain, and scale revenue-producing work.

The results demonstrate substantial enterprise-level economic and organizational effects. Documented engagements produced revenue growth from $0 to $1.3 million, $0 to $2 million, and $0 to $3.3 million over two-year periods. In established enterprises, revenue increased from $13 million to $39 million and from $17 million to $32 million, representing increases of approximately 200% and 88.2%, respectively. A separate human-capital intervention generated $118 million over two years while staff satisfaction increased from 30% to 88%. Additional results included six private B2B contracts valued at $2 million, an 8-of-10 proposal-to-award conversion rate, project-volume expansion from 8 to 24, organizational capacity growth from 1 to 8, $12,000 in operating-expense reductions, $2.3 million in additional contract revenue, and an increase in average contract value from $0 to $2.8 million. Because some financial outcomes may overlap within individual engagements, results are attributed to their respective operating interventions rather than aggregated into a single portfolio revenue claim.

The case finds that enterprise growth was strongest when operating capacity preceded or accompanied expansion. Across different organizational contexts, economic performance improved when people, processes, money, information, technology, authority, accountability, and capacity were designed as an integrated operating system rather than managed as isolated functions. The portfolio therefore positions operating infrastructure not as administrative support for enterprise growth, but as a productive enterprise capability through which organizations create, absorb, and sustain economic value.

detail.abstract: Public transportation plays a crucial role in ensuring sustainable urban mobility and directly affects commuters' quality of life. While service quality, satisfaction, and operational performance have been widely studied, limited research has integrated commuter attitudes and well-being into public transport evaluation particularly in the context of highdensity, multimodal systems in developing countries. This study addresses this gap by examining the interrelationships among service quality factors, commuter satisfaction, travel attitudes, and well-being in Kolkata's public transport network. A mixed-methods approach was adopted, combining an expert survey with a questionnaire-based study of 400 commuters across five key multimodal hubs. Factors such as safety and security, comfort, service quality, and reliability emerged as critical determinants of commuter perceptions. Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modelling (PLS-SEM) revealed that attitudinal perceptions significantly mediate the relationship between service quality and commuter well-being. Overcrowding and safety concerns were identified as major drivers of negative travel experiences, while improvements in safety and comfort were found to enhance both satisfaction and well-being. The findings provide actionable insights for policymakers seeking to design passenger-centric and sustainable public transport systems in congested urban environments.

title: Prepare or Respond? Timing the Activation of Backup Capacity under Diffusing Supply Disruptions

detail.title: Prepare or Respond? Timing the Activation of Backup Capacity under Diffusing Supply Disruptions

detail.abstract: Large-scale disruptions such as natural disasters and geopolitical restrictions can spread across regions and affect suppliers at different times. Firms often hedge against such disruptions by diversifying their supply base, including reserving capacity from backup suppliers. However, if the disruption can also affect the backup supplier, the reserved backup capacity may no longer be available when the firm needs it. Therefore, the value of backup capacity depends not only on how much capacity the firm reserves, but also on when the firm activates it as the disruption unfolds. In this study, we develop a two-stage model in which a firm first chooses safety stock and backup capacity as static preparedness before a disruption occurs and then decides when to activate backup capacity afterwards. This setting allows us to distinguish static preparedness from responsiveness, which we capture through activation timing. We compare three classes of policies: A reactive policy, an efficiency-focused proactive policy, and resilience-oriented proactive policies. The reactive policy activates only after the primary supplier is disrupted, whereas the efficiency-focused proactive policy activates earlier to maximize profitability. The resilience-oriented proactive policies activate earlier to maximize Time-to-Survival or minimize Time-to-Recovery. We show that responsiveness can substitute for static preparedness. Relative to a reactive firm, a proactive firm can activate backup capacity before supply is lost and therefore depends less on safety stock and backup capacity. We further show that the two resilience objectives value preparedness resources differently, with Time-to-Recovery placing greater emphasis on backup capacity than Time-to-Survival. Moreover, the resilience-oriented policies achieve these improvements with only a modest reduction in profitability. Therefore, our study reveals that when firms can use information about disruption diffusion, timely activation of backup capacity can reduce the need for costly static preparedness. Managers should also align their preparedness mix with their resilience objective. Backup capacity is more important when the firm's priority is faster recovery, whereas safety stock and backup capacity can substitute more directly when the priority is sustaining operations before stockout.

detail.abstract: In this editorial, I explain the choices that Retorik has made regarding citation style and the use of generative AI in articles, including its decision not to adopt threshold-based AI-detection cutoffs. I also elaborate on the mandatory inclusion of author statements, starting with volume 14, issue 1. I present the choices that pertain to the form of the journal—such as the preference for Chicago’s notes-and-bibliography citation style—as deliberate attempts to embody something of the journal’s substance, that is, its critical orientation. Although Retorik cannot afford to ignore the requirements of Indonesia’s academic-governance apparatuses, this does not entail passive acquiescence to trends that represent the very objects of cultural criticism. If, as Theodor Adorno wrote, “[w]rong life cannot be lived rightly,” it is nonetheless possible to strive to “live less wrongly.”

detail.abstract: Drawing on the evolution of China's commercial space policies, regional industrial development, corporate ecosystems, investment and financing structures, and satellite manufacturing capabilities, Blurred Orbits: Inside China's Commercial Space Expansion advances a central proposition with a pronounced strategic focus: commercial space is becoming a nexus of industrial capacity, technological autonomy, military modernization, and competition over global information infrastructure, rather than a market sector separate from state power. This review argues that the report's most valuable scholarly contribution lies in shifting the unit of analysis from assets in orbit to the organizational and industrial systems that produce them, rather than in its account of any individual company or constellation. It consequently treats factories, industrial clusters, capital allocation, and production cadence as leading indicators of space power. At the same time, the report's principal inferences involve evidentiary levels that require careful differentiation. Design capacity is not equivalent to actual output; actual output is not equivalent to reliable operations; and infrastructure scale does not necessarily translate into market dominance, military effectiveness, or international political influence. The report's observation that the commercial-state and civilian-military boundaries are blurred has explanatory value, but its conceptual operationalization, causal identification, symmetry in crossnational comparisons, and the verifiability of some sources could be strengthened. Drawing on strategic management, organizational learning, and industrial policy, this review further proposes that China's commercial space sector be understood as a multilevel system combining strategic alignment, local competition, organizational exploration, learning through scale, and selection and exit, rather than reduced to a single model of state mobilization. Future research should develop longitudinal datasets capable of supporting falsifiable claims about capacity utilization, quality and reliability, launch constraints, unit economics, firm heterogeneity, international adoption, and policy shocks.

detail.abstract: This paper proposes enoculation as a distinct term and theory for the application of inoculation principles to cyber security. The term appeared as E-noculation in its first public use; the closed spelling is used here, and both forms refer to the same theory. Inoculation theory, formulated by McGuire in 1964 and extended by Pfau, Compton, Ivanov and colleagues, is among the most reliable approaches to building resistance to persuasion. Its migration into cyber security is intuitive, since social engineering is influence aimed at producing a harmful action. The migration is not clean, however. The cyber attacker conceals persuasive intent, targets behavior rather than belief, adapts continuously, and exploits the single unprotected person or system rather than the average one. Each difference changes what an effective intervention must do. Retaining the word "inoculation" collapses these differences back into the parent literature, and in practice the word does exactly that: the cyber usage keeps reverting to the health and persuasion meaning. Enoculation Theory centers on a cyber-specific practice: the deliberate, controlled exposure of an organization's sociotechnical system, its people, practices and technologies together, to attenuated, realistic forms of attack, paired with preemptive refutation and verification routines, to build durable, organization-wide resistance to social engineering and technical compromise. The paper traces the theory from its first presentation by Treglia and Delia at the 2017 New York State Cyber Security Conference, sets out its components, and offers testable propositions for empirical work.

detail.abstract: Purpose-To investigate the extent to which type of media used affects the efficiency of health-focused PSAs by applying social marketing principles and evaluating exposure, attention and accessibility as three main factors influencing consumer engagement. Research Design/Methodology-An explorative study was completed using a mixed methodology that included both quantitative and qualitative methods. Quantitative data were collected from a cross-section of 278 adults through the use of a survey questionnaire supplemented by qualitative data collected through semi-structured interviews with 20 participants. Statistical data analysis for the quantitative data included ANOVA and multiple regression, and thematic analysis for the qualitative data to achieve a greater understanding of the pattern of consumer engagement. Findings-The analysis indicated that digital media performed better, particularly with respect to consumer attention. It was also found that consumer socio-demographics had a significant impact on both exposure and attention, with gender showing the strongest relationship with attention. Qualitative data provided insight into how consumer engagement was affected by their media habits, perceived credibility and presentation of the ads and how accessibility was a factor across all media channels. Practical Implications-These results suggest that an integrated media strategy that combines both digital and traditional channels will be effective as well as create segmentation strategies to target audiences based on their media use and access. Originality/Value-This study developed an integrated framework that included all three components of engagement, thereby providing empirical support for improving the selection of media channels to use within health communication campaigns.

detail.abstract: Large language models are increasingly used to construct consumer digital twins, yet evidence that synthetic consumers reproduce aggregate market behavior does not establish that they accurately represent the individuals they are intended to simulate. We distinguish market-level validity from individual targeting validity and evaluate both using the Twin-2K-500 dataset. The analysis covers 2,058 consumers, 40 products, 11 price levels, and 82,320 participant-product observations. Personaconditioned LLM simulations reproduced substantial market structure, with the strongest GPT-4.1 configuration correlating with human stated demand at r = .924 across 440 product-price conditions and supporting similar assortment decisions. However, the same configuration achieved a conditional targeting AUC of only .516 when consumers were compared within identical product-price offers. A nine-configuration LLM ensemble improved targeting to .554, but remained below conventional supervised models. Under simultaneous participant and product holdout, demographic and structured models achieved conditional AUCs of .596 and .617, respectively, despite receiving no labeled observations for the target products. Learning-curve analyses further showed that approximately 100 labeled consumers were sufficient to match the LLM ensemble on average, while 200 exceeded it in every repeated training sample. Secondary behavioral outcomes produced similar evidence of weak person-specific correspondence. These findings show that synthetic consumers can reconstruct markets without functioning as equally valid digital twins of individual consumers. We propose decision-specific validation in which person-level performance is evaluated conditional on the marketing stimulus, compared with no-persona controls, and benchmarked against conventional predictive models.

detail.abstract: A simple question drives this paper: why does the same debt-to-GDP ratio imply very different sovereign risk across countries and over time? I build a country-year panel of 195 economies for 1980-2024 that merges the Bank of Canada-Bank of England Sovereign Default Database with IMF and World Bank macro-fiscal series, and I evaluate early-warning models strictly out of sample under a horizon-purged time split: covariates are lagged one year, models are fitted through 2009, isotonic-recalibrated on a window that ends before the test labels begin, and tested on the 2017-2024 default wave. Defaults are measured as materiality crossings with hysteresis rather than any positive stock. The debt ratio alone is a weak predictor: AUROC 0.71 one year ahead, pseudo-R2 0.02 in sample. Adding fiscal, macro, liquidity and currency-structure variables lifts out-of-sample AUROC to 0.84 one year ahead and 0.79-0.80 five years ahead; the paired bootstrap improvement over the fiscal-macro specification is positive in 96-98 percent of 1,000 full-pipeline resamples, and Brier scores beat both ex-ante and oracle climatologies at every horizon. The headline conditional story does not survive: neither the debt x (r-g) interaction nor an out-of-sample subgroup split detects the snowball channel in this design. I then embed the estimated stress model - re-estimated excluding France - in a stochastic debt-dynamics engine built on the security-level ledger of Agence France Tresor and simulate 2,000 paths per scenario to 2050. France's 2026 configuration maps to a stress index of 0.24, the 87th percentile of the leave-one-country-out prediction distribution, above the out-of-sample alert rule (sensitivity 0.92, specificity 0.45) and inside the score band of the actual pre-default observations of 2018-2022 - while scoring essentially the same as Japan 2016, which never defaulted. The calibrated index saturates there and cannot separate those two histories. Median simulated debt reaches 123 percent of GDP by 2030 (IMF official: 121.8) and 142-310 percent by 2050 depending on the scenario. The exercise is a stress-equivalence benchmark, not a literal default probability; the paper's point is that debt becomes dangerous through the whole configuration around it - financing costs, liquidity, currency architecture and data coverage - not through its level.

detail.abstract: This review examines how classified (staggered) boards affect non-financial corporate outcomes and how these outcomes inform the long-standing debate over the value of takeover defenses. We develop a framework based on four competing perspectives: the entrenchment view, the bonding hypothesis, the myopic-markets hypothesis, and the optimal-governance view. These perspectives generate distinct predictions for outcomes that are often obscured by aggregate financial measures such as Tobin's Q and stock returns. We review evidence on innovation, environmental performance, labor investment, corporate social responsibility, corporate culture, inclusion-related policies, and voting premiums, which we treat as direct evidence on managerial entrenchment rather than as a conventional non-financial outcome. The evidence suggests that staggered boards can promote innovation and labor-related outcomes by supporting long-term investment and stakeholder commitment, while also imposing costs in areas such as corporate culture, social capital and corporate social responsibility, inclusion, and private-benefit extraction. Environmental findings remain mixed. Our primary contribution is a mechanism-based synthesis that clarifies when, why, and for which stakeholders staggered boards are likely to create benefits or costs.

detail.abstract: Economics was born for human beings, yet in measurement and policy it pushed them aside as a means of production. GDP measured production; it never measured human lives. This paper defines the essence of distribution economics as human-centered economics and proposes the Human-Centered Index (HCX, 人本指數), which measures human lives in place of GDP. The HCX consists of eight indicators across five dimensions: survival, emotion, relationships, safety and time autonomy. Every indicator is a question a person can put to their own life. The HCX is not an index of theory but an indicator for living. Calculated from 2022 and 2023 data, the HCX places Norway (75.7), Finland (75.3) and Denmark (75.1) at the top. Korea scores 52.6 and ranks 32nd. GDP rankings and HCX rankings diverge sharply. The United States falls from 6th in GDP per capita to 29th on the HCX, and Korea from 19th to 32nd. Estonia rises from 27th to 11th, and Finland from 15th to 2nd. The ranking of production is not the ranking of life. Among the 17 countries whose actual individual consumption (AIC) per capita exceeds USD 40,000 (PPP), the correlation between consumption and the HCX is-0.02. This is the saturation point, beyond which the economy can no longer buy more life. Past that point, what separates human lives is relationships and time autonomy. Working hours remain negatively associated with the scores of the other dimensions (-0.47) even after controlling for consumption. The Life Realization Rate (LRR), which measures how far economic capacity is realized as life on the HCX, is 91.6% for Korea and 79.6% for the United States. Korea falls 8% and the United States 20% short of the life that countries with the same economic capacity enjoy on average. The standard for judging human lives should be the HCX, not GDP.

detail.abstract: This article proposes a theoretical model of long-term social self-renewal. It is based on the hypothesis that the adaptability of a society depends not only on the quality of its institutions but also on its capacity to prevent, periodically, the closure of its mechanisms of social selection (cf. Acemoglu and Robinson, 2012; Olson, 1982). The central proposition of the model is formulated as follows: Any social system requires a mechanism capable of periodically breaking or bypassing the closed loops through which its elite reproduces itself (Alexander Jochim, Stefan Bornholdt, 2025). Historically, this function has repeatedly been performed by war, external threat, revolution and systemic crisis (Marwick, 1974; Scheidel, 2017). Under threats to their survival, societies have temporarily altered their selection criteria, weakened earlier status constraints and granted greater access to resources to people able to solve the problems at hand (Chulhee Lee, 2012). The crisis mechanism, however, carries a high social cost and cannot be regarded as a desirable path of social development.

detail.abstract: A trader cannot buy vega from their own closed trades, but they can try to manufacture it: forecast variance from past reference moves and read an exposure off a regression. This paper shows what is real in that construction, what lies, and what a martingale theorem says about both. On 53,989 identical random entries per machinery across six currency pairs and nineteen and a half years, the variance-news loading c2 orders exit machineries exactly as their geometry dictates: stop-only +17.29 pips per standard deviation at t = 22.3, trail +1.65 at 5.8, symmetric barriers and the naked control at zero, the control exact at b = 1.015. The loading on expected variance, c1, is significant with opposite signs for stop and trail, and both signs reproduce on GARCH(1,1) and t(6) conditional martingales: c1 is a bad-control artefact of holding the realised endpoint fixed, never a market fact. The theorem-clean projection of outcomes on expected variance alone is null for every machinery except a trail residual of-1.01 pips per sd at 2.8 standard errors against the fattest null, one of twelve contrasts examined and reported as suggestive. Exit machinery manufactures variance-news posture; it collects no premium and forecasts nothing.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how structural business-environment constraints and the pace of digital adaptation relate to firm performance among registered, non-agricultural private establishments in Bangladesh. Using the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2022 for Bangladesh-a nationally representative survey of 998 establishments-the paper draws on the survey's published country-profile indicators and its documented sampling and questionnaire design (rather than the restricted-access firm-level microdata file, which was not available for this study) to build a descriptive, comparative picture of the constraints Bangladeshi firms report relative to the South Asia and Lower-Middle-Income country groups. The analysis focuses on four linked domains: infrastructure reliability (principally electricity), access to finance, governance and informality, and the absorptive-capacity indicators-formal training, research and development spending, and firm size-that the literature treats as preconditions for digital and technological adaptation. Consistent with a broader literature on investment climate and firm performance in developing economies, the results show that electricity, access to finance, and corruption are the three most frequently cited constraints on Bangladeshi firms, that these constraints bind unevenly across firm-size classes, and that indicators of absorptive capacity remain low relative to the scale of the constraints firms report. The paper argues that these patterns are consistent with-though cannot, on this evidence alone, causally establish-the hypothesis that structural constraints slow digital adaptation and, through it, firm performance. The paper closes by specifying precisely what firm-level microdata and econometric strategy would be required to move from this descriptive account to causal estimates, and by drawing out policy implications for infrastructure, finance, and digital-readiness programs targeted at Bangladeshi enterprises.

detail.abstract: Spectral risk measures, including conditional value-at-risk (CVaR), generate a family of convex criteria for portfolio estimation. We study how the criterion should be chosen when different criteria share the same population minimizer, and whether the efficient criterion can itself be learned from data. We develop a general asymptotic theory for empirical spectral-risk minimization under estimated linear constraints. Under normal scale-mixture elliptical returns, all spectral risk measures identify the same population efficient portfolio, but their empirical minimizers have different sampling distributions. Their asymptotic covariance decomposes into a common component and a positive-semidefinite component scaled by a functional of the spectral measure, reducing efficiency to an optimization over probability measures. We characterize the efficiency-optimal spectral measure and show that single-level CVaR is generally inefficient. We then construct a fully data-adaptive estimator that learns the radial distribution and optimal spectral measure from the same observations used for portfolio estimation, yet has the same first-order distribution as the infeasible oracle. Simulations and an empirical application illustrate the method.

title: Structural Constraints, Digital Adaptation, and Firm Performance: Descriptive Microeconomic Evidence from Bangladesh's Enterprise Sector
affiliations: National University of Bangladesh

detail.title: Structural Constraints, Digital Adaptation, and Firm Performance: Descriptive Microeconomic Evidence from Bangladesh's Enterprise Sector

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The author declares that there are no financial or personal relationships that could have influenced, or could reasonably be perceived to have influenced, this research.
declarations.ethicsApproval: This study uses publicly available secondary data from the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2022 for Bangladesh. No primary data were collected from human participants, and no identifiable participant-level information was accessed. Therefore, ethics approval was not required for this study.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no specific funding from any public, commercial, or not-for-profit funding agency. The research was conducted independently by the author.

detail.abstract: This paper examines how structural business-environment constraints and the pace of digital adaptation relate to firm performance among registered, non-agricultural private establishments in Bangladesh. Using the World Bank Enterprise Survey (WBES) 2022 for Bangladesh-a nationally representative survey of 998 establishments-the paper draws on the survey's published country-profile indicators and its documented sampling and questionnaire design (rather than the restricted-access firm-level microdata file, which was not available for this study) to build a descriptive, comparative picture of the constraints Bangladeshi firms report relative to the South Asia and Lower-Middle-Income country groups. The analysis focuses on four linked domains: infrastructure reliability (principally electricity), access to finance, governance and informality, and the absorptive-capacity indicators-formal training, research and development spending, and firm size-that the literature treats as preconditions for digital and technological adaptation. Consistent with a broader literature on investment climate and firm performance in developing economies, the results show that electricity, access to finance, and corruption are the three most frequently cited constraints on Bangladeshi firms, that these constraints bind unevenly across firm-size classes, and that indicators of absorptive capacity remain low relative to the scale of the constraints firms report. The paper argues that these patterns are consistent with-though cannot, on this evidence alone, causally establish-the hypothesis that structural constraints slow digital adaptation and, through it, firm performance. The paper closes by specifying precisely what firm-level microdata and econometric strategy would be required to move from this descriptive account to causal estimates, and by drawing out policy implications for infrastructure, finance, and digital-readiness programs targeted at Bangladeshi enterprises.

title: Persistent Problems, Repeated Reforms: Explaining Child Welfare Reform Durability in Tennessee
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Persistent Problems, Repeated Reforms: Explaining Child Welfare Reform Durability in Tennessee
detail.abstract: Child welfare systems frequently confront recurring problems despite repeated efforts to identify deficiencies and implement reform. This study examines whether such recurrence necessarily reflects organizational forgetting or whether previously learned and institutionalized reforms can persist alongside uneven implementation capacity. Using Tennessee's child welfare system as a longitudinal case, this study combines documentary analysis of decades of federal and state oversight, litigation, and administrative reform with analyses of NCANDS and AFCARS administrative data. The documentary analysis identifies four distinct regimes spanning Reform Construction, Constrained Implementation, Institutionalization and Exit from external oversight, and Post-Oversight Durability. Administrative analyses show that these periods also correspond to differences in the temporal relationship between case information and foster care removal, and in the timing and destination of foster care exits. The findings show that recurring organizational problems can coexist with substantial evidence of organizational learning and institutional memory. These findings suggest that reform durability depends not simply on whether organizations retain lessons from prior reforms, but on their continuing capacity to operationalize retained knowledge under changing administrative conditions.

title: Beyond Euclidean Attention: Information-Geometric Deep Learning for Automated Bone Health Classification from Knee Radiographs
affiliations: Department of Robotics and Mechatronics Engineering, University of Dhaka, Department of Robotics and Mechatronics Engineering, University of Dhaka and University of Dhaka

detail.title: Beyond Euclidean Attention: Information-Geometric Deep Learning for Automated Bone Health Classification from Knee Radiographs

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.
declarations.funderStatement: No funding was received for this research.

detail.abstract: Osteoporosis is an insidious skeletal disorder defined by systemic degradation of bone micro-architecture and reduced bone mass. Traditional Dual-Energy X-ray Absorptiometry (DXA) provides static bone assessments but fails to capture microstructural changes that account for 20-40% of the variability in bone strength. To overcome this constraint, we introduce the Information-Geometric Convolutional Neural Network (IG-CNN) for automated three-class bone health staging from knee radiographs. IG-CNN introduces three theoretically motivated components: Fisher Information Attention, which replaces heuristic dot-product attention with a statistically grounded mechanism based on Fisher–Rao geodesic distances; Manifold Curvature Pooling, which uses localized Gaussian curvature estimation to emphasize geometrically informative structural boundaries; and Information Bottleneck Regularization, which promotes compact and generalizable feature representations through variational KL-based optimization. The proposed architecture is trained and evaluated on an assembled dataset comprising Normal (1002), Osteopenia (528), and Osteoporosis (1028) classes, collected from three repositories. Ground truth exhibits heterogeneous clinical rigor across sources. Unlike Kaggle repositories that rely on folder-level annotations, the Mendeley subset (n=239) is selected as a clinically anchored validation cohort because it provides T-score-derived labels and patient-level demographic and clinical metadata. Under identical training splits, IG-CNN achieves a state-of-the-art overall accuracy of 83.54% and a Cohen’s Kappa score of 0.751, comfortably outperforming popular CNN backbones like ResNet-50. Controlled ablation studies confirm synergistic interactions among the components, while attention maps provide anatomically consistent localization, enhancing diagnostic trustworthiness. We emphasize that IG-CNN is intended as a risk stratification tool from knee radiographs. ​

title: A Theory of Participation in OTC and Centralized Markets
affiliations: ESSEC Business School, Johns Hopkins University - Carey Business School and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) - Department of Economics

detail.title: A Theory of Participation in OTC and Centralized Markets
detail.abstract: Should regulators encourage the migration of trade from over-the-counter (OTC) to centralized markets? To address this question, we study a model in which banks make costly decisions to participate in an OTC market, a centralized market, or both markets at the same time. Banks differ in their ability to take large positions, what we call their trading capacity. In equilibrium, intermediate-capacity banks find it optimal to participate in the centralized market. In contrast, low- and high-capacity banks find it optimal to participate in the OTC market, due to an endogenous complementarity. Namely, low capacity banks receive worse terms of trade than in the centralized market but better risk sharing, thanks to the intermediation services offered by high-capacity banks. High-capacity banks receive worse risk sharing than in the centralized market, but profit from the provision of intermediation services to low-capacity banks. While the social optimum has qualitatively similar participation patterns, it prescribes that more customers migrate to the centralized market, and that more dealers enter the OTC market.

title: Do Multinationals or Domestic Firms Face Higher Effective Tax Rates?
affiliations: Michigan State University and University of North Carolina Kenan-Flagler Business School

detail.title: Do Multinationals or Domestic Firms Face Higher Effective Tax Rates?
detail.abstract: To our knowledge, this paper provides the most comprehensive analysis of firm-level corporate income tax expenses to date.  We use publicly available financial statement information to estimate firm-level effective tax rates (ETRs) for 10,642 corporations from 85 countries from 1988 to 2007.  We find that multinationals and domestic-only companies face similar ETRs.  We also find that, on average, ETRs declined by seven percentage points or 20% over the period.  German, Japanese, Australian and Canadian decreases were large.  American, British, and French declines were more modest.  Nonetheless, because ETRs were falling worldwide, the ordinal rank from high-tax countries to low-tax countries changed little.  Japanese firms always faced the highest ETRs.  ETRs for tax havens and countries from the Middle East and Asia (ignoring Japan) were always lower than those for the U.S. and European countries.  These findings should provide some empirical underpinning for ongoing policy debates about the taxation of multinational profits.
